Maroh 14, 1936.
Commander Walter F. Lafrenz, U.S.N., Chairman,
Sub-seotion on Asia House, International Relations Seotion,
Commonwealth Club of California,
San Francisoo, California.
Dear Sir:
It is noted that at the meeting of the Sub-seotion, February 19, Edward C.
Carter, Secretary General, Institute of Pacific Relations, and Frederick F. Field,
Seoretary, American Council of the same organization , explained the plans of the
Institute for introducing into 152 high schools of California and into the publio
sohools of other states certain courses on Pacifio Relations and Japanese Culture.
Because of the importance of the subject, there are offered herewith for
information of the Sub-seotion, in the shape of documents and references, certain
necessary details, which, it is inferred, the speakers did not cover. The plan is
undertaken jointly under mutual understanding between the I.P.R. and the Society of
International Cultural Relations of Japan, and assumes cooperation of educational
authorities in the United States. In the Japan Times and Mail, January 1, 1936,
Count Kabayama, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Society named, explains
Japan's desires in the matter, and stresses the importance of receiving favorable con-
sideration therefor in our institutions of learning which he regards as the real oen-
ters of American culture.
The general plan of collaboration is indicated in an item in the December 4,
1934, issue of the Japan Times and Mail of Tokyo ("English language voice of the
Foreign Office of Japan"), reproduced in C.J.I.C. Doc. #4o9 attached. It is covered
more fully in report of a meeting of departmental heads of the Japanese Government
held on November 21, 1934, as stated in a protest to the Hawaiian Commissioners of
Eduoation, December 11, 1934, (C.J.I.C. Doc. #414 attached).
A practical demonstration of what is intended to bo taught Amerioan students
under the plan is found in the text book on Japan which was in use, notwithstanding
repeated protests, in certain public schools of Hawaii throughout the year 1935, and
which was personally urged by its co-author for general use in public sohools of the
mainland. A general idea thereof may be had by reading the attached copy of a letter
to the Editor of the Honolulu Star Bulletin, Maroh 1l, 1936, and C.J.I.C. Doos. #438
and #443. Copy of #438 was mailed recently to more than 200 members of the American
Counoil, I.P.R..
Copy of the book itself, together with statements and exhibits explaining
fully the charges made were deposited with Vierling Kersey, Superintendent of Public
Instruction of California at Sacramento, on June 21, 1935, and January 15 and 31,
1936, and duplioates thereof are in the office of the Bay region Group, I.P.R. at San
Franoisoo.
Respectfully,
California Joint Immigration Committee,

March 11, 1936.
Mr. Riley H. Allen, Editor,
Honolulu Star Bulletin,
Honolulu, T. H.
Dear Mr. Allen:
This is in response to your letter of February 17, concerning the text
book on Japan which was in use in certain public schools of Hawaii throughout 1935,
and which has been proposed for similar use in California and other states. The book,
joint product of the Institute of Pacific Relations, the Society for International
Cultural Relations of Japan, and the Hawaiian Commissioners of Education, it is charged,
flagrantly misrepresents historical facts and available records in order to serve the
interests of Japan.
Hawaii and California may fairly disagree in matters of opinion and pol-
icy. They should not disagree as to facts in the face of conclusive evidence. Assum-
ing that some of the facts in this book have not yet come under your notice, I take
the liberty of calling your attention thereto with suggestions as to where full de-
tails may be obtained.
You say the book is not now in use by any school in Hawaii. It was,
however, in use in certain public schools there throughout the year 1935, as indicated
by protests made to the Superintendent of Public Instruction as latc as December, l935.
The proper authorities hed notice and proof repeatedly as to the alleged objectionable
features of the book:- In Deoember, 1934, through protest to the Hawaiian Commissioners
of Education; in March, 1935, through petition to the Hawaiian Legislature; in June,
1935, and later, through publicity in California and New York attending the attempt to
secure endorsement of the book for use in continental states; and through notico given
by the co-author of withdrawal of the book pending revision (New York Times, July 14,
1935.).
C.J.I.C. Docs. f430 and #443, ttachod, enumerate a number of misrepre-
sentations made; and full details appe ar in statements and exhibits filed with the
State Superintendent of Public Instruction of California, June 21, 1935, and January
15 and 31, 1936. Copies thereof were filed also with the San Francisco Bay Region
Group, I.P.R., and copy of the June 2lst presentation was sent to Superintendent of
Public Instruotion of Hawaii, O. E. Long, at his request. It is suggested that you
inspect that statcment nd the accompanying exhibits.
It is learned from your letter that the book is now being somewhat
revised and that it will be again used in Hawaiian public schools after that revision
is completed. Meamwhile, however, as stated by the Chairman of the Hawaiian Education
Committee, I.P.R., in the Honolulu Advertiser, January 26, 1936, the co-author of
the book is still urging at New York endorsement thereof for goneral use in high
schools throughout the United States. There is also, he states, concert of action
between the I.P.R. groups in Hawaii and Culifornia looking to preparation of material
concerning Pacific Relations and Japaneso Culture, "for use in over l00 cooperating
high sohools of the state", and a movement "to carry forward this text book project
which had suoh modest beginning in Hawaii"in the hope that in another year units

=== Page 8 === (confidence 0.99)
"may be widely available to American schools". Evidence of that polioy has already
been noted in certain California cities.
The California Joint Immigration Committee, when it learned that the
promoters planned to introduce the book into schools of California and other states,
called attention to the established fects as contrasted with the authors' version in
vertain important matters, suggesting that the showing justifies doubt as to the
uthors' reliability in other matters. The position of the Joint Committee is indi-
cated in its statement, June 2lst, as follows:
None will criticize the claim made that knowledge on the part of
each nation facing the Pacific of the character, conditions, and aspira-
tions of other nations thereon is a necessary foundation for mutual under-
standing and the promotion of permanent peace on the Pacific. It is our
contention, however, that textbooks used in the public schools and relied
upon for suoh information should not be prepared by, or under direction of,
foreign propagandists, even with the aid or approval of American interests,
organizations or individuals; and further, that such books, no matter by
whom prepared, should so present authenticated facts as to assist an intel-
ligent reader in renohing fair conclusions.
Mr. Long, in a letter to the Joint Committec, July 21, 1935, quoted
the paragraph sbove and said: "I am certain I can speak for the Commissioners of
Publio Iustruction when I state that the abovo paragraph states the viewpoint of
this department. * * * * To be effective, however, any instruction in this field
must be entirely free from propaganda."The continued use of the text book in
Hawaii throughout the year 1935 does not accord with the principle thus enunciated.
If the facts are as shown by documentary evidence, the interests of
state and nation, the Joint Committce believes, forbid the uso of this book in
public sohool ourricula. Nor should any necessary ruvision thereof or preparation
of other similar text books be entrusted to egencies responsible for introduction of
the present book, nor to the authors who, after disproof of the statements therein,
reiterate conclusions and criticism which have no foundation save such misstatements.
(See intorview Helen Gay Pratt, New York Times, July 14, 1935.)
Hawaiian public opinion apparently supported the authorities of the
Territory in the policy of continuing use of this book through l935, notwithstanding
protests and evidence submitted therewith and the absence of answer cr denial. That
may have been due to lack of knowledge of the facts or to racial conditions and influ-
enoes which exist in the Territory. But, regardless of other agencies involved,
responsibility for the situation created rests with Hawaii, her constituted authori-
ties and her citizens. Cc.lifornia and other states should not be expected to acqui-
esce, even tacitly, in policy and acts so manifestly injurious to the interests of
state and nation.
I feel sure no issue wil! be raised between us on the points thus
outlined in friendly spirit.
With personal regards,
Sincerely,
V. S. Moclatchy, Exec. Secy.
California Joint Immigration Committee

HAWAIIAN TROUBLES COME TO MAINLAND
Propaganda in Public Schools
In the office of Vierling Kersey, State Superintendent of Public Instruc-
tion, at Sacramento, is a copy of a text book on Japan now in use in the public
schools of Honolulu and urged by its authors for use in the public schools of Cali-
fornia and other mainland states. Accompanying the book is a statement with exhi-
bits from the California Joint Immigration Committee in support of the charge origi-
nally made before the Hawaiian Legislature, that the book misrepresents, in the inter-
est of Japan, certain historical facts and available official records in matters of
material concern to the United States. The book was prepared and issued under joint
sponsorship of the Society of Cultural Relations of Japan, the Institute of Pacific
Relations and the Hawaiian Commissioners of Education.
Superintendent Kersey oalled attention of local school authorities in Cali-
fornia to the matter. As a result he has been asked to investigate special school
courses in two Califoraia cities which, it is charged, may be used to similarly de-
ceive the American students.
The Hawaiian book makes various statements as to the "Gentlemen's Agreement"
its purpose and operation, including the claim that it authorized the entrance of 200
Japanese immigrants annually, which are criticized as at variance with the records.
The Joint Committee's dooument offers also the following analysis of Chapter V of the
book:
In Chapter V, which purports to present a brief sketch of the polioies,
activities and international relations of Japan during the present century, the
conquest of Manchuria, creation of the puppet state of Manchukuo, siege of
Shanghai and occupation of various districts of Northern China are supposed to
be suffioiently covered for the information of inquiring American students by
the following paragraph:--"During the World War and afterwards Japan played a
part in China utterly diffcrent than anything previously known. Japan entered
actively into the internal affairs of that great and disorganized country, impos-
ing the 21 demands in l915, and beginning an economic penetration of the country
by lending money and establishing factories." Korea, which was annexed in vio-
lation of treaty obligations, receives only two brief mentions, one in connec-
tion with the request for two new Army Divisions "to maintain order in Korea",
and another in regard to "the cost of maintaining order in a hostile dependency
such as Korea".
Japan's action under the Nine Power Treaty is dismissed with
the statement that "this treaty dealt with maintaining the territorial integrity
of China and Open Door trade relations with China". The Chapter closes with the
statement that "this brief survey . . . mny serve to indicate the growing com-
plexity of the problems of contemporary Japan and their international significanc

Copy of Item in Japan Times, Tokyo, Japan.
December 4, 1934.
HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS IN U.S. TO BE GIVEN
BOOKS WITH CORRECT INFORMATION ON JAPAN.
The Society of International Cultural Relations at its meeting Monday
afternoon decided on a plan to be followed for the compilation of school text-
books to be used at high schools in the United States for diffusing correct
information on Japan.
According to the plan, the collecting and provisional compilation of
Material on Japan will be undertaken by a committee in this country, while
final compilation will be done by a joint committee including both American and
Japanese members. It was also decided at the meeting to present the draft by
the Japanese committee to Mr. Lasker, chairman on the cultural relations of the
I. P. R.* for his suggestions before sending it to the joint Japanese-American
committee for final compilation.
Material of instruction on Japan will cover almost every phase of modern
Japan, embracing topios on the government, economic and social conditions, art,
etc., which will be presented in a way that will appeal to the average high
school student in America.
*
The "Japan Times and Mail" published at Tokyo under direction of the Foreign
Office.
**
I. P. R. - The Institute of Pacific Relations, whose members in rcoent bi-
ennial sessions - notably at Bunff, Canada, in 1933, were urged by the
Japanese delegation thereto to proselyte for immigration quota for Japan.
For further information in regard to this subject see C.J.I.C. Releases #407 - #408.

JAPAN INVADES THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS
What Hawaiian Students are Taught
In June, 1935, Vierling Kersey, Supt. of Public Instruotion of California, made
publio faots concerning a text book on Japan, then in use in the public sohools of
Honolulu and which was under consideration by the Lincoln Teachers College, Columbia
before the Legislature of Hawaii that the book was an instrument of Japanese propagan-
authoritative statements in July that the book would be entirely rewritten and mistakes
if any, correoted, new protests made in Hawaii in December declare that use of the book
has inoreased (c).
Supt. Kersey has received from the California Joint Immigration Committee an anal-
ysis of certain portions of the book substantiating the charges made (d). It is poin-
Manchuria, oreation of the puppet state of Manchukuo, siege of Shanghai and oocupation
of various districts of Northern China are supposed to be sufficiently covered for the
information of inquiring American students by the following paragraph:--"During the
orld War and afterwards Japan played a part in China utterly different than anything
previously known. Japan entered actively into the internal affairs of that great and
disorganized country, imposing the 21 demands in 1915, and beginning an economic pene-
tration of the country by lending money and establishing factories." * * * Korea,
which was annexed in violation of treaty obligations, receives only two brief mentions,
one in connection with the request for two new Army Divisions "to maintain order in
Korea", and another in rogard to "the cost of maintaining order in a hostile depondency
such as Korea". * * * The Nine Power Treaty is dismissed with the statement that "this
treaty dealt with maintaining the territorial integrity of China and Open Door trade
relations with China". * * * The Chapter closes with the statement that "this brief
survey . . . may serve to indicate the growing complexity of the problems of contempo-
rary Japan and their international significance".
In Chaptor V, and also at pp. 129 and 150, are statements concerning Japanese immi-
gration to the United States and the "Gentlemen's Agreement", which the Joint Committe
declares "are so much at variance vith the records of the facts, accessible to anyone,
as to disoredit the entire book". The toxt book states that the Gentlemen's Agreoment
provided for entrance of 200 Japanese annually; that tho Agreement was sorupulously ken
by Japan; and that the law of l924, excluding all aliens ineligible to citizenship, "was
one of the most unjustifiable and unfortunate pieccs of legislation imaginable". In
refutation of those statements it is pointed out on the published authority of Pres.
Theodore Roosevelt, under whose direotion the Gentlemen's Agreemont was made, that (1)
the Agreement did not permit thc entranco of any number of Japanese immigrants per year
(2) that it was made for the agreed purpose of excluding Japancse immigration; (3) the
to save Japan's "face", instead of mssing an exclusion act, as in the case of Chinese
immigration, the object was to be seoured by Japan so limiting her passports as to ex-
clude all Japanese laborers and to prevent inorease of Jupanese population in continen-
tal United States; (4) that if the plan failed to accomplish those purposes it was to b
replaced by an exclusion act (e).
Offioial records show thet the terms of the Agreement were not complied with. Thou-
sands of male laborers were sent over with passports; they were detained at ports of
entry, but released under habeas corpus by Fedoral Courts, which disclaimed jurisdiotio
the Agreement being noither law nor treaty; the male laberers were followed by thousand:
of pioture and kankodan brides, nearly all of whem came to labor in the fields and inci.
dentally to inorease the population by births. California's protests were unheeded un-
til 1924, when under a nationwide demand, Congress was foroed to substitute for the
Agreement a general law excluding all aliens ineligible to citizenship--the only one of
five plans proposed which would accomplish, without disorimination, the agreed purpose
of the Agreement (f).

PREFACE
For particular help in the preparation of this second book of the Peoples of the Pacific Series, I wish
to express my gratitude to Sir George Sansom who read and discussed with me all but the modern part; to Dr.
Robert Karl Reischauer of Princeton University who criticised the entire manuscript; and to Professor Gregg
M. Sinclair of the University of Hawaii who introduced me to literary sources. This edition differs in im-
portant respects from an earlier mimeographed draft in the preparation of which I had the valuable assis-
tance of Professor Masamichi Royama of the Imperial University, Tokyo, who happened to be in Hawai1 while
the work was in progress, and whose courteous help was much appreciated. Preference of the teachers who ex-
perimented with the earlier outline for a somewhat different form of treatment has made this edition prac-
tically a new attempt to bring the history and the contemporary life of Japan to the understanding of Ameri-
can students.

Contradictions and conflicts are, of course, characteristic of life everywhere, but in Japan they ap-
pear to be particularly spectacular. In a list such as has been just set down, and which could be continued
almost indefinitely, it is plain that there are two t:pes of opposed elements. One is the kind which exists
in fact, and which arises from imposirg western civilization upon an ancient culture, many of wrose charac-
teristics have been retained. The other has its origin in the differences in personal bias of those who
interpret Japanese life. Some of the opposed elements arise from differences in emphasis rather than in
fact.
It 1s obvious that if we take all our colors from one of the lists just examined, we shall have one
sort of picture, while, 1f we take them only from the other, the picture will be very different. Many inter-
preters of Japan do exactly this sort of thing, painting pictures which, laid side by side, appear to be re-
presentations of entirely different subjects. Which of the different items listed on both sides are most
significant? What is Japan?
The clue to the answers - if there is an answer - lies in the past, for Japan alone, of the Asiatic na-
tions meeting the modern west, has adopted the techniques and methods of the outside world, and has, at the
same time, kept her political integrity and retained many national forms of thought and behavior. In the
history of the people, in the nature of the social and governmental structure which was able to maintain it-
self in the face of the impact of the modern west, lie clues to the enigma of Japan. In Japan, however
modern it may appear to be, feudal elements in thought and behavior are still struggling for survival. Out
of this situation arise some of the conflicts and contradictions which are seen in Japan today.

Chaptor 1.
THE NATURAL SETTING
The main islands of Japan - Honshu, (the main land), Shikoku, Kyushu and Hokkaido - curve
outward from the peninsula of Korea and then inward toward the coast of Asia. The position of
this crescent of islands, inclining toward the mainland of Asia, may be considered symbolic,
for from the continent came the Chinese culture on which so much of Japanese culture was built,
and towards the mainland the thoughts and aspirations of Japanese very frequently were directed
in the past - as in the present. Insular pride and tradition were inevitably brought up
against the diverse influences which came from the great empire of China.
The continent, however, 1s not near at hand. At least one hundred miles of ocean separate
Japan from the mainland, a fact of great importance particularly when considered in connection
with China's tendency to expand on land, not by way of the sea. If Japan had been not one
hundred miles from the continent, but twenty miles - as England is - the whole history of the
country would doubtless have been entirely different. Into Japan came no invaders comparable
to the Romans, the Saxons, the Angles, the Danes, and the Normans, who raided, invaded, and
conquered England, and brought waves of new influences into the country when they settled there.
The expanse of ocean between Japan and the mainland was sufficient to isolate the islands to a
great extent and to free them from the threat of invasion. Though some piratical raids were
made upon Japan from the mainland, the only armed expedition on an important scale that ever
approached Japan was one planned and carried out by the Mongols in the thirteenth century.
The 1slands of Japan are extremely beautiful, with mountains rising from the sea, and
swift streams cutting the mountain sides. They give an impression of peaceful beauty which
has served as a Japanese ideal, but in their very nature they offer obstacles to a peaceful,
easy life. The mountains running throughout the crescent of islands break even the largest
of the group into portions which, until modern means of transportation were developed, were
relatively inaccessible to each other, for the swift mountain streams were not navigable.
Isolated portions of the 1slands formed natural strongholds for the rival lords who flourished
and made war upon each other through so much of Japan's history. Again, only about fifteen
per cent of the land is suitable for cultivation; the terraced fields today reach into the
mountain slopes, and intensively cultivated farm lands occupy all the flat plains of the rural
regions, but the greater part of the mountainous land is covered with forests which today be-
long to the emperor. Mountains, rivers, and forests form a charming natural setting for a
battle for existence, which, with every census, 1s obviously more acute. More than 60,000,000
people occupy Japan proper today, yet the country's total area is less than that of the single
state of California, and eighty-five per cent of it is not cultivable.
Still another fact to be opposed to the appearance of peaceful beauty is the existence of
fifty-eight active volcanoes. Earthquakes, often very destructive, are of frequent occurrence.
Since the dawn of Japan's recorded history there have been repeated earthquake disasters.
Betwoen 1597 and 1897 there were 108 quakes of sufficient violence to merit history, and there
1s no record of the number of minor upheavals in that period. In the years between 1884 and
1897, when more scientific records were kept, 17,750 shocks were reported, an average of 3t a
day. The Seismic Disaster Investigation Committee of Japan, a scientific body devoted to the
study of seismic disturbances, estimates that since 8oo A.D. there have been something like
2,o06 major disasters. An accurate estimate is impossible, but these figures give one some
1dea of the frequency and 1mportance of this particular part of Japan's natural heritage.

The geographical position of the islands is such that they are subject to frequent violent
storms - typhoons and torrential rains. Earthquakes especially have influenced architecture and
building. Japanese homes and temples were not made of clay or stone, but of wood. Brick was
discarded after the disaster of l923, and all concrete structures have two and a half times as
much steel reinforcement as is used in the United States. While it would be difficult to esti-
mate the exact effect of recurring earthquakes, storms, and floods, upon people, it cannot be
doubted that there is an effect upon those who experience them. It is not impossible that a na-
tion's whole attitude toward the things to be valued in this world may be influenced by such
acts of nature, but even if the influence is not of the permanent type which affects the temper
of a nation, a mark is left upon the generation affected by major disasters. On the other hand,
the geographical position of the central islands of Shikoku, Honshu and Kyushu in which Japanese
civilization developed gives these islands an even, temperate climate which, in the long inter-
vals between storms and other natural disasters, also influences the life of the people.
Like all 1slanders of history, the Japanese were a seafaring people - until they were for-
bidden,early in the seventeenth century,to have anything to do with the outside world and were
not permitted to build boats which could traverse the ocean or the inland seas to Asia. Before
this, however, they built fishing and trading boats, crossed to the mainland, and made raids
upon the coast and upon islands not yet under Japanese control. One research student of Poly-
nesian life, studying Hawaiian customs and comparing them with those of the rest of Polynesia,
concludes that some Japanese must have reached Hawaii in ancient times, for the Hawaiian kahilis
which were used as symbols of royalty cannot be matched elsewhere in Polynesia, and they resem-
ble very closely the insignia carried before Japanese lords. However, it is certain that any
Japanese reaching ancient Hawai1 were blown there by some storm, and that they did not estab-
lish any routes across the Pacific. In the sixteenth century, however, under the stimulus of
contacts with European traders and explorers, the Japanese built ships in which they traversed
the Pacific Ocean. All of this seafaring activity was ended in the seventeenth century when the
Tokugawa shogun closed the country to foreigners, and forbade Japanese to leave the 1slands.
Thus the natural enterprise of seafaring islanders was imprisoned within closed walls, bringing
new problems of adjustment into the lives of the Japanese people, and helping to dam up energies
which welcomed the outlet supplied by the "opening" of the country.
As a result of the isolation of early Japan, and the natural beauty of island setting, a
copious mythology developed long before Japan had historical contact with the adjoining main-
land. In the words of Sir George Sansom:
A nature worship of which the mainspring is appreciation rather than fear is not to
be dismissed as base and fetichistic animism, and much that is gracious and kindly in the
life of the Japanese today can be traced to those sentiments which caused their remote
ancestors to ascribe divinity not only to the powerful and awe-inspiring, such as the sun
and the moon and the tempest, or to the useful, such as the well and the cooking pot, but
also to the lovely and pleasant, such as the rocks and streams, the trees and flowers.
The worship of such objects has its counterpart in that delicate sensibility to the
beauties of nature which is one of the most endearing characteristics of the modern Japa-
nese. Beyond doubt it is a ciaracteristic deeply rooted in the past.1
Isolated in valleys, cut off from many contacts, the people of ancient Japan felt their re-
lationship with the deified forces of the visible world, and traced their descent from the gods.
The myths and legends of the 1ndigenous religion were handed down by oral tradition and were not
committed to writing until 712 A.D. when the first record of the past was written in a long ac-
count called the Kojiki (Record of Ancient Matters).

The folklore recorded in these eighth century chronicles was particularly emphasized after
the country was opened to foreigners in the middle of the nineteenth century, and after the em-

rooted in the very nature of the land itself, was carried over into the present. In Japan today,
for example, the jewel which forms part of the imperial regalia is considered to be the actual
article given by the Sun Goddess to her grandson, the ancestor of the present emperor. It is
believed that the original mirror and sword are in existence, housed in famous shrines. The
rest of the imperial regalia consists of ancient replicas of the Sun Goddess's gift. Those who
find it difficult to understand how anyone can accept such beliefs forget, perhaps, their own
uncritical attitude toward traditional elements in their own heritage.

The Japanese empire occupies a strategic position in the Pacific and on the mainland of
Asia. This geographical position, combined with such things as the weakness of disordered

What then is the position of Japan in international politics and what is the situation
in the Far East? Japan is the most densely populated country in the world, with 17o per-

The position of Japan, as a nation of the greatest density of population coupled with
natural resources which are poorest among the larger Powers, naturally leads to the fear .
that, unless something be done, the nation will be exposed to starvation and the very exis-

What then is the situation in the Far East? Who is the mistress of Asia that nurtures
one-half of the total population of the world? For many centuries in the past, the conti-

divided up into colonies of European or American nat1ons. And Japan is the only country

struggles to keep up her prestige as a state by playing one nation against the other, al-

Chaptor 2.
THE DEVELOPMENT OF JAPANESE SOCIETY UNDER CHINESE INFLUENCES
(7th-12th Centurles)
We know that in the middle of the nineteenth century, Japan was "opened" to the western
world; that the barrier of isolation set up for nearly two hundred and fifty years was torn down,
and that from that time modern Japan was rapidly built. This was the first time in Japanese
history that foreign pressure had been a factor in forcing change upon the country, but it was
noi the first time that Japan had been profoundly modified by contact with foreign influences.
The earlier influences came from China. These were most important during the most prosperous
and virile periods of Chinese history, as, for example, during the time of the Han when Japan
first obtained some of the advanced arts and crafts of China, and especially during the time of
the T'ang when new ideas of government, literature, philosophy ani religion took root, and the
earlier imported art of writing began to be more widely used. At periods when China was weak-
ened, its influence upon Japan was lessened; and also, Japanese culture became more sure of it-
self, and less imitative. If we take a long view of Japanese history, we see that however
strong were the foreign influences affecting the country, nevertheless certain Japanese elements
persisted. From this point of view, Japanese history appears as a combination of strands, some
of Japanese origin, the others of foreign importation. These strands sometimes are brought
together so closely that their separate identity is almost lost in what appears to be a single
fabric; at other times, they are separated and stand out in contrast to each other.
The idea of the divine origin of the great families and more particularly of the imperial
clan is one of the Japanese strands which runs throughout Japanese history. The idea persisted,
though the emperor seldom exercised the power which would seem to belong to his exalted origin
and though this particular strand was obscured at times by other elements. When the country was
going through the stages of enthusiastic acceptance of Buddhism, the national religion was for
some time in the background, and even the emperors and empresses, devoting themselves to the new
religion, seemed to be at a loss as to how to relate their own ancestors, the gods of Japan, to
the new gods. Again,after the relationship had been established and the national gods had been
honored with shrines in Buddhist temples, the influence of the growing feudal structure of Jap-
anese society, together with the actual rule of the state by non-imperial families powerful at
court, helped to undermine the power of the imperial family. During the period of more than six
centuries when the shogun ruled the country, loyalty to the immediate overlord overshadowed, in
the popular mind, devotion to the secluded and quite powerless emperor. However, the idea of
imperial prestige was never completely lost; it remained sufficiently fixed in the tradition so
that it could be revived, as it was at different periods, for political reasons.
Another of the Japanese elements persisting throughout the history of the country was the
clan system, which knit groups of people together, not only by centralized control, but also by
traditional loyalties, customs, and observances. Class stratification existed - farmers, arti-
sans, merchants and warriors formed hereditary divisions within the clan over which the lord
ruled, but class divisions did not permeate Japanese society horizontally. Thus all the farmers,
all the artisans, all the merchants, all the warriors, did not form homogeneous groups; instead,
a clan embracing members of each class was held in loyalty to the clan leader, the lord. Tradi-
tional behav1or and traditional loyalties were gradually very elaborately developed, so that
groups of the less privileged who might have common grievances were not welded together against
the upper classes. The many conflicts which devastated feudal Japan, the wars and struggles
which, in turn, led to the development of a great literature illustrating and extolling Japanese
tradition, were possible because of the emphasis on loyalties owed to a feudal overlord. This

=== Page 40 === (confidence 0.99)
-9-
literature, elaborated in popular plays during the years of peace which were brought about under
the Tokugawa shogun, the last of the great feudal rulers of Japan, kept alive among the people
the traditions which had permeated Japanese life during the feudal wars. Thus Japan was thor-
oughly imbued with feudal tradition, and it was this Japan which met the impact of the modern
west. Feudalism, as a form of organized society, was abolished, but feudal attitudes did not
die out, and feudal remains in government, in industry, and in the landholding system struggled
for survival. Indeed, in every period of Japanese history, changing economic situations pressed
against feudal traditions; economic influences brought about change in the past and cause us to
examine their possible influence today.
The presence of characteristically Japanese elements in the thoughts and behavior of the
people and in the structure of society, imparted strength to the country. When foreign forms
came in they were modified under the influence of the strong national tradition. On the other
hand, the process of modification was not a simple one and the clash between indigenous and im-
ported forms created problems. This conflict l1es at the root of modern problems of adjustment
within the country, and offers an obstacle to outside understanding of Japan.
In spite of the strength and tenacity of the national tradition, the country of Japan owed
1ts cultural advancement not to these elements, but to Chinese importations, which began quite
certainly as early as the first century A.D. At that time the Han empire held the northern part
of the peninsula of Korea; flourishing Chinese colonies brought the arts and crafts of the virile
China of the Han into a region which was reached by Japanese. Thus into Japan came such things
as silk culture, weaving, and lacquer work. Chinese script probably reached Japan, which had had
no written language, in the fifth century, but very little use was made of writing until the
seventh century. Chinese chronology was adopted in the seventh century, and when the first ex-
tant Japanese chronicle was compiled in the eighth century, Chinese chronology was used to deter-
mine dates for the legendary as well as the more well-established personages of Japanese history.
Thus the date of the legendary first emperor, Jimmu (the great-great-great-grandson of the Sun
Goddess) was set at a date corresponding to 66o B.C., because - according to the Chinese belief -
a large cycle of 1260 years precedes a small cycle of 60 years, 1n the 58th year of wh1ch a revo-
lution 1s l1able to take place. Considering the adoption of Chinese chronology as such a revolu-
tion and counting backward into the mists of legend, a date corresponding to 66o B.C. was arrived
at. Modern historical research however places the emperor Jimmu in the f1: st century A.D., but
the earlier date of 66o B.C. 1s that usec y Japanese in computing the lengh of the imperial
rule. This 1s the basis for the frequentiy reiterated statement that the present emperor, the
one hundred twenty-fourth of the unbroken line, represents a dynasty over 250o years old.
Chinese crafts were important in Japan; Chinese script had to be adapted to Japanese use;
the national tradition which derived a type of exactitude from Chinese chronology was to be in-
fluential, but the influences most immediately effective 1n changing Japanese life were Chinese
governmental forms and Buddhism.
Since 1t was China of the T'ang which profoundly affected Japan, we shall pick up the story
of Japan at the seventh century, the time when 1t met the T'ang culture.
So much of the later growth of Japan 1s to be traced to her borrowings from China un-
der the T'ang dynasty that it 1s necessary to describe, as briefly as can be, conditions in
China and Japan at this time. Politically China was at this moment perhaps the most power-
ful, the most advanced, and the best administered country in the worid. Certainly in every
material aspect of the life of a state she was overwhelmingly superior to Japan. The fron-
tiers of her empire stretched to the borders of Persia, to the Caspian Sea, to the Alta1
mountains. She was in relations with the peoples of Annam, Cochin China, Tibet, the Tarim
basin, and India; with the Turks, the Persians, and the Arabs. Men of many natíons ap-
peared at the court of China, bringing tribute and merchandise and new 1deas that in-

=== Page 41 === (confidence 0.99)
-10-
fluenced her thought and her art. Persian and more remotely, Greek influence is apparent
in much of the sculpture and painting of the T'ang period.. We need not discuss the
extent of these various alien influences, we need only notice that their presence must
have been a stimulus to invention and creation in many provinces of life, and at the same
time remark that the bulk of China was so great, her strength so formidable, that they
could be easily absorbed without disturbing the balance or the individuality of her own
culture. Along the streets of Ch'ang-an there passed in those days Buddhist monks from
India, envoys from Kashgar, Samarkand, Persia, Annam, Tonkin, Constantinople, chieftains
of nomadic tribes from Siberian plains, officials and students from Korea and, in now
increasing numbers, from Japan. It is easy to imagine the effect upon the eyes and the
minds of these last of a capital so rich in interest and excitement, their despair at the
sight of such profusion, their proud resolve to rival it, if industry and courage and
restless ambition could eke out their country's material shortcomings. No doubt with that
tireless curiosity and patient attention to detail which characterized their study of
other alien civilizations with which they later came in contact - those of Portugal, of
Holland, and later of the industrialised Occident of the l9th century - the Japanese set
themselves to observe and report on every aspect of Chinese life, and to consider what
features they might profitably adopt in their own country. First, in the political field,
they would notice that the T'ang sovereign was an absolute monarch surrounded by able
ministers, who were both scholars and statesmen, from whom he exacted and obtained
obedience and loyal service. The country was divided into administrative districts under
governors who were carefully selected for their capacity, and constantly supervised by
inspecting commissions. Officials were selected and promoted for merit. Appointments
were usually limited to those who had passed examinations in the classics, and this test,
though it might exclude certain useful types of vigour and ability, had the inestimable
advantage that it set learning above warfare and gifts above family. The career was open
to the talents: circumscribed talents, no doubt; but none the less society was establish-
ed on an intellectual basis, and to have even attempted to form an aristocracy of brains
is a stupendous achievement. So the Japanese travellers saw, and perhaps understood in
some measure, a centralised, organized state, a vast but united empire, with a great regu-
lar army, victorious against all its enemies except - and this must have afforded them
some hope and consolation - the Koreans, who more than once repulsed Chinese invasions on
a grand scale, notably in 646. The Japanese, then, could not fail to be impressed by the
sheer power of China, and they must have been soon convinced that it was due principally
to her system of government, which was in almost all essentials the exact opposite to
their own aristocratic, caste-ridden tribal institutions.
Less apparent, but equally impressive to the seekers of knowledge, was the prodigious
activity of China in the intellectual sphere... The first T'ang emperor, announcing that
the teaching of the sages was what air is to birds and water to fish, surrounded himself
with scholars, remodelled and enlarged the imperial academy, increased its students to
3,Ooo, and reformed the provincial seats of learning.. Already there existed a long tradi-
tion of architecture and carving.. Now to this was added the delicate skill of T'ang
sculpture and drawing, with which there was compounded a new emotional element furnished
by the tender and refining influences of Buddhist thought as it had by then developed...
It would be too much of a digression to go on to speak of the painting, the bronzes, the
pottery, the coloured silks, the poems and the fine calligraphies. It is enough to say
that ali these arts were blossoming in profusion when the first Japanese missions found
themselves in the T'ang capital... To the Japanese it must have been staggering.....
Priests, artists and craftsmen, brought back to Japan the knowledge and material
objects by which their country was to take over, and fashion to her own requirements, a
superior culture. The process was obviously a defective one, because it operated at a
distance, with little personal contact. Not very far in miles, China was separated from
Japan by great differences of race, language, and custom. For most Japanese, a knowledge
of China was to be obtained only at second or third hand, passing at one stage through the
medium of an alien language. It is therefore to be expected that in its transit it would
be diluted, if not distorted, and that what would reach Japan would be the forms rather
than the essence. In studying the history of the 7th century in particular, one is con-
stantly struck by this feature, as one 1s at the same time struck by the artistic develop-
ment of Japan, which was as rapid and real as the political and social changes were slow.
and superficial. Not that this difference 1s to be wondered at, for the Japanese could
see before their eyes the ravishing loveliness of statues and paintings brought from the
continent or created 1n their midst by Chinese and Korean masters. The other gifts which
China had to offer were intangible or invisible, and tainted with human fallibility. You
might be breathless with adoration before a serene and faultless golden Buddha, but you
could dislike or criticise the Chinese way of thought and the Chinese principles of
government, the more so if they ran counter to your vested interests. Splendour and
beauty are easier to accept than the austerities of reform, and the consolations of philo-
sophy are more welcome than its discipline.1

China of the T'ang had a mature and sophisticated civilization. For over a thousand years,
philosophies had been formulated, discussed, restudied, and reformulated. Buddhism had been in
process of absorption for some five hundred years. Governmental forms of a non-aristocratic
type had been evolving for centuries. A great literature already lay in the past. In Japan, on
the contrary, civilization at this time was unsophisticated. No systems of thought which could
be called philosophies had been formulated by Japanese; governmental forms were simple - and
aristocratic; no national literature existed, and Buddhism was a comparatively recent importa-
tion. The way in which Japanese grappled with the problems of creating a new Japan on the
Chinese model, of taking over new forms of government and religion, of building a new culture in
spite of barriers of language and handicaps of the country's size and resources, is one of the
interesting stories of history. Its close parallel may only be found in the later history of
Japan, in the story of the country's development after the middle of the nineteenth century.
Since it was the power of China which first of all attracted the Japanese, and since this
power was attributed by them to the form of government, it is important to realize that the
governmental forms of China were worked out to suit a country which included great plains in its
vast area. The country was divided into provinces, which were in turn sub-divided, until the
farm lands were reached. These farm lands were re-allotted at intervals, according to the size
of the households involved. One ninth of the produce of the allotted lands was the tax supposed
to be paid to the government. Another aspect of the government was the non-aristocratic non-
hereditary officialdom, appointed by the emperor not from families of aristocratic birth, but to
a great extent from scholars drawn from any class who succeeded in passing the state competitive
examinations.
When Japanese clan leaders who were powerful at court and who practically ruled the country
attempted to remodel Japan on this pattern, they met difficult problems. The very nature of the
land was against them, for the mountainous lands of Japan were not easily allotted and divided
into farming regions from which regular taxes could be figured and collected. The social struc-
ture was against them. Powerful clan lords ruled their districts. If the clan most influential
at court asserted without qualification, that the imperial family owned the land and could dis-
tribute it at intervals, as well as appoint provincial rulers, it would find itself meeting the
opposition of all the other powerful lords. Qualifications and concessions had to be made, to
secure the support of the clan leaders. A beginning had been made in this direction early in
the seventh century, before the era of the government reforms, in order that the ambitious clan
leaders might be placated by the family most powerful at court. At that time, an elaborate
system of ranks was worked out, each rank designated by a cap of a certain color. These ranks
were prized, and were considered important enough to be revised from time to time, until at the
beginning of the eighth century, they reached the form in which they remained. Officials of the
court and in regions near the capital were given the highest ranks, while those of the rural
regions fell into the lower categories. Privilege, exemptions, and prestige were based on
degree of rank. Rank went to members of great familios; it was based primarily on birth. When
from 645 to 718 the changes in government that began with the Taikwa Reforms were worked out,
government officials were chosen from these same families. Thus to privilege, exemptions, and
prestige was added official position with all its special privileges.
In spite of the difficulty of allotting the cultivable fields of Japan, the Taikwa Reforms
provided for such a system of division of the lands, based like the Chinese system on the size
of the households. It was planned that re-allotment should take place with the new census of
every sixth year. Cultivators of rice fields paid a land tax in rice. Rice fields held by
shrines and temples, rice fields from whose produce officials drew their salaries, and rice

=== Page 43 === (confidence 0.99)
-12-
fields cultivated by serfs for the government were exempt from taxation. When new lands were
brought under cultivation, there was a possibility that they might escape the rice tax if they
could manage to remain unlisted.
In addition to the tax on allotted rice fields, there was a labor tax payable in work or
in produce supposed to be paid by all males, but men of certain rank were exempt from this levy.
A tax was also laid upon other produce than rice - workers in a silk district for example paid
a tax in silk.
It is plain that the system of taxation placed the burdens upon the rural cultivators, but
that they might escape their obligations 1f in some way their lands could be attached to those
of an exempt lord or religious establishment, or if they could secure non-allotted non-registered
land. Thus the economic basis of the remodelled structure was fundamentally unsound. It had
too many loopholes - arising from the facts that special privileges had to be given to the
powerful to gain their support for the plan in the first place, and that the way was open to
increase the number of exemptions.
In order further to conciliate the clan leaders, local or district officials in the new
government were selected from the families already powerful in those regions. Officials were
not, as a rule, moved about as they were under the Chinese system; they remained in their own
districts and their position was further strengthened by clan loyalties. The Chinese examina-
tion system of selecting most government officials was very much modified in Japan. The types
of offices open to candidates successful in competitive .xaminations were much fewer in number
than in China and they included none of the exalted posts. The spirit behind the examination
system of Japan was different from the spirit of the Chinese system. In effect, this system
as it worked out in Japan was merely the accompaniment of government, not its basis, and it
gradually fell into disuse.
Because of the concessions given the clan leaders and because of the insecurity of the
economic basis of the new government, the system introduced in the middle of the seventh century
and revised from time to time in the effort to make it work was bound to be superseded. But,
while it was in force it is evident that in the court would be centered all that was attractive
in the life of Japan, at the expense of the rural population.
The first great center of Japanese court life was erected at Nara, where in 71o a city was
built on the model of the Chinese capital. The tax in labor secured the workers for this
enterprise, other taxes supplied the funds, and Nara arose. Life at Nara has been described as
follows:
A settled home was necessary for the growth on native soil of all those alien arts
and sciences which were then being studied with such ardour, and it is for this reason
that their development in the relatively short period of seventy-five years during which
Nara remained the seat of government and the centre of learning, was more rapid and in-
tense than it had ever been befcre. It is difficult to realize how complete a revolution
was effected in all departments of life in the capital. Life in the country went on as
before. Peasants grew their rice, fed their silkworms, grudged their taxes, and worship-
ped their native gods. But in the city all was new, all was foreign. The very architec-
ture of the palaces and the temples was Chinese; the sutras were read in Chinese transla-
tion if not in Sanskrit; laws, ordinances, public documents, official despatches, chroni-
cles, and even poems were in Chinese; the costume of the courtiers, their etiquette, their
ranks and appellations were borrowed from China. The political doctrines of the statesmen
of Japan, the philosophical ideas of her scholars, the religious beliefs of her priests
could be expressed and expounded only in an alien tongue and an imported script; and even
their native speech was now being enriched with words of foreign origin. It is hard to
find a parallel for this curious phenomenon of a small society, busily digesting and
assimilating a superior foreign culture not imposed from without by conquest or proximity,
but voluntarily, even enthusiastically adopted. It numbered probably not more than twenty

=== Page 44 === (confidence 0.99)
-13-
thousand in a city of perhaps two hundred thousand inhabitants, and the total population
of Japan at this period is estimated at six million.2
The writings attributed to Confucius were among the Chinese books studied in Japan at this
time. No investigation has ever been made to show just how much of Chinese philosophy was ever
comprehended and assimilated in Japan. To the modern reader, the essence of the teachings of
Confucius is that part which deals with the relations between man and man; the emphasis on the
responsibility of every person to include the good of others in his own good. The stress
Confucius lays on the personal integrity of a ruler as the only sanction for his rule, stands
out as another essential part of his teaching. These humanistic teachings made less apparent
impression in Japan than the portions dealing with respect for family, for ancestors, and for
ruler, which were particularly congenial to Japanese tradition. It would seem that the forms of
Confucianiam, rather than the teachings of Confucius, influenced Japan, but the study (in any
European language) which would prove or disprove this conclusion has not been made.
The thin and superficial characteristics of some aspects of Japanese culture at this time
arose primarily from the difficulties involved in adapting the Chinese script to the Japanese
language. When Chinese culture first reached them through Korea, the Japanese spoke a poly-
syllabic and inflected language entirely different from Chinese. They had no developed system
of writing, and at first students simply learned and wrote in the Chinese language, as scholars
in Europe learned and wrote in Latin during the middle ages. The Chinese written language was
1deographic, not phonetic; each ideograph represented an idea, rather than a sound. The second
step was taken when the Japanese tried to represent Japanese proper names by ideographs and saw
that Chinese symbols might stand for sounds as well as ideas. They simplified a number of the
ideographs to become purely phonetic signs and thus produced the Japanese "alphabet," which is a
list of signs (known as Kana script) for the fifty syllables that occurred in their speech. It
was possible then to write the native language completely in these signs, and Japanese might
have become independent of Chinese. To write yama, the Japanese word for mountain, for example,
one needed only to employ the kana signs for ya and ma. But the Chinese symbols stuck. In the
first place, the 1deograph for mountain was one symbol, the kana signs, two. In the second
place, the Chinese ideograph was more graphic, perhaps more picturesque. In the third place,
with the acceptance of Chinese culture the Japanese acquired a vast number of terms that had not
existed in their own language, and instead of inventing new words they simply adopted the Chinese
words with the Chinese pronunciation. To write these they naturally used the Chinese ideographs.
It is clear that many problems were involved in making the adjustments of the Chinese system of
writing to the Japanese language, that solving them would take time, and that before the solu-
tions were reached, Japanese students would be absorbed in studying and transcribing a foreign
language.3
Of the writing done by Japanese during the Nara period, three works are important. The
Kojiki and the Nihong1 (the latter written in Chinese) were compiled. At the very end of the
epoch, the Manyoshu (Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves), the only creative writing of the time,
which was a collection of poems written by different persons, was compiled. These poems show
the influence of Chinese poetry, but they were written in Japanese; the Chinese characters were
used phonetically to express the sounds of Japanese syllables, regardless of the meaning of the
Chinese ideograph. The shorter poems of the collection are particularly interesting; they are
known as Tanka, and "consist of five phrases of lines of 5, 7, 5, 7, and 7 syllables. Each of

of all the influences modifying Japan at this time, Buddhism and Buddhistic art were among
the most important. Buddhism had been introduced into Japan at the end of the sixth century.
At first, though a few scholars studied the teaching, the chief attraction of Buddhism was the
temple images and tho prayers. Then the organization and the ritual began to make their appeal.
A prince and regent of the empire had been responsible for the first real interest in Buddhism;
emperors and empresses gave the new religion their support; the imperial house and the great
families gave the church lands, property and wealth; monasteries were erected, and Buddhist
establishments with their property and court recognition were numbered among the privileged
institutions of the land. It is interesting to see that it was not the ethical teachings of
Buddhism, nor the Buddhistic philosophy which was the occasion of any particular difficulty in
Japan. The questions which however had to be settled were the relation between the native gods
and the new ones, and also why the members of the ruling house, themselves gods, bowed before
new gods. The first question was settled by the decision that the native gods were phases of
Buddha. The second was disposed of by taking the attitude that Buddhism was "excellent for
protecting the state." The gods of Shinto (the name Shinto is given to the native religion)
were enshrined in Buddhist temples, or Buddhist priests took over Shinto shrines. Buddhist

The significance of this lies in the evidence it gives of the Japanese willingness to

that although philosophical controversies were avoided, political ones might arise. The
government and the Church were closely connected, and the institution which was "excellent for
protecting the state" might come to threaten the power of other privileged interests. As a
matter of fact, the Buddhist clergy were so influential at court, especially during the latter
part of the Nara period, that this was one reason why the capital was removed from Nara and
constructed elsewhere away from the great monasteries of that city.
Buddhist art was very stimulating to the Japanese. As has been pointed out earlier, art
can be understood without any word. Language is not necessarily connected with artistic expres-
sion stimulated by actual objects. Years before Nara was built, the Japanese had copied
Buddhist images and created beautiful sculpture in wood. In the latter part of the Nara period
Japanese sculpture began to be more than imitative. Buddhistic images of bronze, wood, and dry
lacquer were produced in profusion. Numerous temples, monasteries, and nunneries constructed in
Nara and in the provinces were filled with sculpture of the period, but artistic expression, as
well as the other cultural developments of the time, was confined to a small group.
The Nara period which came to a close in 782 is summarized in the following:
In the Nara period pure cultural development in art and letters and religion outran
economic and political growth. The aesthetic advance was almost miraculous, and bears
witness to the power of the artistic impulse in the Japanese people. Their economic and
political progress was limited by a number of adverse conditions. It was too much to
expect that a rich and varied culture could be, without difficulties and breakdowns,
borrowed from abroad and erected upon a social basis in which tradition was so strong,and an
economic basis which was inadequate to support it. The new culture not only brought a new
and rapidly rising standard of living; it created a numerous class of leisured or at least
unproductive people. The privileged classes, the monks, the nuns, the priests, the orna-
mental officials and soldiers, with all their servants, had to be supported in increasing
luxury by a farming population which, though it also was doubtless increasing in numbers,
was constantly drained of able-bodied men for unproductive work and crippled by taxation.
The measures taken to cope with this situation were bound to fail. The development of new
land merely emphasized the disparity between the rich proprietor and the small cultivator.
The appointment of inspectors to supervise, in the interests of the peasants, the conduct
of local officials merely gave scope for more patronage, already a grave abuse. The
financial expedients of the statesmen were ineffective if they were not dishonest... The
particular example of Fujiwara Oshikatsu (Nakamaro) aptly illustrates the situation in
general. In 76l, on the occasion of one of those temporary transfers of the imperial
residence which were so burdensome to the people at that time, Nakamaro was granted one
million sheaves of rice to meet his expenses. This is equivalent to the crop of 6,0o0
acres of rice field. He received in addition a fief of 3,o00 households and 300 acres of
rice land. At about the same time he was promoted to the highest possible rank, carrying
the highest possible emoluments, and was given privileges which in practice amounted to
the right to mint coins and to collect interest on rice-loans. He issued silver and
copper coins, in exchange for a currency already debased and nearly half of which was
counterfeit, at such rates that the money cost of commodities must have been raised at
least fivefold. Other courtiers and officials received grants and privileges on a lavish
scale, so that it is not surprising to learn, from memorials of the following period, that
the national treasure was diminished by half through the extravagant expenditure of the
court on buildings and gifts in the last decade of the Tempyo era, which ended in 767.6

When the capital was moved to a city constructed on the site of the present Kyoto, the
Heian period (794-ll85) began. During this period, Chinese institutions, 1deas, and cultural
forms were assimilated and a Japanese culture developed. At the same time, the power of the
Fujiwara family which practically ruled the country for the emperor, the growing demands of
other families, and the rise of a militant clergy, together with the economic difficulties
which were bound to arise because of the loopholes in the taxation system, brought about such
changes that military feudalism began to develop at the end of the poriod.
Dr. Anesaki gives a charming description of the setting in which: the court lived in seclu-
sion, devoted to a life of aesthetic enjoyment:
In order to understand the sway that romantic sentiment came to have over the thought
and emotion of the makers of this civilization, we must picture to ourselves the surround-
ings in which they lived. The city of Miyako (Kyoto) lies in a valley, walled in on three
sides by hills that here and there rise to the dignity of mountains and watered by two
beautiful streams that flow southward toward the southern opening of the valley. The dark-
green slopes of the hills are broken by the somber gray of imposing temple roofs and the
overhanging eaves of pagodas. On the banks of the rivers the pliant willows bend their
supple branches, and soft leaves quiver in the breeze while the clear waters reflect their
green images. A thin veil of mist frequently covers the valley and then the gentle slopes
and overhanging precipices are like a long scroll painted in black and white. Those who
live amidst such loveliness would be insensitive if they did not respond emotionally to
such loveliness.
The persons who played their graceful parts on the stage thus set were the refined and
effeminate "moon lords," or "cloud gallants," as the noblemen were called, and the charming
and intelligent court ladies - the "Ladies of the Wisteria Chamber" and the "Ladies of the
Shadow of Willow." The refinement of their literary and artistic tastes was far superior
to their political talent or tneir moral sense; and in their emotional life they found de-
light in a romantic development of the relations of the sexes, and in a sensitive response
to the beauty of nature.7
Architecture also exerted its influence in setting the stage for the court life of the time:
The mansion of a nobleman of this period was built simply of wood and bamboo. The
floor was raised several feet above the ground, and was reached by staircases. The gently
sloping roof was covered with shingles thickly and compactly laid, so that it had the ef-
fect of a soft, brownish thatch. The main building, which contained the rooms of the lord,
was connected by bridge-like corridors with the other buildings - the lady's chamber, the
angling pavilion, the fountain house, and other characteristic structures. On three sides
of these buildings and galleries was the garden, in which there were necessarily a lake and
streams, with winding shore lines that touched the verandas of the various pavilions. In
the lake there was an islet reached by bridges with lacquered railings. The trees and
stones were placed so as to give the garden the effect of a landscape. The view of the
houses from the garden was also picturesque, for it offered the contrast of brown roofs,
grey walls and red railings, seen through the rich green of the trees and through clouds
of pink cherry blossoms or violet wisteria.8
The Genji Monogatari, or Tale of Genji, a long novel written at the beginning of the elev-
enth century by a lady of the court, gives realistic descriptions of the court life of the time;
though the novel is fiction, it serves to give pictures of contemporary life. Here we see the
palace intrigues, the life of the "refined and effeminate 'moon lords' . . and the charming and
intelligent court ladies." There is very little in this long novel to show that other people
existed, outside the court circle. The lack of mention of other classes of the people is sig
nificant. One of the few comments on the life of the people is made in a description of the life
of the hero Genji in exile in the country, where he lived in rustic style. A friend from the
court visited him.

Of this period as a whole, Sir George Sansom says:
If many of the activities of this age were artificial to the point of silliness, they
did, we must remember, express a culture remarkable, probably unique, in that it was al-
most entirely aesthetic. Into the remoter origins of this phenomenon we will not inquire,
but its immediate reasons are plain. For some centuries past Japan had been peaceful and
undisturbed, except by a little frontier fighting and brief factional quarrels that did
not check the smooth flow of metropolitan life. She had been supplied with a religion, a
philosophy, a theory of the state, all ready-made; and since she had no criterion by which
to judge these gifts she accepted them on the whole without reserve. She might have been
more critical or more uncertain had she known other civilizations, but she was isolated,
and her communication with the outside world was scanty and irregular. Though her rulers
were dominated by foreign ideas, as a country she never suffered a violent cultural inva-
sion and the first hostile descent upon her shores of any consequence was the Mongol at-
tack of 1274. The Chinese did not force their customs on her, and she was never stimu-
lated by close contact with other peoples, whereas the history of the rest of Asia and
Europe is one long record of the marching and mingling of tribes and nations.
Therefore - and this is true in greater or less degree of subsequent times - the Jap-
anese of the Heian epoch tended to treat each element of their imported culture as if it
were something integrated and perfected. Yet, while they did not question the perfection
of the whole, for they were acute observers rather than r estless critics, their temper and
their circumstances modified its parts and changed its very essence. So the terms of In-
dian metaphysics became a kind of fashionable jargon, Buddhist rites a spectacle, Chinese
poetry an intellectual game. We might almost summarize by saying that religion became an
art and art a religion. Certainly what most occupied the thoughts of the Heian courtiers
were ceremonies, costumes, elegant pastimes like verse-making and amorous intrigue con-
ducted according to rules. Perhaps most important of all, because it entered into all,
was the art of penmanship. These were the subjects of their literature and in these they
achieved a prodigious virtuosity. Let it be added that, if they transformed whatever they
borrowed and sometimes refined away its essence, they and their descendants also rejected
what was gross and cruel.13
As in the Nara period, art in the Heian period was not a thin and artificial affair. A
characteristic way of painting distinguished the art expression of this time. Scrolls, full of
realism and action, were painted to illustrate, for example, the Tale of Genji.
But what about the state of affairs in the country at large, while the Heian courtiers were
living their lives in pleasant seclusion, occupied with art and literature, manners, ceremonies,
rites and costume?
The legislation of the early Heian period is concerned to an amazing extent with mat-
ters of ritual and etiquette, and it is easy to see that the seclusion of the sovereign
and his constant preoccupation with details of dress and deportment made 1t difficult, 1f
not impossible, for even the strongest-minded ruler to comprehend, much less to cope with,
the urgent problems of government. . . Busy with such matters, occupied for many days of
the year with elaborate rites, the emperor and his ministers could not, if they would, pay
attention to the serious questions, both political and economic, which had begun to arise
as soon as the centralized state had begun to develop. . . They could not fail to be aware

authority. The breakdown of the system of taxation, as administered by greedy provincial
officials, was plain from the emptiness of the imperial chest. The weakness of the mili-
tary authority was plain from the incursions of the Ainu and the ravages of pirates. The
quarrels and rivalries of the great families were only too apparent from the plots and
counterplots which centered around the throne and the succession. But, obvious as were
these abuses, there is little sign of constructive policy to remove them.14
The lords of adjoining manors did not live peacefully and it was necessary for each lord to
have his own troops to protect his estate. Some peasant families proved to be better fighters
than others and the sons of these families became warriors in the troops attached to the clan.
All warriors were exempt from taxation. The fighting men of the northern districts bordering
the lands of the Ainu - those aboriginal inhabitants about whose origin little is known - had
considerable practice in warfare, for the Japanese desired the lands still controlled by the
Ainu. Thus, for one reason or another, a small privileged class of hereditary warriors arose,
the beginning of the special warrior class which was to be so important in feudal Japan. In
794, the commander of the armies fighting the Ainu was given the title of Barbarian-Subduing-
Generalissimo, or Sei-1-Tai-Shogun, the first time that this title, later to be used to desig-
nate the actual ruler of the country, was used. Thus at the very beginning of the Heian period
appeared signs of the changes which were to come much later.
Tax-free estates increased in size and in numbers. The Buddhist establishments, in spite
of decrees restricting the land they could hold, continued to gain possession of more and larger
estates - and these were tax-free. Even about Kyoto, where it was planned there should be no
powerful monasteries whose clergy might interfere with affairs at court, temples and monasteries
arose on every hill top. Many clergy were ambitious men who entered religious establishments in
order to obtain exempt land. Other men, seeking tax-free estates, took over hitherto undevel-
oped land. Small landholders, forced to bear the financial and labor obligations of the state,
tended to place their lands in the hands of some exempt institution or person, and to work their
share of the land on some sort of payment basis which was less oppressive.
As power and privilege passed into relatively few hands, the elaborate bureaucratic govern-
ment attempted under the Taikwa Reforms broke down. At court, the regent who was the mouthpiece
for the emperor came to conduct most of the business of the state. Throughout the Heian period,
the real ruler of the country was this regent, who was always a member of the Fujiwara family.
Thus the highest office in the state became virtually hereditary.
Over against this tendency to centralize control in the hands of one family, were decen-
tralizing tendencies which, combined with economic weakness, were to tear the whole fabric of
government apart. The numerous offspring of the imperial house, all of whom could not be accom-
modated at court, moved to outer provinces which they had been given, and founded new families.
In this manner the Taira and Minamoto clans, and the lesser families related to them, originated.
Gradually the daimyo or "great names" emerged, living on tax-free lands, and a potential threat
to the Fujiwara, particularly since these ambitious daimyo had in their service numbers of here-
ditary warriors while the Fujiwara at the court were not themselves a warlike clan.
The lesser nobility, who could very infrequently obtain rank high enough to enable them to
hold high offices of staie, tended to devote themselves to art, or to enter the military profes-
sion, which, toward the end of the Heian period, had become important. The lowest classes of
the people, including free persons and slaves, gradually merged into one. The distinction be-
tween privileged and unprivileged classes was much more marked than any distinctions between
different groups in the lower orders of society.

-20-
Of the actual life of the people, there is little record. Some idea of their reactions
may be implied from their response to the widespread and popular teaching of a new interpreta-
tion of Buddhism.
The times were evidently ripe for a new movement in religion. A monk named Kuya, who
had preached in the streets of Kyoto during an epidemic in 951, spent most of his life
travelling about Japan, teaching the people to invoke the name of Buddha, so that he was
known as the Saint of the Market Place. These open-air meetings were clearly of a revi-
valist nature, and seem to indicate that there was now room for some popular evangel which
would afford an easy outlet for religious emotion, some satisfying but not exacting faith.
It was a marked characteristic of the Japanese of this period (a characteristic which
shows itself in their earliest native beliefs and which, some think, time has not alto-
gether eliminated) that they were not tortured by a sense of sin, not racked by a desire
to solve the problem of Good and Evil. There was little of the cruel puritanical strain
in them and little of that restless spirit of doubt and inquiry which has driven other
peoples either to seek refuge in quietism or to escape from their thoughts by incessant
activity. They were impressionable and lively, but without metaphysical bent. Being im-
presstonable, they were quick to feel the scrrows and delusions of earthly life, readily
believing those Buddhist preachers who taught 1ts emptiness and dwelt on the terrors of
hell and the glories of paradise. Being lively, they could live happily in the moment,
and pass with an easy reaction from fear of suffering to hope of bliss.is
In the latter years of the Heian period, when disorder marked the troubled times, the idea
of faith as a means of salvation had wide popular appeal. The believer found consolation in the
teaching that if he repeated the name of Buddha, in simple faith, he might hope to enter para-
dise and in that distant "pure land" receive the enlightenment he could not attain in this world.
This interpretation of Buddhism was the one which had the greatest influence on the lives of the
masses.
The last century of the Heian period, from, roughly speaking, the middle of the eleventh
century almost to the end of the twelfth century, was marked by struggles of various types. The
emperor tried to escape the dominance of the Fujiwara. When the Fujiwara were threatened by the
militant clergy about Kyoto, they had to ask assistance from one of the great military families
of the outlying districts, and these, in turn, did not give help without asking a price and gain-
ing power. Both the Taira and the Minamoto families were attempting to increase their holdings
and their power. The rivalry between the Taira and the Minamoto culminated in warfare which
went on for years (1l59-ll85). At first the Taira were victorious, but later under Yoritomo the
Minamoto finally subdued their rivals, in 1185, and inaugurated (in l192) the series of military
dictatorships, the shogunates, which were not abolished until 1867.
Thus, out of the interactions of imported Chinese governmental forms and the indigenous so-
cial structure of ancient Japan, military feudalism began to emerge with all its emphasis on the
prestige of warriors - a form of society and of thought which took deep root in Japan, and which
was quite unlike anything existing in China.
