Chapter 3
SOCIAL CHANGES DURING THE GROWTH OF MILITARY FEUDALISM
(End of Twelfth Century to BegInnIng of Seventeenth)
When Minamoto Yoritomo conquered the Taira, and as shogun set up his capital at Kamakura,
military feudalism was established in Japan and many institutions and customs were overturned.
A contemporary observer, Kamo Chomei, described the time of change and trouble.
"During the forty years or so I have lived since I began to understand the meaning of
things," Chomei wrote, "I have seen not a few strange happenings." He describes a fire which
destroyed a large part of the capital in l175 A.D., a typhoon which wrecked many homes, the re-
moval of the capital, and the ruinous state of the buildings remaining. "And those mansions
that stood so proudly side by side from day to day became more ruinous. Many were broken up
and floated down the river Yodo, while their pleasure grounds were turned to rice fields. And
the fashions changed also in those days, so that everyone came to ride on horseback, while the
more dignified ox-car was quite forsaken. And everybody was scrambling to get land by the
Western Sea and none cared for manors in the north and east." He visited the new capital (at
Kamakura), and observed the unsettled feeling of the people, the unfinished state of the build-
ings. "So the old Capital was already a waste and the new one not yet made," he wrote. "Every-
one felt as unsettled as drifting clouds. And the natives of the place were full of complaints
over losing their land, while the new inhabitants grumbled at the difficulty of building on such
a site. And of the people one met in the streets those who ought to have been riding in car-
riages were on horseback and those who usually wore court costume were in military surcoats.
The whole atmosphere of the Capital was altered and they looked like a lot of country samurai.
And those who said that these changes were a portent of some civil disturbances seemed to be not
without reason, for as time went on things became more and more unquiet and there was a feeling
of unrest everywhere." He went on to describe the growing poverty of the people, and then the
pestilence which killed thousands so that the dead lay unburied by the roadsides. To these mis-
eries were added the destruction and suffering caused by an earthquake. All of these experi-
ences led Chomei to reflect upon the "fleeting evanescent nature of man and his habitation," and
to conclude that the less he possessed, the less would be his misfortunes and cares. So, at
sixty, he retired to the mountains where he lived alone, in a hut ten feet square. "Since I for-
sook the world and broke off all its ties, I have felt neither fear nor resentment. I commit my
life to fate without special wish to live or desire to die. Like a drifting cloud I rely on
none and have no attachments. My only luxury is a sound sleep and all I look forward to is the
beauty of the changing seasons." 1
Many people retired, as Kamo Chomei did, and left the difficult world of affairs for monas-
teries or other retreats. In general, however, it appears that the lords and their retainers
took the opportunity of profiting by the feudal society developing in Japan.
We often think of feudalism as an ordered hierarchy of landholders who owe final fealty to
a king, and to whom lesser landholders give submission in return for protection. Actually, how-
ever, except in countries where supreme control is gained by conquest - as in England under the
Normans - the relationships are not quite so ordered and simple, because when feudal loyalties
and the whole feudal system grow out of existing conditions many other relationships cut across
the feudal organization. Though the Minamoto under Yoritomo became the most powerful family in
all Japan, and though they gained this position through fighting, nevertheless it cannot be said
1. Extracts taken from Sadler, A. L., The Ten Foot Square Hut, Angus and Robertson Limited,
Sydney, 1928.

=== Page 53 === (confidence 0.99)
-22-
that Japanese feudalism owed its characteristic features to imposition through conquest. Con-
sequently, there were many conflicting elements in the growing feudalism of Japan, which arose
out of changes gradually developed within the Japanese social and economic structure, and which
necessarily affected the life of the people.
In a society which does not have a money economy - and this was the situation in Japan
throughout almost the whole of the period we are considering - and in which the aristocratic
principle is strong, two factors are of immense importance. One is concerned with the land-
holding system in which the wealth of the country is centered, and which involves the life of
the cultivators. The other is connected with the various means by which the power and strength
of the lord are maintained. It is obvious that there is a close relationship between these, for
the military feudal lord, if he is to have any power at all, must have warriors; he must draw
income from the cultivators, and he must be able to command the loyal service of both cultivator
and warrior. If the farmer is fixed to the soil, he must make all the payments, in service and
in kind, which are demanded from him, but if he is not, then he may seek the protection of a
less oppressive lord. In Japan, through the period of the growth of feudalism, the farmer was
not attached to the soil. Consequently, the lord was obliged to find some way to command his
service. Ore method used was the emphasis on traditional clan loyalties; this was one of the
chief reliances of the early lords of Kamakura, the Minamoto, who established their capital not
in Kycto, but on their own estates in oastern Japan, far from the diversions and aesthetic ac-
tivities of Kyoto. We find a literary interpretation of these loyalties in the stirring tales
of the feudal wars written in the thirteenth century. These stories may contain an element of
fiction, but they nevertheless gave to later generations the spirit of feudal 1deals. The
Gempei Seisuiki, for example, tells of the struggle between Yoritomo and the Taira, and of his
later conflict with his half-brother Yoshitsune. Yoritomo was jealous of his brother and deter-
mined to capture and kill him. The plight of the fleeing Yoshitsune seemed hopeless when Sato
Tadanobu, one of his warriors, said:
"I will stay here as my lord Yoshitsune. When my arrows are exhausted then I will
commit harakir1, and the start given will ensure our lord's safety."
Tears stood in Yoshitsune's eyes. He felt how much he owed to these brave fellows,
to any one of whom his brother would have given a large fief as a reward for desertion...
"When I think of your brother's death in my stead at Yashima, I cannot endure the idea
of such a sacrifice."
"Without him I cannot face my father," replied Tadanobu, "he would ask me what I had
done and will be only too pleased if I die fighting for my lord."
Then Benkei (another follower) said, "Tadanobu is a true samurai. We are all ready
to die for our lord. There is no taking the backward road. Will our lord graciously per-
mit Tadanobu to carry out his plan?"
"Call yourself Yoshitsune," was the latter's reply to Tadanobu, "and so tell the
Judges of Hell when they ask your name. We will exchange armour." He handed over to
Tadanobu his armour sewn with red thread, his helmet with the gold frontlet and white
stars in sixty-four places, and with the shihi (lion-leopard) surmounting it. Then he
gave him his sword Kimi-Banzai-no-Tomonari (Everlasting-Royal-Reign forged by Tomonari).
Said Tadanobu, "I would only ask that someone would don my armour. It is that of
Tsuginobu, which he wore at Yashima."
"It shall be I," said Yoshitsune. "Never has man been surrounded by men of stronger
faith than these."
Tadanobu dropped to the ground at his lord's feet. "My brother in his grave will
turn with joy."
Benkei hastened the departure. "Put on your sandals backward, so that our trail
will look as if we were going in the opposite direction." Then they took their leave of

-23-
Tadanobu. Sadly he watched them, and tears came into his eyes at the idea of never seeing
his lord again.2
One has only to compare this with the Tale of Genji or with the Pillow-Book of Sei Shonagon,
to be aware of a new atmosphere of life, a new set of ideals of behavior. These ideals were of
immense influence and significance, particularly in time of such an emergency as Yoshitsune and
his followers faced, but they could scarcely supply all the motives which would keep the mass of
the people contented and loyal when there was a degree of peace - or even when there was not.
Moreover, the clan system - that loose organization of numbers of people most of whom are re-
lated by blood, broke down under pressure of increasing numbers, conflicting interests, and
civil war. Out of it emerged the family system, involving single households ruled by the head
of the household and owing fealty to feudal lords unrelated by blood. Also, during the many
years of civil war, individual daimyo were obliged to control most of the affairs of their
estates, since there was no strong central government to which administrative matters could be
referred. Daimyo exercised increasing control over the households, determining whom retainers
should marry, for example; but since allegiance could be transferred to another daimyo, provided
the living conditions were intolerable, the ambitious lords of Japan were obliged to pay some
attention to the prosperity of their vassals in order to have wealth and power. The real basis
of Japanese feudalism was not ideals of feudal loyalties, but economic conditions, which varied
through the centuries.
These economic conditions, as we have seen, were primarily tied up with the landholding
system, and it is necessary to have some notion of the peculiar system of Japan, in order to see
how the lives of the people were affected. Rice, the chief crop, was cultivated by individual
farmers working small plots of land. These farmers did not own their fields; they had the right
to use the land. Numbers of other people possessed rights in the same plots of land - for ex-
ample, the bailiffs who managed several holdings for another person, or the great family which
guaranteed protection to a large number of people. The highest overlord did not necessarily re-
ceive the largest income from his rights. Rights were hereditary possessions, to be passed on
to numerous heirs and sometimes, in the process, to come into the hands of rival overlords. The
whole system was very complicated, and Yoritomo, the first lord of Kamakura, did not attempt to
change existing rights; he simply added new rights to tho list, the rights owned by his own
military administrative officials. These men were in a position to extend their authority and
they founded the ambitious new families which were later to threaten Kamakura. The great es-
tates of conquered lords were added to the Minamoto holdings - the lands of the conquered Taira
alone included one third of the lands of Japan. These confiscated properties were given to
Minamoto vassals, but even in this case all existing rights in the land did not come into the
hands of the new overlords. The samura1, the warriors attached to the clan who had figured so
prominently in the civil warfare and who had emerged from the civil wars as a recognized class,
were sometimes settled on the land, sometimes confirmed in any rights to which they laid claim,
and sometimes given new rights to draw income from land they did not cultivate. The final sanc-
tion for landholding appears to have been force. There seems to have been little discussion
about who actually owned the land but, instead, a recognition of the fact that the strongest
could dispose of it as theirs.
The inheritance of undivided estates (including land rights) by one son was not established
at this time. The feudal lord of Japan followed the old clan custom of nominating his heir, or
heirs, and cf dividing his estates among his numerous progeny. Since polygamy was practiced,

Vo1. II, pp. 231-232.

=== Page 55 === (confidence 0.99)
-24-
there were many claimants to property, and at this time, if the eldest son were passed over, he
could legally demand but one fifth of an estate. The imperial succession might also be a matter
of dispute - as it has very frequently been in the past - for the emperor nominated his succes-
sor. The Fujiwara had generally managed to control such nominations by intrigue; now, since the
military was influential, disputes over the succession were more apt to be marked by war than
they had been. Not until after the strong Kamakura government had become weakened, and had
finally fallen, and years of civil war had disrupted the country, was the whole inheritance cus-
tom changed.
The first lord of Kamakura was a warrior, the leader of warriors. He had no sympathy with
the aesthetic activities of Kyoto. Costume and etiquette held a minor position in the stern
military regime of early Kamakura, though they were more valued later in the period. The new
government was strict; while it expressed no particular interest in the welfare of the people,
it dispensed a certain rough justice, and let the people know where they stood. Any cultivator
who was not in debt was permitted to move from his fields, and a peasant might sell his rights
in the land, while no other person was allowed to dispose of his own rights except by bequest.
The payments required of the farmer were fixed so that a greedy overlord might not unduly op-
press him.
In dispensing justice, the Minamoto house law, a body of regulations regarding relation-
ships between the many members of the clan, was found convenient because it fitted the situation
of the time. Consequently, 1t was applied to larger groups, and by other families, and it came
to take the place of the elaborate codes of law worked out earlier. This house law, for ex-
ample, dealt with inheritance regulations. It is interesting to note that at this time women
were permitted to inherit property, estates, and land rights, and to name their heirs; they were
even allowed to adopt an heir. While these laws appear liberal, in them may be found one cause
for the chaotic social and political situations which developed in Japan, because they led to a
continued shifting of power, and to disputes and difficulties.
Even these few details concerning the Kamakura government make it plain that the men who
managed it followed no imported theory, but, instead, attempted to work out their own solutions
for problems as they arose. The new government followed the type of organization which had
grown up in connection with the management of Japanese manors, rather than copying forms devel-
oped in China. Consequently, the developments of the Kamakura period resulted not from con-
flicts between imported and indigenous ideas and institutions, but from the strengths and weak-
nesses within the Japanese situation. The government did not long retain its early stern sim-
plicity. Hojo regents, members of the Taira family, ruled for Yoritomo's sons and the later
heirs to the shogunate. The shogun lived secluded in their Kamakura palace, just as the em-
peror lived secluded in Kyoto. However, for over a hundred years (Kamakura fell in 1333) while
life at Kamakura lacked the romantic aestheticism of the Heian court, it possessed a vitality
of its own.
We have already referred to the Gempei Seisuiki and similar tales as being literary inter-
pretations of the ideals of behavior which were a part of this vitality. In the brief illustra-
tion already quoted the mention of Yoshitsune's sword is significant, for it gives an idea of
the way in which swords were personified and treasured, and suggests the manner in which crafts-
manship played 1ts part in the life of the time. Like the legendary Excalibur, Japanese swords
of this period were often credited with supernatural powers. Behind all this lay the art of the
sword-makers, for at this time sword-making was an art. It is said that for strength and cut-
ting edge, the Japanese swords of the thirteenth century have never been surpassed anywhere in
the world. Moreover,

-25-
As regards the sword, it was honored in Japan to such a degree as to be considered
the soul of the warrior and the token of his self-respect. Hence the manufacture of
swords was viewed as a holy profession. In the workshops cleanliness was an essential,
the workmen wore fresh garments and were required to fast and to undergo rites of purifi-
cation.3
Stories in present-day government school readers recall the traditions and skill of the sword-
maker. For example, in a story called The Blacksmith, the old blacksmith speaks:
"Nowadays I just work at making kitchen knives, nails, and such things, but there was
a time when I was fairly well-known as a swordsmith. I don't know how many dozen broad-
swords and short-swords I made when I was young. The sword is the soul of the samurai,
they say, and for that reason when forging a sword one nust have the body clean and the
mind perfectly composed."
The Dictionary of Japanese Biography gives some light on the importance of the sword-maker.
About ten per cent of the material in this work deals with sword-makers, who make one of the few
groups for which genealogical tables are given, and the only group placed in a section by itself.
The wars and conflicts which led to the establishment of the Kamakura government offered
inspiration not only to writers and craftsmen, but also to the painters of the twelfth and thir-
teenth centuries. One of these, Keion, painted extraordinary battle pictures and turbulent
scenes full of movement and action. Laurence Binyon, the well-known critic, describes his work:
In his own way Keion is the greatest of Japanese draughtsmen. At a time Kiyomor1,
the Taira chief, was absent from Kyoto, the Minamoto invaded the court and set the palace
on fire, hoping to seize in their turn the sacred person of the Emperor. Disguised as a
woman, the Emperor was smuggled into an ox-cart. Keion has painted the scene, when a
group of armed Minamoto, arriving in the courtyard, surround the ox-cart; one holds up a
smoking torch, others roughly pull aside the curtains of the hood and exclaim with disap-
pointed anger at finding only a woman. The men are alive; we can hear the stamp of their
feet; we can see their swift and menacing gestures. But the full measure of Keion's power
1s seen rather in another scene from the Boston scroll, the "Flight of the Court." What a
fury of fear, what a riot of speed, in the headlong flight of the men, in the mad race of
the ox-carts, some of which are overturned in the wild onrush! 4
The spirit of the age was reflected in certain developments in Buddhism. Nichiren, who
violently attacked all other sects, and who emphasized nationalism, sounded a new note of defi-
ance, of missionary zeal, of national spirit, even of intolerance. On the other hand, the "Pure
Land" teachings, so popular at the end of the Heian period, spread more widely among the people.
Zen Buddhism, brought from China, attracted the warriors. It stressed self-reliance, self-exami-
nation, and self-mastery, as means of enlightenment; it lacked the simple emotional appeal of
the "Pure Land" sect, and for that reason found a following among the warriors who had to depend
upon their own efforts in battle and who felt a kinship with the same idea applied in religion.
These elements, rather than the contemplative side of Zen teachings, won the warriors.
Zen priests reintroduced tea from China. Tea was believed to be a quieting drink and it
was used by those who practiced Zen meditation. Since the practice of drinking tea creates a
need for appropriate cups, porcelain manufacture, as well as trade in tea and porcelain, was
stimulated - just as it was much later when Europe obtained tea from China and tea drinking be-
came fashionable. In Japan, the elaborate tea-cult developed, because of the connection between
tea drinking and religious meditation. The tea-cult reached its height somewhat later, but it
may be described here:
Through the spread of Zen practice, tea-drinking became a necessary part of the daily
life, and gatherings in specially constructed tea rooms were organized by devotees of Zen.

The room was tiny and simple, like a primitive hut or a hermitage in the forest. There
was no other decoration than a single painting or example of calligraphy hanging in an
alcove and a flower in the same recess. Everywhere there was severe simplicity and
purity of taste. This calm and serene mood of the tea room came to permeate Japanese
life, and restrained and refined even the luxurious life of military grandees. . The
tea room was above the ordinary laws of social distinction, for it was retreat from all
worldly cares and troubles. There a military ruler or a great lord sat on the same simple
matting with men of inferior rank, and the subject of their talk was drawn from regions
beyond the routine of daily life. They spoke of the "wind and the moon," the "air and
the stream," or any other subjects that would help to purify and elevate the mind.5
All this sophisticated simplicity seems a long way from the bare simplicity of warlike
Kamakura, and it was. It was a later development, but the beginnings lay in the Kamakura period
when regents exercised the power and the puppet shogun lived in luxury and retirement. To the
shogun's court in Kamakura came some members of the Kyoto circle; and many samura1, whose famf-
1ies had increased but whose lands had not increased proportionately, joined the shogun's court
where well-paying positions were numerous. Members of the warrior class were not uninfluenced
by this contact with Kyoto ideas and learning, introduced to Kamakura by courtiers from Kyoto.
However much the warriors affected to despise luxury and aestheticism, they were human enough to
be attracted by it. A number of influences broke down the narrow standards of the warriors and
made it possible for them to enjoy the sophisticated simplicity of the tea-cult.
Changes in the warrior class and in the standards of life at Kamakura helped to bring about
the downfall of the Kamakura government, but many other factors were more important. The con-
trol of the country by regents for a shogun, supposed to represent the emperor, made government
increasingly cumbersome. It was tending to break down of its own weight, as it were, when twice
in the thirteenth century the Mongols attacked Japan. In the history of the Mongols this was
but one of their military enterprises which did not succeed, but in the history of Japan it was
a tremendous thing, straining all the resources of the country and leaving it weakened and dis-
rupted. A costly defensive war gave the lords of Kamakura no new lands with which to reward
their followers, and both lay nobility and clergy demanded payments for their efforts in keeping
the invaders from conquering Japan. It was impossible for the Hojo regents, who were not Mina-
moto, to appeal to clan loyalties, and by this time even the shogun was not a Minamoto. The
emperor seized the opportunity to attempt to do away with the military shogunate and to re-es-
tablish civil government directly under him. Contending elements gathered their forces; in 1333
Kamakura was burned and the Kamakura government came to an end.
The ambitious strove to make the most out of the fall of Kamakura. The emperor failed in
his attempt to re-establish civil government; military feudalism was entirely too strongly en-
trenched for any such effort to be successful. From 1336 to 1392 there were two emperors, one
in the north and one in the south. A member of the Ashikaga family was shogun, appointed by
one of the contending emperors. The whole period of disorder was marked by a series of private
wars between lords contending for lands and power.
Affairs throughout the country were so confused that the daimyo began to settle many mat-
ters previously referred to Kamakura. Weaker lords "commended" themselves to the more powerful,
in order to obtain a degree of security. In these days of civil war, it was a poor policy to
divide estates, or to allow women to be the heads of families; hence women were no longer per-
mitted to inherit, and the chief share of an inheritance went to one son, the individual most
able to manage fighting men. The whole basis of Japanese society was shifted.
The ideal of the time was the maintenance of the family, the preservation of its
property and the enhancement of its prestige; and by family is here meant not the prolif-

erating clan but the small household. . Supreme over each group was a powerful warrior,
usually the constable of a province, and attached to him for protection were less power-
ful families holding land within the territory which he ruled, but not necessarily re-
lated to him or to one another. The business of the overlord was to consolidate his
power for offense and defense against other overlords, by conserving the strength of each
family unit in his domain while preventing its use in any combination unfavourable to
himself. The business of the lesser warrior was to secure the prosperity and the continu-
ance of his own family. So we find on the one hand constant interference by the overlord
in the family affairs of his vassals, and on the other hand a sacrifice of the individual
to the interests of the family. . . Particular care was taken to ensure that land or
rights should not, through adoption or marriage, fall into the hands of a vassal of an-
other lord. A watchful eye was kept upon the marriages not only of knights and their
sons and daughters, but also of the better class of peasants and craftsmen, so that the
lord should not lose their land or their service to another fief. The members of a fam-
ily depended even for sustenance upon the head of the house and must obey him, whether he
was their father or their brother or even an adopted stranger.
The development of the family as an economic and social unit so profoundly influenced
Japanese life that the civil code now in force embodies certain survivals of medieval no-
tions as to property and succession. The new constitution of society made it the chief
duty of man to consider first not his own individual interests, but those of his house.
It thus placed high in the scale of virtues obedience, patience, and sacrifice; it encour-
aged a habit of respect for age and authority, of courtesy in speech and demeanor; and it
stimulated the holder of the name to keep 1t unsullied. These ideals of conduct were not,
of course, new, for they grew naturally out of ancient beliefs and customs; but feudalism
tended always to single out for emphasis those conceptions of morality which seemed to
contribute to its own survival, and to neglect, 1f not to discourage, all others. Its
code, though strict, was therefore narrow. Since it aimed at preserving an economic unit,
its basis was in essence material rather than ethical . . . Since the interests of the
family are paramount, the movement of its individual members is fettered, and the most
trivial decision can be reached only after prolonged consultation and discussion. A piti-
less social pressure strangles independence of thought and behaviour, makes servants of
younger sons and chattels of women. Only the stimulus of warfare, which needs quick judg-
ment and bold action, could keep suon a system from decay.6
Under this system, and in conditions of warfare, the people suffered much. The security
which they had experienced under the Kamakura government was shattered. Daimyo who managed al-
most all the affairs on their estates could exact irregular payments from the people. Contend-
ing forces destroyed homes and crops. Many peasants left their fields to join armies or to be-
come brigands. The economic basis of life was so disrupted that it became necessary for indi-
vidual lords to attempt to make better conditions for the people.
While private war was being waged over Japan, from the court of the southern emperor came a
document invoking the national tradition, and seeking to gain popular support against the Ashi-
kaga regime on the basis of this argument:
Great Yamato 1s a divine country. It is only our land whose foundations were first
laid by the divine ancestor. It alone has been transmitted by the Sun-Goddess to a long
line of her descendants. There is nothing like this in foreign countries. Therefore it
is called the divine land. . . It is only our country, which from the time when the heav-
ens and earth were first unfolded has preserved the succession to the throne intact in one
single family. Even when, as sometimes naturally happened, it descended to a lateral
branch, it was held according to just principles. This shows that the oath of the gods
(to preserve the succession) is ever renewed in a way which distinguishes Japan from all
other countries. . It 1s the duty of every man born on the Imperial soil to yield devoted
loyalty to his Sovereign, even to the sacrifice of his own life.7
This particular announcement went unheeded in the feudal warfare of the time when it was
issued, but these ideas had great influence much later, when Japanese thinkers were formulating
national philosophies in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and when the emperor was re-
stored in 1868. Because of the many times they have been repeated since then, these words have
a familiar ring.

The Ashikaga, with their retinues and followers, settled in Kyoto where they built elab-
After the succession dispute was settled in 1392, and when the lords of Japan came to desire
larger revenues to support them in their new life of luxury, they not only attempted to secure
increased revenues from their lands, but they also turned to trade with China as a source of
profit. Japanese swords and raw materials were shipped to China and exchanged for goods which
were sold in Japan for two or three hundred times as much as they had cost. Seaport towns and
merchants flourished, and the lords, the monasteries, and the shogun who backed the China trade
reaped huge profits, which, however, did not reach the common people who suffered from the de-
mands made by public officials and landlords. About l425, local riots against oppressions began
to take place. In l467, a civil war began which lasted ten years, and which was particularly
destructive. Finally, in 149l, the whole of Japan was swept by war which continued for a century,
and of which perhaps the chief cause lay in the fact that neither shogun nor emperor possessed
enough power to hold the lesser lords in check, or to provide for the economic security of the
people. The century of civil war was a time when all the lords of Japan fought for supremacy,
lands, and wealth.
This long war could not be carried on without revenues and food. Consequently, the trade
with China continued during most of the period, and prosperity was by no means unknown. More-
over, rice fields do not form a convenient battle ground, and therefore rural economy was not so
disrupted as one might expect. The great families, however, were almost all wiped out. Only
the strongest survived, and obscure men of ability rose to positions of power. Of these the most
famous were Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu, all of whom rose to power dur-
ing the latter part of the sixteenth century.
Nobunaga, the son of a small rural lord, managed to make himself the most powerful war lord,
and to conquer about half of Japan. Hideyoshi, at first a common soldier in Nobunaga's armies,
then a general, followed Nobunaga. Although he never obtained the shogun's rank, he became a
military dictator and succeeded in subduing the portion of the country which Nobunaga had not
conquered. In 1592, he sent an expedition against China by way of Korea, and in 1597 another
expedition to Korea. Both were unsuccessful, but the fact that they were undertaken shows the
expansive ambition of the man, arising perhaps from his meteoric career, and from the circum-
stances which could make such a career possible.
In the latter years of the sixteenth century, Japan was in a ferment. Portuguese ships had
come to Nagasaki,on the 1sland of Kyushu. Japan was interested in extending her foreign trade and
new foreign goods were fashionable. Portuguese Jesuits had arrived; Japan was not opposed to a
new religion - provided it did not have political effects; but it became apparent that European
traders and European missionaries were not unconnected with European politics. However, the
Jesuit missions obtained converts among the lowly as well as among the great of the land, and
the new religion spread, particularly in Kyushu to which the Portuguese had first come. Fire-
arms had been brought from Europe but they had not been widely used. The Japanese preferred
their traditional swords, although they built great feudal castles whose defenses had some ref-
erence to the effect of firearms. Hideyoshi, for example, caused the huge fortress of Osaka to
be constructed in a very short time; 1t is said that he used the labor of 3o0,ooo people to get
this castle finished as he desired. The patient people of Japan were not unaffected by the rest-
less spirit of the time, and by the fact that the growing prosperity of the ruling classes was
not, to any extent, reaching their lives.
Hideyoshi, anxious to consolidate his own power and to prevent other obscure men from ris-
ing to threaten him, forbade samurai to transfer allegiance from one lord to another - a custom

=== Page 60 === (confidence 0.99)
-29-
which had been frequent in the years of warfare and shifting control. Farmers were forbidden
to leave their fields, and subordinates to leave their place of employment without the lord's
permission. As we know, lords had long possessed the right to interfere in the family affairs
of their vassals; now they controlled the persons of their retainers who could not, as they had
done. seek the protection of another lord if they were dissatisfied where they were. To fix the
people more firmly in their niches, landholders were forbidden to protect wanderers. Farmers
were obliged to surrender their weapons; no one but a samurai might wear the warrior's swords.
In the early Kamakura days, the samurai often was, in the intervals between wars, a peasant cul-
tivating the soil; the many years of civil war had helped to break this condition down, but now
legislation separated samurai from peasant. Hideyoshi also began to make laws restricting the
spread of the new religion, since he observed that not only were the foreign churchmen ambi-
tious, but that also Japanese Christian lords might form a combination threatening to him, be-
cause of their divided loyalties.
Before Hideyoshi's legislation had gone very far, he died, and there was war over the ques-
tion of succession. Ieyasu conquered Hideyoshi's son and in 1603 was appointed shogun, (being
descended from the Minamoto he was eligible for this post). He was the first of the Tokugawa
shogun who ruled the country until after the arrival of Commodore Perry.
Two lines of action were open to Ieyasu. He could fall in with the changing spirit of the
times and cope with the new problems of a Japan which was taking its place in the world with
which it had come in contact. Or he could follow the example already set by Hideyoshi with re-
gard to expelling foreigners and regulating Japanese life. He chose the latter course in order
to keep his family in power indefinitely. When peace came under the Tokugawa, Hideyoshi's le-
gislation was supplemented by other regulations all tending to hold each man in his place and
each class apart from other classes. Much attention was given to the formal rules of conduct
which should be observed by the members of each class, in relation to each other, and to other
classes. Thus the feudal wars not only consolidated feudalism but led to the creation of formal
barriers within the feudal society. Any flexibility which had existed was wiped out, and a
static rule of life substituted.
Hideyoshi had begun to restrict foreign trade and religion; the Tokugawa shogun carried
this much further. They finally closed the doors of Japan to all but the Dutch, whom they per-
mitted in the port of Nagasak1; they forbade any Japanese to leave the country, and they caused
the Japanese Christians to be persecuted until the foreign sect was wiped out. Thus, as we
shall see, Ieyasu and his successors proceeded to attempt to set Japanese life in a rigid mold.
The restless and enterprising leaders of Japan, to whom new things had always been attractive
and welcome, were now cut off from new influences. A people who had been engaged in almost
constant warfare for centuries was now at peace. A nation whose economy had become dependent
to a large extent upon foreign trade, was forbidden to engage in such trade except in very small
and carefully regulated degree. All of these bonds were to endure for two hundred and fifty
years.

Chapter 4
THE YEARS OF SECLUSION
(Seventeenth Century to the Middle of the Nineteenth)
The Tokugawa shogun wished to make their own power secure. They attempted to create
stability by preventing change - but economic forces were too strong for them. In spite of
laws and regulations designed to keep the military feudalism of Japan intact, feudalism stead-
11y declined during the Tokugawa period, and each of the carefully compartmented classes of
Japanese society was affected. Formality was encouraged, to preserve unchanged a society which
was being steadily undermined by changing economic conditions. Even if Commodore Perry had not
visited Japan when he did and caused the country to open its doors to the hosts of new influ-
ences which resulted in great changes, there is little doubt but that the Tokugawa regime would
have gone down before economic pressures, and that economic forces alone would have destroyed
feudalism. The new influences entering Japan in the middle of the nineteenth century gave
direction to changes which were inevitable; they were by no means the sole cause.
In their desire to make themselves secure, and to create stability in Japan, the Tokugawa
had first to deal with the daimyo, who numbered about two hundred and fifty. They kept the
great lords content by permitting them to receive large incomes and to continue to administer
their estates. The people were required to act with the utmost servility toward the daimyo.
When a daimyo passed, everyone knelt - beside the road, in the fields, in the streets. Issa,
a peasant-born poet, gives glimpses of the way in which the people viewed the lordly ways of
the daimyo. For example:
Just bent on viewing cherries when - "On your knees, on your knees." (That is to say,
some daimyo has come riding past and all the common people have had their pleasure in-
terrupted to get down on their knees).1
Daimyo took precedence over other people, even in small matters. Issa gives an idea of a type
of situation which doubtless was not infrequent:
After being beaten, I learned it was the daimyo's chrysanthemum. (That is to say, all
competition is futile when you're matched against a daimyo - even at a chrysanthemum
show.) 2
Issa gives the impression that the common people kneeling before the lords of Japan were not,
at heart, completely subservient. For example, he says:
A kotatsu, from which to watch a daimyo soaked to the skin. (A kotatsu is a small stove.
Here Issa pictures himself, warm and comfortable, in some inn perhaps, enjoying the sight
of the daimyo arriving "soaked to the skin.") 3
However, the people were required to show outward respect to the daimyo, and they did. Daimyo
made contented with large incomes, estates, and prestige, might have threatened the Tokugawa,
so it was ordered that every great daimyo spend part of each year in Yedo (the present Tokyo
and the Tokugawa capital). When the lord returned to his estates, he was required to leave his
family behind in Yedo. Daimyo thus had to spend a considerable part of their incomes on the
great retinues with which they travelled to Yedo, on the palaces they built in that city, and
on the servants they kept in both city and country establishments. And, of course, while they

might have been willing to spend everything they had left on war, they were not likely to plan
to attack the Tokugawa stronghold in which their own families lived. The Tokugawa plan made
the Japanese war lords into men of peace who did not threaten the Tokugawa rule.
In this situation, however, the attention of the privileged class of daimyo turned to new
wants and desires. The lord of Japan who could no longer go to war, but who could wring addi-
tional payments from the cultivators, could have more luxury goods - silk, embroideries, ivory
carvings, crystals, cloisonne, lacquer, porcelain. Thus the daimyo became extravagant, the
rural population was oppressed, and the city craftsmen and merchants prospered. The whole
metabolism of Japanese society was affected and eventually every class was involved in the
changes resulting from these conditions.
As the daimyo grew more extravagant and demanded more goods, trade increased; and as trade
increased, money began to take the place of rice as a medium of exchange. When the use of money
takes the place of payment in kind, one of the essential elements of feudalism disappears.
Feudal ideas, ideals, and customs may continue to exist, but the organization of society is modi-
fied. Merchants who manage the trade of a country come to handle its wealth - no longer ex-
pressed in terms of agricultural produce, but in the more complex medium of money. In Japan,
daimyo who wished ready funds to support them in the cities and to enable them to purchase the
articles they wanted frequently sold their share of the rice crop to the city merchants. The
price of rice was manipulated by city speculators, and consequently the daimyo, who despised
trade and affected to be entirely ignorant of it, usually profited little from their transac-
tions, while the traders became rich. Daimyo who were in financial difficulties began to "bor-
row" from their samurai, deducting from their salaries a portion of what they were supposed to
receive.
At this point, we should have some 1dea of the regulations governing the life of the samu-
ra1 after the feudal wars were ended under the Tokugawa. Deprived of their occupation as war-
riors, and long since detached from farming, the samura1 were given special privileges and regu-
lar Incomes. Active and vigorous men, they had little to do. Some of them managed estate af-
fairs for their daimyo, and many acted as local administrators, thus establishing a reputation
for executive ability, and gaining experience in government. Both of these were to be important
when many samurai were influential in the government after the downfall of the Tokugawa. How-
ever, under the Tokugawa, all the samurai could not be employed. Always wearing the two swords
which were the badge of their rank, many samurai were involved in frequent fights and brawls.
Early in the Tokugawa period, feudal traditions were revived to keep this potentially dangerous
group in check, and the old ideal of frugal living was again inculcated into the warriors. It
was hard for all the unemployed members of the samurai group to find complete satisfaction in
stern traditions. The masterless samurai, or ronin, were particularly difficult to control.
The most famous instance of this involves the forty-seven ronin who, in l7o3, took it upon
themselves to revenge their lord's death; after murdering the man they regarded as their enemy,
they gave themselves up and were ordered to commit harakiri. This exploit was made the basis
of one of the most popular plays and it still remains a favorite in Japan. The government,
which had to admit that under the feudal code the samurai had done no more than their duty,
nevertheless felt that the warriors must be kept from taking the law into their own hands. Af-
ter the forty-seven ronin had given themselves up, the argument was advanced that "Confucian
principles must be observed in the light of the law, and not interpreted by individuals at their
own fancy." Though this was the legal interpretation, it was not the popular one; the self-
sacrifice of the forty-seven heroes represented the popular conception of right action. When,
however, daimyo began to reduce the samurai's income, feudal loyalties became a little strained.
They were further weakened when samurai were reduced to d1smissing their followers, to accepting

commoners - for a price - as retainers, or to adopting - also for a price - the son of some
wealthy commoner. The traditional pride of family and connection which was a distinguishing
mark of Japanese feudalism was, to an extent, broken down by these developments. Divisions
appeared within the samurai class itself. Some warriors adhered with pride to all the strict
traditions of their caste; others voluntarily entered trade or the professions, and circum
stances made it impossible for still others to follow their own desires in this matter. An idea
of the dilemma facing many samurai at the end of the Tokugawa period is given in the words of a
famous Japanese when he dascribed his own father:
My father was a samurai (retainer) in the service of Okudaira, the daimyo (overlord)
of Nakatsu in the province of Buzen on the island of Kyushu. . My father was really a
scholar. And the scholars of the time, different from those of today, disdained to spend
any thought on money, or even to touch it. My father always longed for a secluded uncon-
taminated life with his books and noble philosophy of the ancient sages. Yet he was
forced to attend to the most worldly affairs, for as an overseer of a treasury, it was his
duty to associate with merchants, and to count money, and to negotiate the contraction of
debts for his lord. Sometimes when his lord was in difficulty, my father had to bargain
with the rich money-lenders like Kajimaya and Konoike of Osaka.
In this work he was unhappy, and so when it came to bringing up his children, he
tried, it seems to me, to give them what he thought was an ideal education. For instance,
he once sent them to a teacher for calligraphy and general education. The teacher lived
in the compound of the lord's storage office, but having some merchants' children among
his pupils, he naturally began to train them in numerals: "Two times two is four, two
times three is six," etc. This, today, seems a very ordinary thing to teach, tut when my
father heard this, he took his children away in a fury.
"It is abominable," he exclaimed, "that innocent children should be taught to use
numbers - the instrument of merchants. There is no telling what the teacher may do
next.. ."
One may easily see that he was a very strict father who never compromised on what he
felt was just. From the writings he left, I know that he was a disciple of Confucianism
to the very heart. Among the great scholars on Chinese philosophy, my father had a par-
ticular respect for Ito Togai, and was literally living the old saying, "When one's heart
is true, and the mind is just, a broken thatch is no shame." 4
This very brief picture of a single samurai gives an idea of a changing society in which
traders and money-lenders played no small part, but in which they were despised. During the
Tokugawa period, wealth and power tended to pass from daimyo to merchant - though the merchant
was obliged to kneel before the passing daimyo. or to accept meekly the rough t gatment of a
samurai. "The samurai still had their dignit., the consciousness of high social standing; but
the commoners had most of the money and most of the fun."
Before we descrite life among the craftsmen and merchants of the towns, we need to have
some idea of the life of the cultivators. The situation of the Japanese farmer was difficult,
because of the way in which the taxes were levied and collected, and because heavy payments were
exacted from him.
All the land in a domain was carefully surveyed by officials of the overlord, and its
yield was estimated in accordance with its position, the nature of its soil, the number of
1ts cultivators, and in certain cases the harvest obtained from a test area. The overlord
then took his share of the crop, which was divided in the customary ratio, generally,
". . .four to the prince and six to the people," but sometimes even two to the prince and
one to the people. In the surveying, the assessment and the sharing there was ample room
for abuses, and in many fiefs the oppression of corrupt or over-zealous officials goaded
the farmers into revolt. Their lot was wretched enough at the best of times. . .On the
whole it is true to say that the peasants were heavily oppressed by members of the knight-
ly order, who soon in their turn were exploited by the rising class of merchants. Then,
as the daimyo and samurai attempted to transfer their burden of debt to the already over-

laden shoulders of the farmers, the agricultural economy broke down, and was replaced by a
mercantile economy which Japan was unable to support without calling upon the outside
world. 5
As standards of living rose in the cities, as money came to be used more and more widely,
and as speculation affected the price of rice to an alarming degree, the condition of the farmer
became steadily worse.
(To quote from a work written before 175o) the farmers were treated by officials and
tax-gatherers "as a cruel driver treats an ox or a horse, when he puts a heavy burden on
the beast, and lashes it mercilessly, getting all the angrier when it stumbles and whip-
ping more violently than ever, with loud curses." . . Nor can it be said that the rulers
of Japan were blind to these abuses. They tried to remedy them, and to understand them
within the limits of their knowledge. . It is remarkable that, at least until the early
part of the l9th century, even the most penetrating minds among them failed as a rule to
grasp the truth, that the wealth of Japan was adequate neither in amount nor in distribu-
tion to the needs of her society. Some of them saw it dimly, but most of them proposed
only neat ethical solutlons of the terrible equation of supply and demand. Peasants must
work hard and respect their betters, merchants must be honest and content with small prof-
its, and samura1 must not be extravagant.6
Peasants who were deep in debt often were forced to give up their rights in the land to
some creditor; they then farmed the lands under the landlord creditor, and, as may well be
imagined, this situation provided the basis for endless disputes and oppressions. Tenant farm-
ers of this type are numerous in Japan today, the result of similar situations caused by poverty
and powerlessness. There were many peasant riots and disturbances caused, like previous ones
and like similar disturbances today, by local dissatisfactions and oppressions. Many peasants
abandoned their lands - though they were not supposed to do this - and looked for employment in
the cities. Here, though they might be poorly paid in small manufactories or in the houses of
the wealthy, they were in general better off than they were in the rural regions, and city life
appealed to them because it was more amusing and diverting. Flight from the land was one reason
why the rural population of Japan remained stationary in the Tokugawa period. Infanticide was
another; this, in spite of regulations forbidding it, was a common practice among the sorely
pressed rural households of Japan.
A little poem of Issa's suggests the life of the patient farmers of Japan:
Here is suggested the anxiety of the mother working in the fields, longing to tend her neglected
child, and unconsciously planting towards the infant. She may not leave her work, . . for work
must be done.
Though there was much suffering among the farmers of Japan, and though local uprisings
against oppression were not unknown, the Japanese peasants of this period should not be thought
of as a rebellious group. The Japanese farmer was exhorted to be hard-working, obedient, and
unquestioning, and to show his superior the same loyalty expected of samurai to overlord. Feudal
traditions were strong, and they held the people of Japan in a firm grip. The forms of thought
and behavior which permeated Japanese society rested with traditional authority upon every class
of the people, and were in general accepted.
Only in the cities, which saw the rise of the new merchant class, was life less bound by
tradition than elsewhere. Under these circumstances, a gay and unrestrained life developed in

As a revelation of human nature there is nothing so illuminating in all Japan as the

From the novel Hizakurige by Ikku Jippensha (died 1831) we get an impression of the care-
free life of the road, a life which, in spite of efforts of the Tokugawa to restrict travel, was
very attractive to many. In this tale two friends, Yaji and Kita, decide to see the country.
The story begins:
Now 1s the time to visit all the celebrated places in the country and fill our heads
with what we have seen, so that when we become old and bald we shall have something to
talk about over the teacups. Let us accept the invitation of these bosom friends and go
with them on their long long journey. . . Theirs is the easy life of the bachelor. No
more than the rats are they required to waste money on rent, and as all the property they
have is tied up in a bundle they have no anxiety about that. It is true that they had to
make a small offering of rice at the family temple, and besides that pay a hundred coppers
to get a travelling permit. Moreover, instead of paying what they owed to the landlord,
they had to get their papers to pass the barriers. However, they made some money by sell-
ing to a second-hand dealer what they had of value, leaving the rubbish in the house for
the next tenant to return thanks for. The stone weight for the pickle tub and the knife
for scraping pots and pans they left next door, and the house opposite got the torn sun-
shades and the oil jar. Nothing is left, but there is still the difficulty of paying the
rice bill and the sake bill. They are very sorry to go away without paying them, but then
as the old poem says,
Whether in this life or the next we cheat
In either case our punishment we'll meet.9
The new life developing in the merchant towns was regarded unsympathetically by the upper
classes, who were holding on to old privileges, old arts, and old ideals of living.
It is easy to see that such an irresponsible way of life, such frank indulgence in

As an example of the traditional pursuits which were followed by the conventional, the No

describing action, of songs commenting on the scene described, and of dances appropriate to it.
For example, in one play the ghost of the dead Atsumori, the hero of the Taira clan, is repeat-

In the early part of the Tokugawa period, the No drama was kept as an aristocratic diver-
sion, but common people learned the songs and dances, the Kabuki theatre was influenced by the
No, and gradually the No plays became no longer the peculiar property of the privileged. Indeed,
"most of the cultural prerogatives of the former dominant class. . lapsed into formalism and
kept their vitality only in so far as they were enlivened by contact with the commoners' activi-
ties." Another way of saying the same thing is that some of the commoners, for the first time
in Japanese history finding themselves in a position of some security, pressed against the forma-
lism of life as it was set by the upper classes, and discovered that they had the power to create
plays, or color prints, or novels or poetry, as the case might be.
Bashō (1643-1694), of samurai origin, popularized the hokku, or poem of seventeen syllables.
The writing of hokku was widespread, but few, if any, of Bashō's followers possessed his skill.
For Bashō, hokku writing was not a trick; the hokku was a means of expressing the right attitude
toward life. For example, when one of his pupils wrote:

The spirit of the age, however, was not as mystical as Basho's poetry might lead one to
think. The most famous poet after Bashō, Chiyo (1703-l775), was sensitive, appealing, and
witty - but not mystical. For example, after the death of her little son, Chiyo wrote:
I wonder in what fields today
He chases dragon-flies in play -
My little boy who ran away. 14
If we look back over these few selections from the literature of the period, we have a
glimpse of a lively impressionable people striving to find some way in which to express their
feelings and emotions. But actually, wherever they turned, they met some new rule to restrain
them - laws stating how much they might spend, whether or not they could employ a hairdresser,
what the colors, patterns and fabrics of their kimono might be, how many new costumes they
might purchase. Within the family, the services to be rendered the head of the household by the
other members were defined by customs as rigid as law. The whole household, for example, was
supposed to assemble to greet the master on his return; the wife was expected to show the husband
the utmost deference - but, and this may be noticed in all the formal codes of behavior of the
time, the emphasis lay always upon duties and obligations of inferiors, and there was little
recognition of the principle of the responsibility of superiors.
Even in the cities, where life was comparatively free from some restrictions, craft guilds
and organizations of merchants prevented the development of flexible institutions. All manufac-
ture of luxury goods or consumption goods was carried on in homes or in very small establishments
in which apprentices learned their crafts while the master workman sold the commodities and re-
ceived the payments. As trade increased, guilds of workmen tried to monopolize trade in their
particular products; these guilds restricted the number of apprentices which could be admitted
to full guild membership and prevented in so far as they could the rise of competition. Appren-
tices who did not receive recognition as master workmen became wage laborers, working for manu-
facturers employing labor; but establishments depending on wage labor were very small and not
numerous.

life of the workman and present pictures of the methods employed. For example, we see the
cooper making a huge wooden cask; women carding cotton and spinning it on a hand wheel; men

In considering the life of the Tokugawa era, and the attempt to keep life formal in the
face of changing conditions, we should note that the Tokugawa were not satisfied with trying to
control, by law or custom, the things which people might do; they also attempted to dictate what
people should think. They themselves were formal Confucianists; the more rigid interpretations
of Confucianism suited their ideas, and they encouraged Chinese scholarship. However, as soon
as the Japanese began to delve into Chinese philosophy, they began to disagree over ways of in-
terpreting it, and over its actual significance. We do not need to go into the philosophical
disputes of the time, but we should notice the kind of ideas which was expressed by those stu-

Yamaga Soko (1620-1685).
Many Chinese scholars in Japan at the time of Soko considered China superior to Japan
in every way. Soko was one of the few who felt that Japan was superior to China. He
called Japan the "Central Kingdom of Civilization," and wrote an article on "The True Cen-
tral Kingdom." In one of his works he says: "To learn is to investigate things, and to
perfect knowledge. It does not consist in following foreign customs. Therefore superior
men especially will not imitate foreign customs."
....Speaking of how he came to esteem his own country so highly Soko said: "I do
not know the books which have been issued recently, but until ten years ago I read nearly
all the books that came from China; I was well informed in thin's Chinese. At that time I
thought our country was inferior to China in everything. We not only had less land, but
all the sages appeared in China. This opinion is not modern, but all scholars from olden
times have been inclined to exalt China at the expense of Japan. Recently I became con-
vinced that this was a serious mistake. It is a common mistake to believe what one hears,
and to disbelieve what one sees; to forget the things that are near and look only on those
that are far away. Until the time of the Fujiwara family, there were many great retainers.
This shows that bad men were few. This was because the race of our emperor was very in-
fluential. . . Our emperors are all descendants of the Sun Goddess. There is no foreign
blood in our veins. In bravery our country is respected by other countries and has never
been conquered. She has never had to give up even a small tract of land. Wisdom, benev-
olence and courage are three virtues which belong to a sage. When we compare our country
to others in regard to these virtues, Japan is superior. Truly she deserves to be called
the Central Kingdom of Civilization."15
It is easy to understand why the Tokugawa, who had taken from the emperor the last vestige

Other influences were also at work preparing the ground for change. Early in the eight-
eenth century, European books - provided they did not deal with religion - were permitted in
Japan; these were chiefly Dutch, since the European language with which Japanese had contact
was Dutch. Slowly and with great labor, Dutch scientific works were translated into Japanese.
Though the Japanese who dealt with the Dutch at Deshima (a small island in Nagasaki harbor to
which the foreigners were restricted) were forbidden to tell anything about their own country,
or to find out very much about the world outside, nevertheless information and ideas from abroad
filtered into Japan, and foreign goods found a ready market. However, the influence of European
1deas and things reached a very small proportion of the people, and it reached it under protest,
as it were, for the Tokugawa never encouraged the spread of anything which contained the slight-
est threat to the stability which they wished to maintain forever.
Of course this stability, because of its very rigidity, was bound to be overturned, though
the fundamental cause of the change which was to come was not the new foreign influences or the
revival of national tradition.
The country was full of restless spirits, dissatisfied with their condition and
thirsting for activity. There were nobles who wanted independence and foreign trade, to
develop the resources of their domains; samurai who wanted opportunities to use their
talents, whether as soldiers or as officials; merchants who wanted to break the monopolies
of the guilds; scholars who wanted to draw knowledge from new springs; humble peasants and
townsmen who wanted just a little freedom from tax and tyranny. Every force but conserva-
tism was pressing from within at the closed doors; so that when a summons came from with-
out they were flung wide open, and all these imprisoned energies were released.17
The summons came when Commodore Perry arrived in 1853, and the Shogun, realizing that re-
sistance was useless, opened the doors of Japan to a world which had developed tremendously dur-
ing the two hundred and fifty years of Japan's seclusion. How did the nobles of Japan, "who
wanted independence and foreign trade, to develop the resources of their domains," go about get-
ting their desires, when they became aware of a world whose factories were pouring out commodi-
ties which could not be absorbed in the countries in which they were produced, a world in which
modern science had developed new techniques and means of production? How did the samurai who
"wanted opportunities to use their talents, whether as soldiers or as officials," find a place
in a Japan affected by a world in which the great powers had obtained colonies, and were seeking
new markets and new sources of raw materials? How did the "merchants who wanted to break the
monopolies of the guilds," respond to a world in which foreign capital was already seeking places
of investment abroad, a world in which much more powerful and extensive monopolies than any
known in Japan at that time were already in process of development? How would the scholars,
"who wanted to draw knowledge from new springs," meet the stimulus of western governmental forms,
modern science and technical achievement? How would all the inevitable changes for which many
people in Japan were ready, affect the lives of the "humble peasants and townsmen who wanted
Just a little freedom from tax and tyranny?" The doors of Japan were opened - what was this to
mean to the institutions and the ideas of Japan, and to the lives of the Japanese people?

Chapter 5.
THE MODERNIZATION OF JAPAN: THE FERMENTATION PERIOD
(1853-1895)
The time between 1853, when Commodore Perry first arrived in Japan, and 1895, when the
Sino-Japanese war ended, may be regarded as a period of fermentation in the development of
Japan. During these years, western techniques, 1deas, inventions, sciences and education poured
into the country, and from the flood of new influences, combined w1th the existing institutions
of Japan, Japanese leaders shaped the direction in which the country was to develop.
We have seen how in every period of Japanese history, great clan families directed the
course of events - how the Fujiwara managed to control the He1an court and the government
bureaucracy; how the lords of Kamakura established a military feudal rule which absorbed the
functions of the earlier bureaucracy and under which the emperor was secluded in Kyoto; how the
Ashikaga shogun who followed the Kamakura government went down in the clan wars; and how the new
family of the Tokugawa took up the reins of government. Now, after the Tokugawa shogun had
opened Japan to foreigners, the ambitious daimyo of the distant western provinces, who had never
given the Tokugawa any but the most grudging allegiance, seized the opportunity to overthrow
them. These western lords - the lords of Satsuma, Choshu, Tosa, and Hizen - backed the slogan,
"Honor the Emperor and Expel the Foreigner." They attracted to their side many of the disaffect-
ed elements in Japan - the court nobles who had so long been powerless, the ronin, the daimyo who
wished to have some share in the power so long held by the Tokugawa, the reactionaries who were
opposed to opening the country, the men who believed in the abolition of the shogunate.
In 1867, the emperor died and his son Mutsuhito, only fifteen years old, succeeded to the
throne. The Shogun, at the request of the powerful western lords, but also doubtless because of
his own conviction that the day of the Shogunate was over, then 1ssued a statement, indicating
that the presence of two heads to the government - the Emperor and the Shogun - was proving it-
self a cause of weakness, and hence he resigned. His words are wonth quoting:
My ancestor received more confidence and favor from the court than any of his
predecessors, and his descendants have succeeded him for more than two hundred years.
Though I fili the same office, almost all the acts of the administration are far from
perfect, and I confess it with shame that the present unsatisfactory condition of
affairs 1s due to my short-comings and incompetence. Now that foreign intercourse be-
comes daily more extensive, unless the government 1s directed from one central authority,
the foundations of the state will fall to p1eces. If, however, the old order of things
be changed, and the administrative authority be restored to the Imperial Court, and 1f
national deliberations be conducted on an extensive scale, and the Imperial decision be
secured, and 1f the empire be supported by the efforts of the whole people, then the em-
pire will be able to maintain 1ts rank and dignity among the nations of the earth. Al-
though I have allowed all the feudal lords to state their views without reservation, yet
1t 1s, I believe, my highest duty to realize this 1deal by giving up entirely my rule
over this land.1
The abolition of the shogunate was not carried through so peacefully as these words might
lead one to think. The shogun's statement was followed almost 1mmediately by an announcement
from the court nobles and feudal lords present at Kyoto, abolishing the shogunate, and taking
the guardianship of the palace from the Tokugawa. The intention to restore the emperor was
stated, and a provisional government under court nobles and daimyo was set up. The shogun could
scarcely take this without resistance, and a short civil war followed in which the Tokugawa

The new government which displaced the shogunate was under the control of the four western
clans which had made a temporary alliance in order to dispose of the Tokugawa. The leaders of
the four clans were by no means in agreement as to what the new government should be. They had
advocated "Honor the Sovereign and Expel the Foreigner," in order to win support for their
actions, but they actually did not all wish to expel the foreigner and lose foreign trade and
foreign goods. "Honor the Sovereign" was a battle cry which attracted followers, but which
might, or might not, mean anything definite. The lords of Satsuma, Tosa, Hizen, and Choshu,
together with their retainers, wanted most of all to make their own control secure. Gradually
1t became apparent to them that fighting among themselves at this time would be disastrous.
They set up a bureaucratic government after the model of the old Nara and Heian governments, and
divided the offices among themselves and the court nobles. They perceived that if the emperor
were restored, the different clans, as well as the people, would have some unifying 1dea to hold
them together, and to prevent quarrels which might prove disastrous if added to foreign aggres-

famous Charter Oath containing in general terms this statement of intention to liberalize govern-

1nconce1vable in 1867.2

A few months later, those daimyo who had not voluntarily surrendered their fiefs were
ordered to do so; the old orders of nobility were abolished, and the feudal lords were created
district governors in those regions which they had previously held as fiefs. In return for the
surrender of their lands and revenues, the daimyo - numbering about three hundred - were given
compensations amounting to about half their previous incomes. Since this was a certain income
from which no deductions, such as payments to samura1, had to be made, most of the daimyo were
better off than they had been for some time. (It must not be thought that all feeling of finan-
cial responsibility of feudal lord to retainer became at once a thing of the past. To the pres-
ent day, instances of assistance given familles of former retainers by the family of the former
feudal lord are not uncommon.)
There were some 1,500,000 samura1 who, as retainers, had for centuries been supported by
the daimyo. The government offered all samura1 who voluntarily surrendered their feudal stipends,
a payment equivalent to five years' income, payable half in cash and half in government bonds.
When all samurai did not respond, their stipends were discontinued. The warriors' swords, the
distinctive badge of the samura1, could now be worn by anyone; they were no longer a proud mark
of caste. The actual compensation received by each samura1 was relatively small, while their
pride, as a class, was deeply hurt when they were deprived of the outward badges of their rank.
However, it must not be forgotten that many samura1 families had had long experience in political
administration and in financial management of estates. They were not slow to perceive the new
opportunities opening before them in the new government, in banking, and in the management of in-
dustrial enterprises. They despised merchandizing and trade, and were not successful in this
type of business; but some samura1, notably Ito, Inouye, and Yamagata, sought places in the new
government and rose to positions of the greatest power, while others became bankers and company
directors. Still others joined the Satsuma rebellion of 1877, while many members of the class,
failing to adjust to new conditions, sank into poverty and obscurity. The fact that Japan
possessed a privileged class, many of whose members had had valuable experience in the bureau-
cratic government of the Tokugawa regime and in the management of estates, was an important fac-
tor affecting the development of Japan as the country was modernized. Another characteristic
aspect of Japanese life 1s also worth emphasizing - the fact that the masses of the people had
had long experience in being governed by an upper-class bureaucracy.
When feudalism was abolished, feudal rank was also abolished, but a new nobility was created
a few years later, when five hundred men were given new titles. It is interesting to note that
in this list all but thirty-five were daimyo or court nobles of the feudal regime, and that the
new members of the ennobled class were samurai who had already shown their ability in the govern-
ment. Thus we see that though feudalism, as 1t had existed, was abolished, old feudal lords held
office in their old provinces, or other positions in the new government, and that they formed the
bulk of the new hereditary nobility. In so far as they could adapt thenselves to the changing
conditions of l1fe in Japan, the doors of privilege and power were as open to them under the new
situation as in the past.
What happened to the cultivators? With the abolition of feudalism, peasants who had been
bound to the soil were free to move about. They were at first permitted to obtain titles to the
land they cultivated, but this system was changed to the older method of registering land within

the district. Peasants were permitted to sell or to mortgage the lands they cultivated. To
provide revenue, the fields of Japan were carefully surveyed and a land tax levied. This was
based not as formerly on the crop, but upon the probable value of the land itself, considered in
terms of productivity. The land tax, amounting to about three per cent of the value of the land,
was assessed upon all cultivable fields; house lots, including city estates of lords, were taxed
at a lower rate, and waste land - which belonged to the government - was not taxed. One would
say that, with the abolition of feudalism, a better day dawned for the farmers of Japan. They
became a free people; but what this freedom would mean, depended upon the governmental, social
and economic structure taking the place of the old feudal society.
In every change made in the government, the old aristocratic clan influence was dominant.
When the Tokugawa lands were confiscated, imperial supporters were appointed to fill the vacated
offices. The chief seaport towns and all the Tokugawa fiefs were thus placed directly under the
central government, which was a clan bureaucracy. This organization of local governments was
soon extended over the whole country. When feudalism was abolished, the old fiefs were re-
arranged, and the number of prefectures was reduced from 302 to 72. In 1873, a Department of
Home Affairs was created.
From that time until the present every matter of importance which concerns a locality
has to be brought before the Home Office by the local authorities, and the action to be
taken is decided virtually by the central Government. Thus, 1f a city wishes to bestow a
franchise upon a street-railway company or a gas company, the consent of the Home Minister
must be obtained before any action can be taken by the city authorities.4
The clans powerful in the Government made room for their retainers and followers in govern-
ment offices. This fact, together with the rapid changes made arbitrarily, created a good deal
of resentment particularly among those samura1 and lords who were not profiting from the new
system. Moreover, there was a difference of opinion in the Government over the policy to be
pursued with regard to expansion and internal development. Difficulties with Formosa, the Ryukyu
Islands, and Korea, caused the dissatisfied elements to criticize the Government for hesitating
to enter upon the course of expansion which they had expected would immediately follow the im-
perial restoration. Sa1go of Satsuma was displeased with the course taken by the government; he
left Tokyo and returned to Satsuma, where he was joined by dissatisfied samura1. In 1877 the
Satsuma rebell1on broke out, but the old feudal forces were soon conquered by the new imperial
troops. This was significant, for the new army, conscripted from the people, and taking the
place of the warrior class, had not had much prestige before this.
From 1877 forward an absolute monarchy served and ruled by an oligarchy, the two in a
firm alliance, dominated the nation. In this combinat1on of apparently incompatible ele-
ments, an absolute monarch and a ruling oligarchy, the dualism represented in pre-Meij1
times by the Court and the shogunate reappeared, the only important difference in the
situations being the absence of feudalism and the presence of a free nation.5

into existence, the central bureaucracy would be in too strong a position to be threatened by
any such assembly. For example, the new nobility was created partly for this purpose and to
provide a group from which the upper house could be appointed. A cabinet was formed, and the
Privy Council, or group most closely in touch with the emperor, was reorganized. Ito, originally
a samura1 of the Choshu clan, headed the cabinet, whose members were, with the exception of two,
Choshu or Satsuma men.
As time passed, the emperor commissioned Ito to prepare a constitution. Ito had made con-
siderable study of constitutional governments elsewhere, and now he went to Germany where he was
particularly impressed with the German form of government because 1t was oligarchical and not
democratic. When he returned, he prepared the constitution in secrecy with the assistance of
only four men. When the document was finished 1n 1889, it was promulgated by the emperor, who
read it before a small group of government leaders. Any criticisms or comments were forbidden
when it was announced; it immediately had the force of unchangeable law since it had been
announced by the emperor.
The form of government defined by the Japanese Constitution has several notable and 1m-
portant characteristics. The Constitution represents an attempt to fix forever the institutions
of the country in accordance with aristocratic principles of the strongest type. Only the
emperor may propose a change in the Constitution, which states:
The Empire of Japan shall be re1gned over and governed by a line of Emperors unbroken
for ages eternal.
The Emperor 1s sacred and inviolable.

emperor was given the force of law - a fact of immense significance. An American authority on
Japanese government and politics raises the question which occurs to our minds at this point:

The devices adopted by the constitutional oligarchy - the diligent cultivation of a
