After the Constitution went into effect and the first Diet was convened in 1890, four years
of struggle followed in which one government clan leader after another went down before the
forces of opposition determined on the revision of the Constitution. Finally, in 1894, the
government played the card which 1t has found useful more than once since then when internal
troubles became acute - 1t declared war, this time on China. All the discontented elements in
Japan got behind the war; the Diet assented willingly to the government budgets - which it had
been rejecting - and political differences were forgotten for the time being.
The war with China arose because of differences in Korea. Korea was in a curious position.
Many times in the course of its history it had been completely controlled by China; at other
times it had paid tribute to China; and sometimes 1t had been independent. At this time, Korea
was supposed to be tributary to China, but China, with many troubles of her own and with a
weakened dynasty at the head of the country, did not actively assert her control over the Korean
kingdom. The militarists in Japan emphasized Japan's interest in a region adjoining the island
empire and refused to recognize China's rights over Korea. Korea was in a state of complete
decay; the country was disorderly and the government corrupt. It was unable to resist outside
pressure, or to keep order. Both Japan and China had troops in Korea and the two countries had

In 1895, the treaty of peace was signed; Japan was given the lease of the Liaotung peninsula

The effects of this war can scarcely be overestimated: the conflict may be regarded as a
turning point in Japanese history and in the Far Eastern situation. In Japan, the basis of clan
control shifted from the government bureaucracy to the military. In l885, a civil service system
had been instituted, thus cutting down the number of civil positions which could be given by
government leaders to their supporters. The navy had come under Satsuma control and the army
under Choshu leadership. In 1894, 1t was provided that cabinet ministers of the Army and Navy
departments could only be chosen from officers in active service of at least the rank of Lieu-
tenant-General or Vice-Admiral, and such was the control of Satsuma and Choshu over the appoint-

tion of such prestige that he was able to secure from the emperor the right for the ministers of
War and Navy to approach him directly, and thus to advise the emperor even without the knowledge
of the other ministers. This right separated the High Command of the forces of Japan from civil
control. It introduced the possibility that army or navy leaders could unmake a ministry by re-
fusing to submit the names of qualified officers to a new prime minister. It introduced the
possibility of cabinet difficulties in case the ministers of war or navy opposed the prime
minister on matters of policy or finance. It caused clan government to come to mean a government
by the military. Against this situation political parties in the Diet might struggle, but they
would struggle in vain for they possessed no such means of controlling the executive as did the
m11itary.
This shift in power was but one of the results of the war. Formosa was the first colonial
possession of Japan; Yamagata attached the colonial governors to the list of offices under the
Army and Navy, and thus created the military colonial administrat1on system which Japan has
followed ever since when 1ts colonies were extended. Still another result of the war was the
shift in attention from constitutional revision to expansion on the mainland; Japan's ambitions
were increased, and the determination to gain possessions on the mainland was fed by the way in
which territory which had been gained had been snatched from Japan through the interference of
other nations. Another result was the increase in taxes necessitated to meet the expenses of
the war, and the receipt of an indemnity which might have paid for the war, but which was, in-
stead, applied to the development of industry.
In the Far East Japan's victory called attention to the weakness of China, and in the years

obtaining concessions and spheres of interest. This again had repercussions in Japan; with every
advance of European powers on the mainland of Asia, Japanese militarists became more convinced of
the necessity of getting what they could for Japan. Again, Japan's victory increased Japan's
prestige in foreign eyes; all foreign nations now surrendered the extra-territorial rights they

Government leaders early perceived the need for establishing schools in which the learning

Another foundation laid by Japan to ensure the welfare of the country had to do with the
army. It was apparent to the leaders of Japan that military weakness was one reason why China
was being encroached upon by foreign nations, and 1t appeared that military prowess seemed to
command high respect among foreign nations. The beginnings of a foreign trained conscripted
army have been mentioned in the discussion of the Satsuma rebellion. By 1894, when Japan was at
war with China, the Japanese army, well trained and equipped, cons1sted of some 200,o00 men.
Still another foundation essential for Japan's progress was the development of modern means
of transportation and of modern industry. Japan's feudal industry was not centralized; the
various 1solated communities of the country produced much of what was consumed there. Luxury
goods were made in Kyoto or Tokyo or Osaka and adjoining reg1ons, porcelain for the luxury trade
was made in the districts where the best clay was found, but in general all industry was widely
scattered. Roads were few and poor. The government alone could at first command the capital or
provide the conditions under which modern railways, modern ships, and modern industrial estab-
lishments could be built and operated, and it was hampered because the foreign control of Jap-
anese tariffs prevented it from levying customs duties to protect home industry. However, in
1870, the government arranged for the building of the first railroad, and at about the same time
also took over the first shipyards and transferred them to the navy. In the l88o's, private con-
cerns were granted land and loans for building railways, and the shipyards in existence, except
the navy yards, were rented and then sold to the Mitsubish1, a wealthy family which had been en-
gaged in commercial undertakings in the Tokugawa period. The government gave subsidies to en-
courage shipbuilding, and permitted the Mitsubishi to fix freight rates in silver at a time when
the yen was depreciated, thus further stimulating private enterprise in this industry.
The first modern factories established in Japan were cotton-spinning mills. Modern cotton-
spinning machinery was brought 1n by feudal lords before the Meij1 restoration, but not until the
government took an active hand in the text1le industry, in l879, did cotton-spinning begin to
expand. After the government had imported machinery and established several model mills in
different districts, private concerns entered the cotton-spinning industry. The reeling of silk
was improved after the government, in l87l, set up a model silk-reeling mill. This was purchased
some twenty years later by the Mitsu1, a merchant family which had been a financial backer of
the shogunate, had supported the movement for the restoration of the emperor, and had rendered
important aid in the founding of the ministry of finance under the new government.
The government took the lead in mining, operating mines in existence and opening new coal
fields. By 1880, the government had withdrawn from mining, and had sold 1ts interests to the
Mitsu1 family. The iron and steel industry which began at the Kama1sh1 mine was bought by the
government in 1874 and sold to private owners in 1887, who in turn sold 1t later (1924) to the
Mitsu1 fam1ly.
While the government took the initiative in the industrial development of Japan, and while
1t continued, after disposing of many of its interests, to take an active part in fostering in-
dustry, it did not continue to engage directly in industry and to build state socialism. Instead,
it gave so many privileges to a few wealthy families that a purely Japanese form of capitalism
was, by 1895, beginning to develop. It was not unconnected with the special privileges of feudal
grants. An enlarged sphere of action, combined with government aid and special privileges, gave
to a few families a great deal of power, and caused modern Japan to begin to emerge as a particu-
lar type of capitalist state. In the government of this state, old clan leaders exercised power
through their control of the army and navy, and the ministers of army and navy were powerful be-
cause of their unique position in the cabinet.

Chapter 6.
EXPANSIONISM: ONE ASPECT OF JAPAN'S DEVELOPMENT SINCE 1895
Since 1895, political changes of great importance, particularly 1nvolving Japan, China,
Russia, Germany, Great Britain and the United States, have taken place in the Far East. Japan
has obtained a.dominant position in territory previously a part of China and is steadily in-
creasing the area under her control, while reducing to a minimum the influence of other powers
in these regions. Foreign nations whose trade 1s adversely affected by those developments re-
gard the advance of Japan as threatening to world peace, and the Soviet Union openly considers
them ominous of war. Japanese action has been one of the factors retarding the peaceful settle-
ment of China's internal problems. Since the international significance of the Japanese expan-
sion on the mainland of Asia is so great, 1t is necessary in this chapter to consider the actions
of the Japanese government since l895, and to shift emphasis from the life of the people of
Japan to the events of political history which have a bearing on the present situation in the
Far East.
The main events we shall consider are: the scramble of the powers to gain concessions
from China after 1895; the acceptance by the powers of the United States notes formulating the
"Open Door" pol1cy; the Anglo-Japanese all1ance; the Russo-Japanese war of 1904-1905; the Jap-
anese annexation of Korea in 1910; the Chinese Revolut1on of 19ll; the preoccupation of the
European nations, and later, of the United States, in Europe during the World War, and the con-
sequent Japanese pressure on China during this period; the Japanese intervention in Siberia
after the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917; the Washington Conference of 1922 and the subsequent
treaties and agreements regarding the Far East; the Tsinan "1ncident" of 1928; the Japanese ad-
vance into the Three Eastern Provinces of China - He1lungkiang, Kirin, and Liaoning, the region
known as Manchuria - in September, 1931; the organization of these provinces and the province of
Jehol into the Japanese-controlled "empire" of Manchoukuo; and, finally, the Japanese advance
into north China, south of the Great Wall, in 1935. In this chapter we shall examine only the
events outlined, leaving for later consideration the internal changes in Japan which have a bear-
ing on Japanese expansion.
After the Sino-Japanese War had demonstrated the weakness of China, the powers hastened to
secure additional spheres of interest in Chinese territory. The advance of Russia into the
Three Eastern Provinces was, in 1ts effect upon Japan, and hence upon the Far Eastern situation
today, the most important of the actions of the powers at this time. This advance proceeded as
follows:
1896 - Russ1a secured the right to build and operate, under a Russ1an syndicate - known as
the Chinese Eastern Ra1lway Company - a railroad across north Manchuria to form a short cut
connecting the Trans-Siberian ra1lway with the Pacific.
1898 - Russ1a obtained a twenty-five-year lease of the southern port1on of the Liaotung
peninsula, and the right to build a railway south from the main line of the Chinese Eastern road
to the ports of Dalny and Port Arthur. Russia secured the exclusive right to adminster the en-
tire railway zone adjoining the 1mmense T formed by the Chinese Eastern Ra1lway and 1ts southern
branch, to police the reg1on, to mine coal and cut timber required for the upkeep of the railway,
and to fortify the ports as well as to keep warships in the southern harbors.
1899-1900 - The Un1ted States, alarmed at the way in which the powers were securing exclu-
sive spheres of interest in Chinese territory, sent the "Open Door" notes to the different powers
1nvolved. The text of the notes varied in the case of the different nations to which they were

Chinese territory, but that instead trade should be open to all nations. Each of the powers hav-

their acceptance of the principle set forth in the Open Door notes, though Russia alone stated

1902 - Great Britain and Japan, each alarmed at the As1atic expansion of the Russian empire,
signed a treaty of alliance. The treaty recognized the Open Door principle when it stated that
the two countries were "interested in maintaining the independence and territorial integrity of
China and Korea, and in securing equal opportunities in those countries for the commerce and
industry of all nations." It went on to say, however, that Great Britain had special interests

country was to safeguard 1ts own special recognized interests in these regions, even to the
point of intervening if necessary. In the event of such "intervention" by one of the signing

this case, the neutral country would come to the assistance of 1ts ally. In l905, the treaty
was renewed and changed; the new arrangement provided that if any country made an unprovoked
attack on one of the parties signing, the other would 1mmediately come to 1ts assistance. In
1911, the treaty was again renewed, but its scope was not widened.
Ever since the Sino-Japanese war, Japanese had been extending their 1nfluence in Korea. The

Of recent years, Japanese have emphasized the fact that Manchuria 1s a "life-line" essen-

With regard to the first of these Manchoukuo has proved valuable, and Japan's exports to Man-
churia have more than doubled since 1928. However, the exports of Manchuria have declined in
the same period. The world demand for soya beans, the chief product of the region, has fallen
off and Japan cannot absorb all the beans of Manchoukuo as payment for the manufactured goods
exported there. With regard to raw materials, Manchoukuo also offers wheat, a little cotton,
and coal. But since l932, Japan has raised all the wheat consumed in the country, so Manchurian

Chapter 7.
INDUSTRIAL CONDITIONS IN JAPAN SINCE 1895
After 1895, modern industry in Japan developed rapidly, stimulated at intervals by wars.
The Sino-Japanese War created a sudden demand for war materials and supplies and showed the
need for Japanese-built ships, while the indemnities paid by China after the war provided the
government with funds which were used to subsidize industry. After l899 when international
treaties were revised and Japan was permitted to control (to some extent) its customs duties
the government levied tariffs designed to protect home industries. It further favored industry
by a system of taxation which rested lightly upon the industrialist. The Russo-Japanese War
gave another sudden spurt to Japanese industrial enterprises, partly through the temporary stim-
ulus which war gives to industry, and partly through the new needs created by the Japanese pos-
session of the lease of the South Manchuria Railway and Kwantung Province.
The World War had a tremendous ffect upon Japanese industry and trade.
The war created for Japan an enormous market for war necessities of all sorts, both
in goods and services, gave to her, by its crippling effect on shipping on the ocean trade
routes, an overwhelming advantage in the neighboring Western Pacific markets, and opened
to her fresh markets farther afield. .. For industry in general the following percentages
of increase were recorded: number of factory workers 63 per cent, units of industrial
power 34 per cent, electric motor capacity 206 per cent; in the cotton industry the number
of spindles increased by 44 per cent, the output of yarn by 55 per cent, the steel and
iron industry, thrown on its own resources, developed still more rapidly, the cutput of
pig iron rising by 143 per cent and that of the principal steel products by ll6 per cent. .
À most important development occurred in the chemical industry in its applications partic-
ularly to dye-stuffs, soda, the manufacture of artificial silk, and the extraction of at-
mospheric nitrogen.
Foreign trade reflected the effect of the War in an increase in value of exports be-
tween 1913 and 1918 from 632 mill1on to 1,962 million yen and of 1mports from 729 million
to 1,668 million yen. While Japan's trade with Europe decreased roughly by 10 per cent,
her trade w1th As1atic countries increased 78 per cent, with North America 427 per cent,
and with Africa 385 per cent.1
The tremendous expansion of industry during the World War was followed by depression. In
order to enable Japanese industry to cut the costs of production and to continue to compete suc-
cessfully in the new markets opened up during the period of the war, the government encouraged
a system of rationalization - that is, of forming large combines of the small independent con-
cerns and, under the improved organization, replacing old machinery with new more efficient ma-
chines, improving technique, and reducing wasteful competition in production, management, and
marketing. A law was passed in 193l giving the Minister of State the power to force a minority
of persons engaged in staple industries to participate in agreements concerning production or
sales made by the majority interests engaged in the same industries. The system of rationaliza-
tion decreased output in some industries, increased it in others, and cut costs. Export goods
produced under a definite plan which had markets in view, and produced more cheaply than before,
found a market abroad; the aim of the government plan was attained as far as the export of Japa-
nese goods was concerned; but, partly because of the wider use of improved machinery, requiring
the labor of fewer workers, unemployment increased.
The development of Japan's industry has been accomplished in spite of Japan's shortage of
the raw materials essential to industrial development. With amazing confidence and energy the

export trade - top-heavy industries that may in turn threaten the entire structure of the na-

Heavy industry, involving the manufacture of machines and tools used in other industries
and the building of ships and munitions of war, is considered the foundation for industrial de-
velopment and national defense. Without this foundation, light industry must rely on imported
machinery, and national defense becomes a precariously dependent affair. Iron, coal, oil, and
minerals used in the manufacture of steel are the raw materials essential to heavy industry and
to national defense. What is Japan's position with regard to these materials?
Let us assume, for the moment, that Japan is cut off from all foreign sources of
minerals, and must rely on her own resources. Immediately her blast furnaces must reduce
operations; not only is their output greatly curtailed, but their span of life 1s short-
ened. The entire iron-ore reserves of the Japanese Empire - assuming all the ore to be of
a uniformly suitable grade - would last only some thirty years, at the present rate of de-
mand. But Japan depends upon foreign sources for pig iron as well as ore. Cut off the
six or seven hundred thousand metric tons of pig import, and the requirement for pig from
domestic ore is stepped up. The life of the iron reserves is thereby reduced to little
more than twenty years.
As her resources are scarce and her industrial age is young, Japan lacks the vast
secondary resources of a country like the United States, where scrap metals are abundant.
She is therefore supplementing her imports of ore and pig iron by increasing imports of
scrap - 1,554,000 tons 1n 1934, mainly from the United States. Cut off this supply, and
the blast furnaces, and the output of steel are still further reduced.
These furnaces require suitable coking coal.Japan's known and estimated coal re-
serves, adequate for some hundreds of years at the present rate of consumption in the Em-
pire, are admittedly of only fair quality, and only a very small percentage is metallur-
gically valuable. Dwindling iron reserves are matched by small and uncertain supplies of
coking coal.
For a steel industry, to the above requirements must be added manganese, nickel, and
chromium, as well as other reserves. Possibly Japan could supply manganese, as it occurs
frequently though in no large deposits throughout the Empire. But as the country imports
a large amount, 1t would seem that domestic production to meet total demands is a costly
undertaking, to be justified only in time of emergency.
So little nickel is produced in Japan that no returns on 1t are available. Most of
it 1s a by-product from copper refining. Therefore domestic production to meet the many
industrial demands would be costly, and a national emergency might accentuate the scarcity
of the material. Several Japanese mining and other industrial companies now refine nickel
ores 1mported from New Caledonia, and there has even been some talk of purchasing the
nickel deposits outright. Transporting the ores over such a distance would involve haz-
ards in a time of conflict.
Chromium ore exists in Japan, and is produced in some quantity. But cutting off the
country's foreign supplies would seriously hamper industry; it is doubtful whether self-
sufficiency could be attained. . . .
Japan cut off from foreign supplies of petroleum would present so serious a problem
that the Government has already taken a number of steps to remedy the situation. It has
encouraged prospecting, intensive development of local resources, domestic refining of
1mported crude; it has attempted to enforce the Oil Law, providing for the storage of a
six-months' supply of petroleum products within the country - a provision which has
aroused so much opposition on the part of both foreign and domestic firms in the country
that the date of enforcement has now been postponed until June. Without imports of crude
oil, the refining industry would soon collapse, for about 9o% of Japan's refined petroleum
products are derived from 1mports. Again, petroleum refined in the country supplies less
than half the country's demand. Take away imported petroleum, crude and refined; tax to
the utmost the producing power of the Empire; and within a few years the Japanese navy
alone would drain the country dry.3

As far as light industry is concerned, Japan lacks raw materials. For example, the manu-
facture of cotton textiles which has risen to a position of importance since the World War de-
pends largely upon imported raw materials. About half the raw cotton used in Japan's manufac-
ture comes from the United States; in 1932, the percentage imported from the United States was
71.4; in 1933, 59.5; in 1934, 47.9. The only raw material produced in abundance in Japan 1s
811k.
The conditions which have enabled the forced growth of Japanese industry under the short-
age of raw materials together with the lack of colonial sources of raw materials or colonial
markets to absorb the manufactured products of Japan, are complex. Two hundred and fifty years
of a life of seclusion during which the people of Japan lived upon an agrarian economy, had
demonstrated the fact that the land of Japan could support not more than 30,o00,o00 people
(under the agricultural conditions of the Tokugawa period, at least). Whenever the population
rose much above the 30,Oo0,oo0 mark in Tokugawa times, there was a famine. Disease and recur-
ring famines in different regions helped to keep the population static; in addition, the people
practiced infanticide, and the Tokugawa made laws restricting the marriage of younger sons.
With the modernization of Japan, however, modern medicine reduced the number of deaths by ep1-
demics; new means of transportation made it possible to send famine relief hitherto difficult
to supply; and modern codes of law ended the practice of infanticide and restrictions on mar-
riages. The population increased rapidly; it no longer remained static as in Tokugawa times.
But it was known that an increased population could not be supported entirely on an agrarian
economy, and hence, in spite of natural disadvantages, industrialization was considered neces-
sary. Industrialization proceeded in spite of the unfavorable conditions mentioned, through the
support and encouragement given industrialists by the government in the form of subsidies, favor-
able tariffs and taxes; its growth was assisted by the centralization of control. To these it
is necessary to add the simplicity of the standards of living among the people, the poverty of
the farmers, and the survival of traditional ideas, attitudes, and methods of production of in-
dustrial goods, all of which contributed to the industrialization of Japan.
In spite of the rapid growth of Japanese industry and trade to a point where they are con-
sidered threatening to the other exporting countries of the world, agriculture continues to be
very important in Japan's economy. Moreover, there is still a close connection between industry
and agriculture. Many people who leave their villages to engage in industrial work return later
to the rural districts to live; village households support the members of their families who are
unemployed because of industrial depression or changes in production which throw industrial
workers out of employment; many farming households carry on small-scale manufacture. Before,
however, we consider the life of the people in the rural regions we shall examine some of the
characteristics of Japanese industry and trade, and the life of the industrial workers.
In the industrial expansion of Japan, the part played by a few families is significant.
The concentration of financial power in a few hands 1s not unique to Japan; but the degree of
this concentration is particularly marked in Japan. In addition, the financial power of a few
families is given a peculiar quality because of the fact that the management of the huge volume
of business centered in family groups is based on principles dating back to feudal days. As far
as concentration is concerned, the 1934 Japan Year Book gives as an illustration the Mitsu1
interests, which, among other things, handle half of Japan's export trade.

The story of the house of Mitsu1 describes the organization and control of these vast
business enterprises:
In l673, seventy years after Japan had entered upon the long peace of the Tokugawa
Shogunate, Mitsu1 Hachirobei, then aged 52, left the obscurity of a provincial shop and
established in Kyoto a. new business which was extended to Yedo, the seat of the new gov-
ernment. He died twenty-two years later, the father of many children to whom he left a
gift more valuable than the wealth he had accumulated.
Before he died Hachirobei had set up collateral families for his sons whom he made
partners in his business, and in his will he defined the principles on which his children
were to govern his inheritance, . .
It has been modified to meet the needs of changing times, but the spirit of the in-
herited family code remains the essential core of the constitution, which today governs
the Mitsui family and firm with its worldwide interests, and the Omotokata, the central
administrative body, has become the incorporated Mitsui Gome1 Kaisha, the Mitsui Partner-
ship Company. Its partners are the heads of the eleven Mitsui families and no others,
and its directors are chosen by them. . In the Gome1 Kaisha all the far-flung cords of
the Mitsui enterprises - banking, trading, mining, trust and insurance business, shipping
and ship-building, warehousing, etc., - come to a common centre under the united control
of the eleven families. At its head is the direct descendant of Hachirobei, the head of
the main family.
...
Hachirobei's will, as already stated, is the basis of the present constitution, ampli-
fied by precepts added in 1722 by his son Sochiku. In 1900 the entire document was re-
drafted and it is the constitution of the House today. Every member of the Family, on
coming of age, swears allegiance to it at a religious ceremony in a prescribed form of
oath, of which the English translation runs as follows:
In obedience to the precepts of our forefathers, and in order to strengthen the
everlasting ancestral foundations of the families of our House and to expand the en-
terprises bequeathed by our forefathers, I solemnly vow in the presence of the August
Spirits of our ancestors that, as a member of the House of Mitsui, I will observe and
follow the regulations handed down in the Constitution of our House, and that I will
not wantonly seek to alter them. In witness whereof I take the oath and affix my
signature thereto in the presence of the August Spirits of our ancestors.5
Other great families - notably the Mitsubishi and the Sumitomo - have feudal histories not
unlike that of the Mitsui. Like the Mitsui they direct diversified present-day concerns in
which they gained a head start because the government gave them special rights, just as in
feudal times feudal grants were made to the lords of Japan. As a result, the Mitsubishi, the
Sumitomo, the Yasuda, and the Mitsui together have in their hands about half the banking capital
of Japan and most of the industrial enterprises of the country. Monopolies of the type which
elsewhere appeared after a long period of development in capitalism came quickly into existence
in Japan, partly because of the persistence of forms of thought and behavior dating from feudal
days.
In spite of the growth of Japanese industry and of the concentration of the control of
mining, manufacturing, shipbuilding, shipping, trading, and banking, all Japanese industrial
production is not, as might be expected under these circumstances, carried on in large factor-
1es. The situation is such that a clear-cut picture cannot easily be presented. For example:
The export goods labelled "Made in Japan" come from every type of organization: from
small family industries and small or medium-sized handicraft units, more or less linked up
with family enterprises; from super-handicraft plants, representing the greater part of
medium-sized industry; from large factories based on peculiarly Japanese semi-feudal so-
cial organization; from similar factories organized on Western lines.
Very small units, employing less than five persons, are not included in the Japanese
Factory Statistics. These small workshops still have an important share in the total in-
dustrial production. According to the Chamber of Commerce in Tokyo, they produced in 1931
18.8 per cent of the total output of cotton textiles; 28.8 per cent of woolen textiles;

In 1932, the last year for which a census was comp1led, 13 per cent of all registered
workers were in small industrial establishments employing from 5 to 9 persons - the smallest
units included in the Japanese Factory Statistics.
Twanty-six per cent of all workers were employed in workshops with from 10 to 49 employ-

smaller industries. Altogether, therefore, small industries employ about 39 per cent of
Japan's industrial workers.
Medium-sized industries, as we shall arbitrarily call those plants employing from 50 to
500 workers, absorb a further 36 per cent of Japan's industrial labor.
T1s means that in the large factories, employing 500 workers or more, only 25 per cent
of Japnese workers are employed.6
A line cannot be drawn between the type of establishments producing for the export trade and
the type prolucing for home consumption. Cotton spinning, for example, a step in the manufacture of
the cotton textiles which are invading world markets, is carried on in great mills - while the manu-
facture of tabi, or Japanese stockings, an article used only by Japanese, has been taken from small
plants to large factories. Pencils, which are produced both for export and for home consumption,
are made in tiny establishments employing less than five persons, and a large proportion of the
reeling of silk for the export trade is done in households.
The matter of chief concern to us is the effect of the different industrial set-ups on the
life of the worker. What are the conditions of labor, the hours of work, the protection given the
worker, the wages received, the sex and age of the worker? What, in brief, is the life of the indus-
trial laborer in Japan? Since the conditions affecting the life of the worker vary with the type of
industrial astablishment, generalizations can scarcely be made, but life under the different situa-
tions can ba described.
Cotton spinning, one of the most important industries organized almost entirely on a large-
scale basis, offers an illustration of one type of set-up - the kind in which there are many sur-
vivals of the paternalistic forms of control of earlier days even though the machinery is modern
and the fatory large. Over 8o per cent of the workers in cotton spinning mills are girls and young
women from 15 to 20 years of age, recruited from the country for a definite period of time. At the
end of the.r period of service. they expect to return to the country to live. While they are engaged
in factory work, they live in dormitories on the factory premises, and may not leave the grounds with-
out the permission of the management. The factory management provides the recreational and education-
al influences which reach the lives of these young people. Few, if any, opportunities exist for modi-
fying rural forms of thought - except along the lines favored by the management; and, as is natural
under the circumstances, the management is careful to see that the ideas which reach the young workers
are such as will keep them docile and contented. A recent description written by a visitor to one of
these cotton spinning mills will show the sort of influence which is brought to bear upon the young
girls in t.he factories:
Nine hundred Japanese girls sat on the matted floor, their feet tucked under them, while
an old gentleman addressed them on "Mutual Love." The sermon over, a younger man - in shirt-
sleeves, for it was noon and hot - recited sentences from their scriptures. The girls made the
appropriate responses. He turned to an altar on which a white lily shone among the duller
Budihist emblems, and prayed for the old folks at home.
He had touched a sensitive chord, and with clasped hands and closed eyes the girls remem-
bered the farms in the deep country whence they had come. Then they sang three songs and dis-
persed, chattering, to their dormitory rooms. At 2 o'clock they reappeared, wearing, instead
of their Japanese dress, a "gym" costume of short serge skirt and white blouse, and streamed
across the campus to the factory of the Fuji Cotton Spinning Company. . .

"Welfare" work in a factory of this type includes providing some medical care, bathing and wash-
ing facilities. light and airy workrooms, and meals at low cost, as well as some school instruction
and recreational opportunities. However, it is clear that any system of housing and feeding factory

Some of the dormitories are quite pleasant places, except that they are all under the
shadow of their factories. They are clean and airy and they have small gardens about them,
careful sanitation according to Japanese standards, and various social features. But some are
not well kept. Too many girls are crowded together into one room for sleeping quarters. The
night and day shifts share the same quarters, the same bedding. This is not often true, but
it does happen. Sanitation is careless. The food is bad, or if not bad, unpalatable.
In the best factories, the food is a source of dissatisfaction and unrest. The usual meal
consists chiefly of rice, potatoes, daikon (a kind of pickled radish) and tea. . .
An investigation into the physical condition of operatives living in factory dormitories
in Tokyo City in May, 1930, made by the metropolitan police with the assistance of diet experts,
disclosed the fact that a large number of occupants of factory dormitories are badly under-
nourished. The police and the experts pointed out to the factory management that it was often
not so much a question of the quality of food served as the lack of variety in the menus that
led to the undernourishment of the operatives. One large factory dormitory, it was said,
served miso-shiru (a bean soup) and pickles at breakfast, salted salmon at dinner, and miso-
shiru and pickles at supper; and the same menu had been served for years.8
Wages (which do not include everything received by the workers, and which are only one factor
in judging living standards) are low, averaging 80 sen (a sen 1s 1/lo0 of a yen) for a working day
of from 8 to 10 hours or more; from this 80 sen, 13 sen a day are paid by the employee for the fac-
tory meals. Dormitory accommodations are furnished without charge, as are the various "welfare" ser-

He goes on to say that when hours of work are taken into consideration the low wages

Some reasons why the girls from the villages are persuaded to enter factories and to live under
conditions which limit their freedom and pay them little, are the poverty of their parents and the
fact that the Japanese girl of the rural regions has relatively little freedom at any time. Brought
up in an environment in which the family system, controlled by the father or other male head, 1s
still strong and the wishes or desires of individuals are subordinated to the welfare of the family
group as a whole, she expects to do whatever seems best for the family. Though the factory wages are
small, the money which can be sent from her wages to her family makes an appreciable difference in
the small budget of the Japanese farmer.

cotton textile industry of Japan has remained largely untouched by any Japanese labor movement, and

Though the manufacture of cotton textiles is the largest industry of Japan, Japanese do not
consider its labor conditions typical. Textile manufacture can make use of unskilled labor, and it
1s contended there is justification for treating unskilled young workers in a paternalistic manner.
The newer chemical industries which employ skilled labor, it is asserted, are more typical; here the
workers are better paid, the turnover less, and the methods more advanced. However, in industries of
this type, continual technical improvement results - as elsewhere in the world - in increased unem-

culture or other rural work, the number of unemployed remaining in the industrial districts is, com-

of support is another factor contributing to the weakness of the labor movement in Japan.
All industrial workers in Japan are not so docile and easily man ed as the girls of the textile
mills, but it is to the advantage of both government and industrial leaders to emphasize traditional
attitudes which will keep all workers fairly contented with thei situation. The attitude which is
highly appreciated is expressed in the words of a Japanese industrialist:
The rapid industrial progress which Japan has achieved during the past half century is,
indeed, phenomenal, and the causes are not far to seek. First is the spiritual discipline in
which the Japanese people have been tempered for centuries and the excellent workmanship re-
sulting from such discipline. The energy and industry of the people, the simplicity in Japa-
nese mode of living and the system of cooperation they display in industry may be counted as
other contributing factors. ..
I have at one of my factories a very efficient worker whom I consider the leading expert
in the paper manufacturing industry in Japan. I sent him abroad with the 1dea that he might
learn something more in his profession. I was told that he took a dagger with him when he left
Japan for the United States. One day I asked him why he took the weapon with him when he went
to America. He hesitated to tell me the reason, but finally owned up that he was going to end
his life if he could not maintain his honor among the American workers as an efficient repre-
sentative of his craft in Japan. My instructions were simply for him to go to America to study
more about the industry, but he had taken his task very seriously and went on his mission with
the great determination not to tarnish the reputation of what is meant by an efficient Japanese
worker.1o
The existence of such traditional attitudes and points of view is one reason why the labor move-
ment in Japan is relatively undeveloped. Other causes for this have just been mentioned - the rela-
tively small number of the unemployed, and the small size of the proletarian class, due to the fact
that young girls, temporarily employed, form so large a proportion of the textile workers. Still an-
other factor influencing the labor movement is the government control of the majority of the labor or-
ganizations. Trade unions enroll less than ten per cent of the industrial workers, and all but a very
minute fraction of this small number belong to unions which are controlled by the government. These
organizations, known as "Right Wing" unions, are much less concerned with securing higher wages and
better conditions of work than with backing the policies of the government, and they are thus entirely
opposed to fundamental social and economic changes. When, for example, the assistant director of the
International Labour Office visited Japan in 1934, he had a number of interviews with persons in dif-
expressed opinions which showed a remarkable degree of agreement. Government leaders said, for example:

Labour leaders made a sta+ement including the following:
It is very deplorable for the cause of the peace of the world as well as for the progress
of mankind that a campaign against the expansion of Japanese overseas trade is being organized
in various countries, especially in Europe and America. And the most regrettable thing in more
than one sense for us is that, as one of the reasons for that agitation, the wages of the Japa-
nese workers are being cited as low wages. . .
Even when an improvement of working conditions has been obtained, it is quite possible
that the conditions of employment in Japan may still not be "nominally" the same as those pre-
vailing in Europe and the United States. From that point of view, which is purely one of fig-
ures, Japanese wages will continue to be low. In order to understand this fact it is not suf-
ficient to take into account the conditions of labour and industry. Allowance must also be
made for the climatic, geographical and demographic conditions prevailing in Japan, its his-
torical traditions, the racial traits of the Japanese people, their mode of living, and also
the international situation.
In the matter of food, housing and clothing, the Japanese are a people of simple and fru-
gal life . . . This, however, does not necessarily mean a low standard of living, but simply a
qualitative difference between the life of the West and that of the East. The simple, frugal
life of the Japanese means a comparatively cheap cost of living, and it 1s here that the real
significance of the relatively low wage rates must be sought.11
In addition to the "Right Wing" unions which join with the government in presenting a "united
front" when explaining Japanese labor conditions, there is a small "Left Wing" organization which
had in 1935 a membership of only about 15,000 persons. Leaders of this group do not defend 1abor
conditions in Japan in terms of the simple frugal life of the people; they believe that labor has
been exploited to serve political purposes and to enable the expansion of Japan's overseas trade.
They have for their goal the betterment of the life of the workers, but they have to steer a diffi-
cult course and avoid any suspicion of being unpatriotic. Hence they do not advocate fundamental
political, social and economic changes. They desire merely a fairer wage and better living condi-
tions.
Radical groups advocating socialist or communist ideas are illegal and must work underground.
Members of any such organizations are always under threat of arrest or imprisonment. In l932 alone
over 8,ooo people were arrested and imprisoned for suspected connection with radical organizations.
The suspects were not all workers; many were young students or university graduates. The strikes
which occur in Japan - and there are many - generally take place in individual factories, in protest
against particular situations; they are not the expression of a growing political consciousness among
the workers of Japan. Since radical thought must work in secret, the extent of the spread of poli-
tical consciousness among the proletariat cannot be estimated.
It is clear that the labor movement in Japan is undeveloped and 1mmature. It seems reasonable
to conclude that it will remain immature so long as: (1) so many of the workers are women tempora-
rily recruited from the rural regions where traditions are strong; (2) the government succeeds in
controlling the majority of the labor organizations; (3) radical organizations are suppressed; (4)
unemployment is not a pressing cause for unrest because of the fact that rural families care for
their unemployed members; (5) industrial workers are relatively better off than the farmers; and (6)
household and small-scale industry (in which many of the workers earn most of their living elsewhere)
plays so prominent a part in the industrial set-up.

What about the life of the workers in small household industrial establishments? In the words
of a recent observer:
In a small industrial town, at the foot of a beautiful mountain range, a small wooden
house stands among rice fields and mulberry groves. In the house are six broad looms, of the
usual size, which are worked by electricity. The staff of this small home industry consists
of the owner, his wife and the neighbor's child, and they are all very busy.
They begin work in the morning at six o'clock. Three times a day they rest: twice for
fifteen minutes and once for thirty minutes. The machines are stopped in the evening at half-
past six. Then next day's work is prepared; the woman cooks a meal and the man writes his
letters. Twice a month they take a day off.
There 1s no door between the family's bed-sitting-room and the workshop where the looms
are rattling. The floor of this room is somowhat raised and is covered with a mat. There 1s
a low table, a few cushions and a small iron bowl to hold glowing charcoal. Beyond 1s the
kitchen.
Each of the second-hand looms costs 90 yen. They are sold in the village street just as
elsewhere bicycles might be offered for sale. The man owns the looms, but he is 300 yen in
debt. His creditor is either a merchant or a factory owner of whom he buys his yarn and to
whom he sells his cloth. . . .
The man and his wife earn about llo yen a month. The electricity they use, very cheaply
generated by water power, costs them about.....15 yen a month. The neighbor's child is paid
40 yen a year... The taxes are not much more than 6 yen a year.
The average daily production of this home industry is 30o yards of good cloth, woven in
many-coloured patterns. Most of the orders received are for the export trade. Therefore this
man is better off than his neighbor who manufactures kimono materiai for home consumption.
This neighbor uses ten narrow looms, which he has bought second-hand for 50 yen each. He, too,
has debts amounting to 3oo yen; and he, his wife and his brother work from six o'clock in the
morning until seven o'clock in the evening. He has two small children to support and his total
monthly income varies from 50 to 70 yen.
In a small wooden house in a side-road in Tokyo, behind a latticed sliding door, which
serves as a window as well, a man, a woman and a young girl are seated on the clean, mat-cov-
ered floor. They bundle and label pencils, which are brought to them from a factory near their
home. The pencils are tied together in neat little packages of twelve with gay pictures on
top. The family works with quick, automatic movements.
They work from early in the morning until late at night, and when the small children come
home from school they spend eight hours, so the mother says, helping the older members of the
family bundle and pack... The whole family, five people, earn on an average 50 to 60 yen a
month.
Forty families near the factory are employed in a similar manner. Before they get the
pencils, many other families in Northern Japan, in Hokkaido, a district rich in wood and
graphite, have worked under similar conditions making the unfinished pencils which are sent
to the Tokyo factory in huge bundles.
The factory itself is merely a large handicraft plant laid out in thinly walled wooden
workshops of somewhat improvised appearance. The machinery is more or less primitive. The
forty men and women employed in this factory are mostly young and they earn between 15 and 30
yen a month. Only the finishing of the pencils is done here; they are painted, polished and
the name is printed on them. In all, the factory sees to the planning of the work of about a
hundred smali family enterprises, from the purchase of raw materials to the distribution of the
finished pencils. .. .
A mechanic at the "pencil combine" . . . told us about this complicated family budget. . .
This man has two sources of income. As a mechanic he earns 33 yen a month. He works
every day from seven o clock in the morning to six o'clock in the evening, with an hour's rest
at noon and two free days a month. While the export trade is as prosperous as it is at pres-
ent, he receives a month's wages as a bonus every six months.
He earns a second income as a small employer. He and his wife work at home for the pencil
factory, and they employ three neighbors' children to help them. When he comes home from the
factory he rests for a short time, and after his wife has seen to her two little children and
the household, she and her husband work three hours in the evening. They also devote most of
the two free days a month to this homework. After the man's wages have been paid, this man has
14 yen a month from this second source of income, his total earnings being 47 yen, excluding
bonuses.
His house, near the factory, is small and old. It has room for 10 mats, and the rent 1s
only 9 yen a month. He spends about 3 yen a month on coal, gas, and electric light. He pays
O.60 yen a month for his health insurance; the factory pays the other half. His wife and
children are not insured.

This family's average daily expenditure for food is O.60 yen. They spend about 4 yen a

The illustrations selected are, in the opinion of the writers quoted, typical of situations in
certain kinds of Japanese industrial establishments. Thus it would appear that industrial workers
in Japan in general work longer hours for smaller pay than the workers in other exporting countries,
and that young girls do a considerable proportion of the work in large textile mills, and both women
and children assist in household industries. It would also seem thit the standard of living is low,
but this statement cannot be made without the type of qualification indicated by the Government and
Labour leaders whose opinions were quoted earlier. The diet of the Japanese people is different
from the diet of western countries; it includes afmost no meat, butter, or milk, all of which are
expensive - and a great deal of cheaper foods such as rice, pickles, bean products (the chief pro-
tein element in the diet), and some fish. Household furniture is simple and inexpensive; bedding,
mats, cushions, low tables, rice bowls and cups equip a home in comfort. House-building 1s simple
and not costly; the same room serves for living, eating, and sleeping, since the bedding laid on the
floor is rolled up and put away during the day. Japanese clothing is not necessarily expensive.
While the apparently simple Japanese home of the wealthy may represent the expenditure of a great
deal of money - costly woods, carefully selected panels, delicate porcelain, priceless scroll paint-
ings - the home of the poor may be suitably equipped, according to Japanese standards, at little cost.
Privacy is scarcely known in any Japanese style home, with its sliding paper partitions, and hence
the lack of privacy in the crowded homes of the workers does not necessarily indicate tenement social
conditions. Because of the general simplicity in living, "a given unit of purchasing power represents
probably more civilization in Japan than elsewhere in the world." 13
Also, while the whole set-up
may seem to indicate a low standard of living, the standard of living of the urban worker is higher
than that of the farmer.
The production of silk differs from the types of manufacture already examined in that it overlaps
both agriculture and industry. In its earlier stages it involves the work of farmers, and rural fam-
1lies often carry through the production of raw silk to its final stages. Any examination of working
conditions in this industry takes us naturally to a consideration of other aspects of rural life. An-
other reason for considering the silk producers of Japan is that silk, as late as 1929, accounted for
thirty per cent of the exports of all Japan and, in spite of the lessened demand for silk on account
of the world depression and the development of rayon as a substitute for silk fabrics, silk still rep-
resents over one quarter of Japan's exports.
The mulberry trees which furnish the food for the silk worms are raised on mountainous slopes
which are unsuitable for the cultivation of rice. The raising of silk-worms, which is exacting and
demands painstaking care, is a seasonal occupation limited to the time when the mulberry leaves are
young. Women and children can do the work required and thus add to the family income. In 1932,
2,065,000 rural households in Japan were engaged in the industry.
When the eggs are hatched, the tiny worms are brushed off the egg sheet into shallow trays which
must be kept in a place where the temperature is carefully regulated. For the first few days of their
1ives, the worms must be fed very frequently, perhaps every hour of the day and night. The leaves
must be picked fresh, but they must not be damp. The fresh leaves are chopped into very fine pieces
at first; as the worms grow larger, the feeding times are not so frequent, and the leaves may final-
1y be given whole. During the beginning stages, then, the persons responsible for raising the silk-
worms are almost continually busy, and constant attention is required until the silk-worm spins its
cocoon.
After the cocoon is completed, a few days may elapse before the silk is reeled. If the cocoons
are to be transported to a filature for reeling, they are packed in bales. Otherwise, the reeling is

In the silk reeling industry, 92 per cent of the workers were women, and of these over 18 per cent

meals and rest, while two rest days are given per month. All of these figures exclude the household
establishments where the returns are less, the hours longer, and the labor of children may be used.
The picture of working conditions in this industry would be incomplete if it consisted only in
descriptions of the labor involved, the wage scales, and the hours. The existence of other factors
1s suggested in the words of a Japanese writer:
The author once saw a pair of votive lanterns dedicated to the tutelary gods of a certain
silk filature. On one of these lanterns were engraved the characters, "On the Occasion of the

numbered among the few that could turn out the yarn of that specific quality. In gratitude
for this, the girls collected money from among themselves and had these lanterns erected for
the benefit of those who might come to the shrine when it is dark. The lanterns are therefore
lights in the dark literally and figuratively.14

Chapter 8
THE FARMERS OF JAPAN
Farming is still the chief occupation of the Japanese - about half the people of the country
are included in the households of the farmers. Rice, the chief crop, is the staple food of the
people, and Japanese rice is different from varieties raised in other countries. Not until the
preferred variety was cultivated in Korea and Formosa did rice from the colonies find a ready market
in Japan.
The farmers of old Japan developed a very fine technique of rice culture. They terraced and
diked the patches, irrigated the plots, fertilized the soil, and planted, cultivated, harvested, and
husked the crop by laborious hand labor. Modern science could offer some improved techniques to les-
sen the labor and increase the yield, particularly along the line of commercial fertilizers, systems
of seed selection, and power machinery. This last, however, has a limited sphere of usefulness under
Japanese conditions. Machinery is suited to large-scale agriculture on flat lands, and such lands
are not only scarce in Japan, but most of them are divided up among numerous cultivators. Power
pumps could replace irrigation devices run by man-power, and they have to some extent, but such ma-
chines are expensive and man-power is cheap. Consequently, Japanese farming has not been modernized
and improved to the same extent that industry has; the farmers of Japan, while they use commercial
fertilizer and improved methods of seed selection, still follow traditional methods.
Since the beginning of the Meiji era, the population of Japan has doubled, and is increasing at
the rate of approximately 1,000,000 a year. The lands under cultivation have increased in the same
period by about 25 per cent, but the general opinion seems to be that all the land suitable for cul-
tivation 1s now being utilized. It was mentioned much earlier that only about 15 per cent of the
land is cultivable. When this small area is divided among the millions of rural households, small
holdings result, averaging about 2 acres per household. The average is not, however, the most com-
mon holding; 69 per cent of the households have less than the average, and 34 per cent have less than
1: acres from which to wring a living. These small holdings are not in one place, but are made up of
scattered patches, some very small. The nature of the land and the way in which rice is cultivated
have something to do with this uneconomic arrangement; other reasons may be found in the original
division of the lands under the feudal system. It will be remembered that when feudalism was abol-
1shed, the farmers were allowed to continue to work the fields which they had been cultivating; as
time went on, they might lease new patches, or sell part of their holdings, or bring some new patch
on the mountain side under cultivation, and thus accumulate a holding which consisted of scattered
fields.
Attempts have been made to consolidate the scattered holdings in regions where the nature of
the land permits this, and to use large-scale methods of cultivation on the larger paddy fields thus
obtained. Several things have retarded this development. One 1s the high price of agricultural
land; in 1920 the price per acre averaged about $1200 and in 1931 $800 (figuring the yen at par in
both cases). Another is the high rate of interest charged rural borrowers by money lenders; this
rate varies from 10 to 12 per cent, a higher rate than that charged other borrowers in Japan. Sti1l
another factor 1s the cost of machinery which would make the cultivation of consolidated holdings
profitable. Under these circumstances, the creation of large consolidated holdings would involve
the outlay of considerable capital which the farmers of Japan do not possess and which they could
only secure at ruinous rates. Capitalists in Japan hesitate to invest their money in agriculture
since the tax on incomes received from agriculture is much greater than the tax on the same income
derived from industry or trade. For example:

These conditions help to perpetuate small-scale intensive cultivation in Japan.
The preferential income tax applies not only to larger incomes but 1s extended to the lowest
incomes on the tax lists. In amount and in proportion, the landlords and peasant proprietors pay
much more in taxes than the most prosperous manufacturers and traders.
The contrast is amazing, as appears from recent figures compiled by the Imperial Agricul-
tural Association. In the annual income group of 300 yen, peasant proprietors pa1d 35% in
taxes, while manufacturers paid 1.5 and traders 12.5. In the 500 yen group, landlords pa1d 51,
peasant proprietors 31.5, manufacturers 18 and traders 14% approximately.2
The origin of the tax discrimination in favor of industry and trade was the government policy
adopted when modern industry was beginning, when Japan "was then predominantly agricultural. Nothing
was more natural, therefore, than that it should tax farming, directly and indirectly, to pay the
costs of industrialization. The first industries were aided with Government subsidies, paid by the
farmers. They were given tariff protection. Again the farmer paid. He is still paying, even though
industry is prosperous and he is sinking into a quagmire of debts." 3
In 1931, 26 per cent of the households engaged in farming owned no land at all and worked on
rented land, for which they paid 50 or 60 per cent of the crop raised as an annual rent. Of the re-
mainder of the farming households, 42 per cent owned some land and rented other fields which they
cultivated. Tenants and small tenant-owners paying rent in produce have little, 1f anything, to do
with the marketing of their crop. Owners, on the other hand, needing cash for taxes, are most fre-
quently obliged to sell their crop as soon as it is harvested, at a time when the price is lowered
because the market is glutted. In l932, according to surveys made in Japan, the average annual in-
come per farm household of five and a half persons was 388 yen. In that year, the average household
went 22l yen deeper into debt, making the average indebtedness 837 yen. Tenant farmers, under such
conditions, desire reduction in rents; but the owner, forced to sell at an unfavorable time and
obliged to pay disproportionately high taxes, 1s not disposed to lower the rents. Agrarian disputes
which have marked recent years have had their origin largely in the demand of the tenant for rent
reductions; in the attempt of the landowner to raise the rents when leases were renewed; or in the
refusal of the owner to re-lease to old tenants because the lands were going over to new tenants or
were to be worked by the owner employing hired labor. The following figures show the growing dis-

and economic reform which would make the farmers' situation more bearable would be too revolutionary
to appeal widely to the Japanese peasantry who merely ask for some favorable modification of local
conditions. One observer of life in the rural regions sums up the situation in these words:
Japanese aestheticism, the victorious army and navy, the smoking chimneys of Osaka, the
pushing mercantile marine, the Parliamentary and administrative developments of Tokyo and a
costly worldwide diplomacy are all borne on the bent backs of...the Japanese farmer and his
wife. The depositories of the authentic Yamato damashi1 (Japanese spirit) are to be found
knee-deep in the sludge of their paddy fields.5
Throughout Japanese history, as we have seen earlier, the farmers contributed the greater part
of the revenue which maintained the state. The toiling farmer and his wife, "knee-deep in the sludge
of their paddy fields," have been familiar elements in the Japanese scene for centuries - but the na-
tional and provincial expenses of the state have increased enormously at a time when the farmer was
being deprived of old sources of subsidiary income, and being made less self-sufficient. Cotton
cloth used in the rural household used to be spun and woven in the household; tabi, sandals, clothing,
were made in the home. Now cotton spinning 1s carried on entirely in large factories, which are tak-
ing over more and more of the cloth weaving as well. Tabi, the universal footgear, are produced en-
tirely in factories. Silk culture, a very important source of subsidiary income, is uncertain; it is
dependent upon foreign market conditions, and when the demand for silk or the price of silk drops,
some 36 per cent of all the farmers of Japan are deprived of a large part of the additional income
which enables them to get along. Moreover, as we have seen, while there 1s still a large amount of
hand reeling, the trend is toward machine reeling in factories. But rice farming alone cannot sup-
port the rural households, under the present circumstances.
In Japan, as in all other industrial countries, the farm problem is a chronic one. The situation
in Japan is particularly acute because of the shortage of land; government leaders make much of the
argument that emigration is one essential solution. But, as we pointed out much earlier in this bock,
emigration alone has never yet solved a population problem. Moreover, there are certain factors in
Japanese life which restrict emigration. Until Hokkaido was developed in the Meiji period, Japan had
no frontier to attract the enterprise of the adventurous; there was no outside stimulus to the pioneer
spirit. Also, the family system of Japan emphasized the subordination of the individual to the group:
Personal initiative was alien to the Japanese tradition which gave the people no opportunity to devel-
op ideas of freedom and independence. Consequently, even when a frontier region was available, as it
was in Hokkaido, the farmers of Japan were unwilling, perhaps unable, to take advantage of the new op
portunities and to emigrate on a large scale. Manchuria has not attracted Japanese farmers. These
facts lead many authorities to conclude that Japanese would not emigrate, even if all immigration re-
strictions existing in different foreign countries were removed.
Immigration restrictions, however, exist, and are resented in Japan, not only because they pre-
vent the Japanese from settling in such favorable regions as Australia, New Zealand and the United
States, where the pioneer spirit is no longer called for and which therefore might attract them; but
also because these restrictions are regarded as an insult to the Japanese people. Probably the great-
est resentment is that felt against the United States, which in 1924 terminated the Gentlemen's Agree-
ment and barred Japanese immigrants on the same basis on which other Asiatics had long been barred.
The Gentlemen's Agreement made in 1907 was an understanding by which the Japanese government provided
not to 1ssue passports to laborers desiring to go to the continental United States. During the years
the agreement was in force, approximately l20,o00 Japanese entered the United States, and approximate-
1y 112,ooo departed. Under the terms of the agreement, the wives of Japanese living in the United
States were permitted to join their husbands, and many thousands of "picture brides" came in under
this provision. The custom of sending "picture brides," the establishment of Japanese families, and
the consequent increase in the size of the Japanese population concentrated in agricultural regions
on the west coast of the United States, were regarded with alarm in these states particularly since

The influence of Congressmen from the coast states feeling strongly on the matter of restricting
Japanese immigration had a great deal to do with the passing of the law of 1924. An unfortunate note
from the Japanese Ambassador at Washington,in which he seemed, on behalf of his government, to threat-
en the United States with dire consequences if this measure were passed, had the effect of hastening
the action of Congress. Since the position of the coast states at the time the law was advocated has
been given, it is only fair to state that today there is a considerable body of opinion, even in the
western states, in favor of some arrangement which, while fully maintaining the actual exclusion of
Orientals, would be less hurtful to their pride.
The farmers of Japan not only show an unwillingness to leave their crowded fields for districts
which are open to them, but they are much less vocal concerning their difficulties than are, for ex-
ample, the farmers of the United States. The American farmers of the great western plains were ad-
venturous pioneers; the American tradition emphasizes independence and personal initiative - and
American farmers do not remain silent about their problems. Moreover, universal manhood suffrage
has existed in the United States ever since the country was founded. But in Japan, a property
qualification for voting automatically shut out the masses of the people from exercising the suf-
frage, until l925, when universal manhood suffrage was granted. Consequently, by tradition and prac-
tice, the Japanese farmer is not politically-minded, nor independent.
When the patient farmers of Japan did become vocal, and in l9l8 and the years just following
there were rice riots all over the country, the Government began to take some steps to relieve the
chronic troubles of the peasantry. A system to control the price of rice was tried in 192l, changed
in 1931, and revised again in 1933. Rice price control had two aims - to prevent the price from
falling too low and thus injuring the farmers, and to keep the price from rising so high as to create
discontent in the cities. In l931, the Government was empowered to buy rice when the price reached a
minimm, and to sell when 1t reached a maximum; but minimum and maximum prices were to be determined

Other measures taken by the Government have aided the farmers to a degree. For example, a
tariff on wheat prevented foreign competition with Japanese-grown wheat. Wheat grown as a winter
grain on paddy fields provided the tenant farmer, who paid his rent in rice, with additional income,
and helped the other farmers as well. Since 1932, Japan has produced the wheat consumed in the coun-
try, so this source of additional income cannot be further expanded.
It 1s evident that Government measures taken to relieve the farmers are inadequate in extent and
in scope; they represent a compromise between the interests of the farmers and the cities. They do
not deal with fundamental difficulties, such as unequal taxation, the landholding and renting systems,
the uneconomic small-scale methods of agricultural production. They do not make it possible for the
farmer to become permanently more well-to-do; they do not permanently increase his security, his com-
fort, or his purchasing power. They perpetuate the small home market which makes necessary the des-
perate struggle for foreign markets for manufactured goods.
More than one foreign writer analyzing the situation of the Japanese farmers feels that, sooner
or later, they must rise in revolt. Such a forecast may be correct, but at the same time the strength
and tenacity of Japanese traditional forms of thought and behavior, and the influences brought to bear
upon the rural population to keep these traditions alive and vigorous, are elements which can not be
entirely ignored. A few concrete illustrations may help to give an idea of these factors.
From time to time there are such things as tenants' strikes. Mr. Yamasaki assured me that
the problem of the rural districts can be solved only by appealing to the feelings of the people
in the right way. He said that "the Japanese are largely moved by feelings, not by convictions.
In some coastwise counties, someone told me, a hurricane destroyed the crops to such an extent
that the tenants could not pay rent, and the landlords who depended on their rents were impover-
ished. Things reached such a pass that a hundred thousand peasants signed a paper swearing
fidelity to an anti-landlord propaganda. Then Mr. Yamasak1 went, and, sitting in the local tem-
ple, talked things over with both sides for days. He got the landlords to say that they were
sorry for their tenants and the tenants to say that they were sorry for their landlords, and
eventually he was allowed to burn the oath-attested document in the temple.
One day, when I was staying in a rural district, I was invited to a remoter part in order
to see something of the discipline that the members of a group of young men's associations were
1mposing on themselves... Nearly six hundred young men were in the parade... The physical con-
dition of the young fellows was good and their evolut1ons with dummy "rifles" were smart and
skillful. The paraders seemed lost in their desire to do their best for their credit's sake
and their own good. . . The secret of this surprising display far away in the heart of Japan
was that the work of the young men had been done under the direction of two fit, be-medalled
army surgeons, reserve officers, who were present in order to answer my questions.
Every morning half an hour before sunrise these Y. M. A. (Young Men's Association) members
assemble in the grounds of their Shinto shrine or of their school, where they exercise until
the sun shows itself. In the evenings after work they also fence, wrestle, lift weights, and
develop their wrists.
The members endeavour to cultivate their minds as well as their bodies, and they also ob-
serve in their dress a self-denying ordinance. . .
The object of all this varied discipline is to develop physique, self-control, self-re-
spect, and what the Japanese call the spirit of association, or, as we might say, good fellow-
ship.. .

For seven years in succession the men, old, middle-aged, and young, who had done the

culture and the Home Office. . . .
Some of the audience used to weep as the older men told their tales. The farmer's would
sit up late around a farmer or a professor who was telling about some subject that interested
them. The originator of these gatherings. . . told me that he was "more than once moved to

The addresses of the earnest Tokyo officials and the Governor were directed towards urging
on the farmers increased production and increased labour, and the duty was pressed upon them,
as I understood, in the name of the highest patriotism and of devotion to their ancestors.
One of my hosts, who was thirty-two, hoped to see all his tenants peasant proprietors be-
fore he was fifty. The relation of this landlord and his tenants was illustrated by the fact
that on my arrival several farmers brought produce to the kitchen "because we heard that the
landlord had guests.".
This landlord's family had lived in the same house for eleven generations. The courtesy
of my hosts and his relatives and the beauty of their old house and its contents are an inef-

to do anything for us. The ladies of the house cooked our food and the landlord and his younger
brother brought it to us. The younger brother waited upon us throughout our meals, even peeling
our pears. At night ne spread our silk-covered futon (mattresses). In the morning he folded

When on our arrival in the house we sat and talked in the first reception-room we entered,
I noticed that outside the lattice a company of villagers was listening with no consciousness
of intrusion, in full view of our host, to the sound of foreign speech. It was a Shakespearean
scene.
The rural policeman is not only a paternal guardian of the peace but an administrative
official. He keeps an eye on public health. He is charged with correctly maintaining the rec-
ord of names and addresses - and some other particulars - of everybody in the village. It is
his duty to secure correct information as to the name, age, place of origin and real business
of every stranger. He attends all public meetings, even of the young men's and young women's
associations, and no strolling players can give their entertainment without his presence. . .
At the houses of well-to-do people I was struck by the way in which the local police officer
.. . called with the headman and joined our kneeling circle in the reception room. Nominally
he came to pay his respects, but his chief object, no doubt, was to take stock of what was go-
ing on.

More than half the expenditure of many a village is on education, which in Japan is com-

I spent some time in a typical inland village. The very last available yard of land was
utilized. The cottages stood on plots buttressed by stone, and only the well-to-do had a yard
or garden; paddy came right up to the foundations. Now that the rice was high no division

I asked a landowner who was in a comfortable position what societies there were in his

society of householders, such as is mentioned in Confucius, which met in the spring and autumn,
and ate and drank and discussed local topics "with open heart.". . . The householders' meet-

There were in the village, in addition to the householders' organization, the usual reservists'

(Story told by a blind headman in a village)
"Although I thought it important to advance the economic condition of the village it was

same, it was necessary to bring about an understanding. I began by asking landowners to contrib-

rice as the priests do. . . In the fourth year a hundred tenants came in a deputation to me.
They said:
This gathering of rice is for our benefit. . . So please let us contribute every year.'.
I was very pleased with that. But I did not express my pleasure. I scolded them. I said,
Your plan is good but you think only of yourselves. You do not give the landowners their
due. When you bring your rent to them you choose inferior rice. It is a bad custom.' I ad-
