tenant and landowner.
In the next year the tenants exerted themselves and the landowners were pleased with them.
hus the relation between landlord and tenant became better. The landowners in their turn be-
came desirous of showing a friendly feeling toward the tenants. Some landlords came to me and
said, If you wish for any money in order to be of any service to the tenants, we will lend it
to you without interest.' I received some money. I lent money to tenants to buy manure and
cattle, to attack insect pests, to provide protection against wind and flood and to help build
new dwellings nearer their work. By these means the tenants were encouraged and their welfare
was promoted. The landlords were also happier, for the rice was better and the land improved.
The landlords found that their happiness came from the tenants. There was good feeling between
them. The landlords began to help the tenants directly and indirectly. Roads and bridges and
many aids to cultivation were furnished by the landlords. A body of landlords was constituted
for these purposes and it collected money. My 1dea was realized that the way of teaching the
villages is to let landlords and tenants realize that their interests agree and they will be-
come more friendly."
(A concrete illustration of the working of the Japanese family system, which is still es-
pecially strong in the rural regions. . . .)
"A married B. B dies without having any children. A next married B's sister, C. Then,
because of the necessity of having a male heir for the maintenance of the family, and because
he thought it unlikely that his wife, C, would have children as her dead sister, B, had had
none, he adopted his wife's younger brother, D. But the wife, C, did have children. Conse-
quently, not only is A's wife his sister-in-law and lhis eldest son' his wife's brother, but
his children are his eldest  son's' nephews. The eldest of these children, E, is legally the
younger son. He says, I am glad that instead of an uncle I have an elder brother. I am much
attached to him and he 1s attached to me. I am not sorry to be younger instead of elder
brother, for when my father dies my adopted brother will become head of the family and he must
then bring up his younger brothers and sisters, manage the family fortunes, bear the family
troubles and keep all the cousins and uncles in good humour by inviting them occasionally and
at other times by visiting them and giving them presents.'

"It is obvious that our family system, for speaking in criticism of which officials have
been dismissed from their posts, puts too much stress on the family and too little on the in-
dividual. The family is the unit of society. Any member of it 1s only a fraction of that

and you seldom find such a thing happening among farmers. The family system, by which all is

The Young Men's Association described in one of these quotations grew out of local organizations
of Tokugawa days, when, in the years of seclusion, local clubs interested themselves in community wel-
fare and in providing amusement and recreation for the young men of the rural districts. with the
abolition of feudalism and the resulting changes in the rural regions, these youth organizations did
not find a new sphere of usefulness until the foreign wars of Japan appealed to their patriotic emo-
tions. The local clubs then undertook to make articles needed by the soldiers at the front, or to
assist in farming the fields from which the laborers had been called to the army, and the Government
began to encourage local governors and officials to support the youth organizations. Army reserve
officers have been very active in directing and assisting the club enterprises which include social
meetings, lecture meetings, athletics, excursions, repairing roads and bridges, caring for shrine
and temple grounds, establishing libraries, and engaging in agricultural experimental work. The
organizations, now known as the Young Men's League, had in 1933 a membership of over 2,700,000. By
far the largest number of these were young men of the villages, who had not entered the middle or
nigher schools after completing their primary education.
The nature of the Japanese family system, and its persistence in the rural regions, is suggested
in the last quotation. We have seen that very much earlier in Japanese history family headship was
given to some male member of the family group, to that person who could best look after the interests
of the family during the disorders of the feudal wars. Since under these circumstances women were
not, in general, either an economic or administrative asset, their position was subordinated to that
of the men of the household. Obedience to the head of the family and subservience to the husband were
inculcated in the Japanese woman.
The Japanese family system embraces relatives of varying degrees of kinship, not necessarily
living under one roof, or even in the same region. When a decision is to be made concerning the mar-
riage of a son or daughter, or the education of children, or choice of vocation or occupation, or
similar matters, the family council is called, and the decision made in terms of the good of the fam-
1ly group. Individuals brought up under this system expect to agree with the group decision; they in
turn expect the support and encouragement of the family in case difficulties arise later in their own
lives. The family system offers a sort of social security which has both its good and less good as-
pects - it provides for the care of dependents, and sometimes, unfortunately, encourages lack of
responsibility among those who are unwilling to do their share. The family system is the psycholog-
ical basis of the group loyalties which are so marked in the Japanese people; carried over from the
family to the nation, it gives to the Japanese sentiments of devotion to the state their peculiar
strength and quality. While western ideas of individualism have broken down the family system to
a degree, the change has been most marked in the cities, not. in the rural regions.
Another influence making for conservatism is Shinto. In the villages the Shinto shrines have
many functions, and are centers for community life. Ancient religious festivals are observed, and
loyalties which give strong support to the present government of Japan.

The picture of the life of the farmers as a whole is that of a simple people valuing tradition-
al forms of thought and behavior, shut off from new or radical influences, and sincerely trying to
meet new conditions in the spirit of their traditions of frugality, loyalty, obedience, and industry.
Without fundamental changes which, under present circumstances, can come only from the government -
changes in the systems of taxation, of landholding, and of credit, for example - it appears that the
earnest efforts of the farmers themselves to deal with their problems cannot be effective enough to
relieve their pressing need. But, because of the strength and tenacity of tradition, and because of
the numbers of governmental, military, and educational influences de: .gned to perpetuate these tradi-
tions, it appears that revolt among the farmers of Japan is still remote, in spite of the unfair condi-
tions imposed on them, and in spite of the pressing nature of their difficulties.

Chapter 9
CONFLICTING CURRENTS IN PRESENT-DAY JAPAN
The swift building of modern Japan is one of the interesting stories of history, but it has not
run so smoothly as might be thought from superficial observation. Preceding chapters have suggested
some of the problems which have developed as the country was modernized, but before we summarize
these we shall mention some of the outward contrasts which attract attention.
Contrasts of a noticeable type are most numerous in the cities. Here are modern department
stores and tiny traditional shops, large public buildings and streets lined with small houses, wide
thoroughfares and narrow alleys, great factories and busy household manufactories. Kimono-clad
women enter modern stores, are waited upon by clerks in western costume, and return to a Japanese-
style home. Outside the door of the home stands a row of footgear - sandals, clogs, western shoes -
removed by different members of the family when they entered the house. Inside the simply furnished
Japanese room may stand a foreign chair and desk, the property of a schoolboy son or of the business
man or professional man who is the head of the family. The pretentious home may boast a room or a
series of rooms furnished entirely in foreign style, overlooking the secluded Japanese garden. The
business man, the student, the teacher, the employee in the store or restaurant returning at night
changes into his comfortable kimono at home and joins the members of his family as they sit on cush-
ions on the soft padded floor mats before the low dining table set in Japanese style. If it is
cold, the room may be heated by a small stove burning oil, or wood and charcoal, or coal, instead of
by the charcoal brazier of earlier days. All of these western furnishings are relatively expensive,
and are not found in the homes of the poorer classes whose tiny dwellings are equipped only in Jap-
anese style.
Thouga the contrasts are most noticeable in the cities, the great dailies of Japan, most of
which are city publications but which circulate widely in the country, carry to the outlying dis-
tricts certain information concerning the changing life of the cities. The four large dailies, pub-
lished in Tokyo and Osaka, have estimated circulations of well over a million each, while smaller
papers published in the same cities have estimated circulations ranging from 100,000 to 600,000.
The combined number of daily newspapers in the two largest cities 1s, according to the Japan Year
Book, 25 per cent of all and their combined circulation covers almost all parts of the country.
These widely-read papers offer many concrete illustrations of the contrasting cultures in the
country.
The press, for example, gives such glimpses as these of the various sports enjoyed by the Jap-
anese:
In the Japanese fencing and Judo tournament of teams from all parts of the country, Chita
prefecture policemen won in Japanese fencing. Tokyo Metropolitan police won in Judo.
The baseball match between Waseda and Keio Universities will be held today and tomorrow.
Not only in Tokyo but all over the country, W and K stand gazing at each other. Waseda has
won 20 games out of the 37 games held with Keio in the past, has made the best record in the
whole League games of this season. Both teams are silent about their plans for today's battle
so that they can win the victory and make their mother school's prestige shine.1
Western sports are immensely popular. The Japanese desire to compete internationally on favorable
grounds with the nationals of other countries, and they have thrown themselves into the business of
developing world champ1ons in games, field sports, swimming and athletics in general. Physical
training and sports usually are encouraged by a militaristic regime, and sports and games have a
natural appeal. For these various reasons, Japan has made great strides in sports.

The developments just mentioned have brought with them changes of some significance in the life
of the Japanese woman. The girl swimmer in her brief costume, the feminine track champion in shorts,
appear to be a long way from the bowing young girl in the kimono greeting her father or her husband.
They are some distance even from the school girls of the last years of the Meiji period, as described

the wife of the Meiji Emperor:
Our royal guests watched our athletic exercises from beginning to end: Swedish gymnastics,
graceful minuets and square dances with orchestra accompaniment, and maple hunting - a dance
with purely Japanese music. About six hundred girls from five to seventeen took part in the
events of the day.

is no more marked than that between the American or European tennis players and swimmers of a few

recreational activities, would seem to open up a new mental horizon for the Japanese girl. One Jap-

The effect of all these forces upon a girl cast in the original mold of the medieval
tradition is incalculable. No woman who has ever mingled in the hurley-burley of economic

surfaces of the modern world, can be again the limited creature that she was before. Her
life opens up in a thousand directions at once. New ideas creep in, new wants develop. old
restrictions are thrown out. She is refurbished in a hundred ways; most of them superficial,
of course, but a few profound.

Yet in spite of the power and penetration of these disrupting forces the integrity of
the old traditions remain surprisingly firm. Their influence cannot be eradicated even from
the most Westernized Japanese woman. Quietness and self-effacement are her external qualities.
The formerly non-existent virtues of individuality, initiative and firmness are not easily cul-
tivated in a soil which is st'll conventionally inimical to them.4
The outward contrasts to be noticed in contemporary Japanese life are striking and picturesque,
but the significant conflicts lie elsewhere in the problems which modernization has brought to the
government, to international relations, to industry, and to agriculture.
The westernization of Japan's government involved developing parliamentary forms in the face of
feudal survivals, and modern government has been unable to resist completely the strong pressure
exerted by earlier clan leadership. Thus in spite of the "restoration" of the emperor, in spite of
his unique position in the Japanese state, he is so surrounded by a host of councillors and advisers
that he himself is not much more of an active factor in government than he was in the days of the
shogun and regents. Also, in spite of the machinery of parliamentarianism - political parties,
elections, and a national Diet - the Diet remains relatively powerless. Clan influences, not dis-
similar to those which shaped the essentially democratic governmental forms of China of the T'ang
into the bureaucracy of the Naii and Heian periods, have modified government institutions imported
recently into Japan, by adding them to the aristocratic bureaucracy which had been for centuries a
characteristic institution in Japan. However, parliamentary institutions do exist; they have as-
serted themselves at times and wrested control from the bureaucracy whenever strong public opinion
has been aroused in support of liberalism.
The modernization of Japan's industry involved industrial development on the basis of small-
scale feudal manufacturing, - which still persists. Paternalistic forms of control dating from feudal
days have been perpetuated in large industry as well as in small-scale manufacturing. Industrial
privileges have been granted to a few families, in much the same way as land grants were made in
feudal times; and thus financial power has come into the hands of these families not as a result of
competition, but as a gift from the Government. However, the proletariat of Japan, though small and
poorly organized, does exist, and it is possible that this group may cease to respond to the tradi-
tional forms of thought and behavior which are pressed upon them, and may take a more actiye part in
changing the conditions under which they live and work.
The farmers of Japan have been called upon to support the expensive program of political and in-
dustrial expansion. Their economic position has not been materially improved and they have been en-
couraged to continue to remain satisfied with frugal living. As a result the home market has not
developed in proportion to the industrial growth of the country. This has necessitated Japan's
search for foreign markets which has intensified the fierce competitive struggle of industrial na-
tions in the markets of the world. However, the literate farmers of Japan are becoming aware of the
way in which they have not shared in the prosperity of the country or in the profits of Japan's ex-
panding foreign trade.
This brief sumn.ary of the situations existing in government, international relations, industry,
and agriculture, shows that the conflicting currents in present-day Japan include more than the con-
trast between the new and the old, though this colors the whole, provides emotional drives, and con-
tributes to the tenseness of the general situation. But these conflicting currents involve as well
the struggle among various powerful groups - bureaucrats, army leaders, capitalists and landowners;
they include also the struggle between vested interests and the less privileged.
As illustrations of the conflicts among the groups in power, may be cited the differences be-
tween liberal political leaders and army heads; between army and capitalist families; between land-
owners and city capitalists. The more liberal political leaders, as we have seen, opposed military
expansionism on the Asiatic mainland; they questioned, for example, the high-handed actions of the

Kwantung Army in Manchuria and the disproportionate budgets demanded by the army, and they have
attempted to oppose the control of cabinets by the military. The army, many of whose younger of-
ficers were of rural birth, promised (in 193l-1932) to develop Manchuria for the benefit of the
people and to prevent the exploitation of the region by the capitalists of Japan. Thus the army
appeared to be opposed to the financial powers; but when it became apparent that the money needed
for the development of Manchuria could come only from the capitalists, the army heads ceased to em-
phasize the need of improving the economic status of all the people and began, instead, to admonish
the Japanese peasantry in familiar language, urging them to work harder and to be more frugal. When
the rural districts asked for relief, the government proposed measures which would benefit the land-
owners, not the poorer peasantry, and immediately the industrialists opposed this; they wished the
custom of favoring industry at the expense of agriculture to be continued. Thus landowners and city
capitalists were brought into opposition.
The struggle between vested interests and the less privileged was intensified when industry was
"rationalized," and industrial workers were thrown out of employment. Those who returned to the coun-
try brought new notions of unrest to the countryside at a time when the people of the rural districts
were themselves disturbed over their pressing economic problems. When great combines were formed,
thousands of small manufacturers and shopkeepers were squeezed out. When, under all these circum-
stances, the lower middle classes, the peasantry and the industrial workers showed signs of unrest;
when they began to respond as never before to radical propaganda, all the different vested interests
of Japan forgot their differences for the time being. They combined and presented a "united front"
against radicalism. Appealing to the traditional patriotism and sentiments of the Japanese, and us-
ing repressive measures as well, they "converted" young, radicals and brought them to see the error of
their ways, and won the support of the masses.
They were the more able to do this on account of the feeling aroused in Japan because of foreign
actions and opinions, a feeling kept alive by reactionary groups in Japan. The history of this feel-
ing goes back to the beginning years of contact with the western world, after 1853; emotions which
ran high long ago are invoked today and aggravate new irritations. In a recent book published in
Japan we read:
Heretofore, the world has witnessed the conquest, by the white peoples, of the colored
peoples. Japan, too, was once treated as if she were a dominion of the white races, having
been subjected to extra-territorial jurisdiction on the part of Occidental countries. Japan was
even forced by powerful foreign countries to return territory legitimately acquired as war
indemnity.
The author goes on to cite the refusal to grant the principle of racial equality in the Versailles
Treaty as another instance of insulting treatment, and says:
Our country has thus long put up with insults on the part of the white races, but we can-
not stand for such forever. In the Manchurian affair, Japan was completely isolated, 42 coun-
tries having unanimously ranged themselves against her.
Under the circumstances, our country finally withdrew from the League of Nations. At
present it stands in a solitary position, internationally speaking.
The foreign countries of late have been doing all in their power to exclude Japanese goods
by raising the tariff wall and adopting an import quota. They are also enforcing a racial ex-
clusion policy against the Japanese through prohibition of Japanese 1mmigrants and instituting
economic restrictive measures.5
All of these accumulated grievances, added to others such as the 5-5-3 naval ratio, and the re-
fusal of the world to accept Japan's idea of her "mission" in China, have been interpreted in Japan
in language which excites emotions. The Japanese press has played its part here in helping to weld
together the conflicting vested interests of Japan and to enlist the support of the peasants and work-
ers. (In matters touching foreign relations, there is little expression of dissenting opinion in the
Japanese press, though on internal affairs there is considerable freedom of speech.)
5. Quotations taken from translation in Contemporary Opinions, published by Tokyo Informa-
t1on Bureau, No. 54, Nov. 29, 1974.

=== Page 116 === (confidence 0.99)
-85-
However, the conflicting interests are facts, and they remain very uncertain elements in the
metabolism of the country. Moreover, the apparent unification of Japan around a policy of narrow
nationalism has not occurred without violence. There are many super-patriots in Japan who regard
themselves as the modern ronin of the country, and who commit deeds of violence on their own ini-
tiative, or hire out their services to those who can pay them. There are also many societies orga-
nized for super-patriotic action, and the "blood-brotherhoods", or the societies, or both together,
have been responsible for many political assassinations. In l930, for example, Premier Hamaguchi
was shot. In February, l932, a former finance minister was assassinated; in March, Baron Dan, the
head of the Mitsui interests, was killed; and in May, Prime Minister Inukai was assassinated, while
"bombs were hurled at the residence of Count Makino, at the Tokyo policy headquarters, the Mitsu-
bishi bank, and the offices of the Seiyukai party, and an attempt was made to blow up the metropoli-
tan power stations. These acts were carried out by several terrorist societies, composed of young
naval officers, military cadets, students, and peasants." 6
From 1932-1935, the deeds of violence
were directed at newspaper editors and writers, many of whom were killed or injured; pressrooms were
attacked and machinery destroyed.
In February, l936, an outbreak of a new type occurred. Young officers and men of the Tokyo
garrison who were soon to entrain for Manchoukuo and who therefore had been engaging in night marches,
started out on what appeared to be but another night maneuver and hence attracted little attention.
It turned out to be, however, a violent attempt to purge the government of all undesirable influences,
of all who were not, in the opinion of the men involved, considering the welfare of the people, and
who were hence betraying the emperor. Marching to the house of Premier Okada, the soldiers called
for him and shot the man who answered the summons, supposing him to be the Premier. Entering the
bedroom of the aged Finance Minister, Viscount Takahashi, they shot him three times and then attacked
him with the sword, almost severing one of his arms. The minister, eighty-two years old, died a few
hours later of his wounds. General Watanabe, Inspector-General of Military Training, and Viscount
Makoto Sato, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal, were killed in their homes, but Prince Saionj1, the last
of the Genro, was warned in time to escape death.
These deeds of violence sprang from a number of causes. The movement was purely an army one,
representing one side of army sentiment. The election which had just taken place had shown popular
support for liberal candidates, and many men opposed to Japan's continued expansion on the continent
of Asia had been elected to office. Young army men, stirred by the popular expression of disapproval
of policies initiated and supported by the army, took the method of violence to show their determina-
tion that the army should continue to control the government, whatever the expression of popular opin-
ion. The Finance Minister was assassinated because he had not supported the huge budget demanded by
the army. Viscount Makoto Sato was a liberal, and a former admiral, and the Japanese army and navy
have seldom agreed upon foreign policies.
The difference of opinion dates back to the days when the army represented the Choshu clan, the
navy the Satsuma; it has been fed by the navy's desire for over-seas trade - which would necessitate
a large navy - and the army's determination to win a continental empire for Japan. But one of the
commanding generals was assassinated at this time - because within the army itself there is division.
Younger officers of peasant birth are opposed to older generals of aristocratic descent, and being
peasants, they desire an improvement in the life of the farmers and thus feel that the army should
take an active part in internal politics. The premier was attacked because of the feeling that
civilian officials have played into the hands of industrialists and neglected the welfare of the
people. Whatever the various causes back of the assassinations, the aim was the establishment of a
military dictatorship under the emperor, and the sweeping away of all opposing influences.
6. Bisson, T. A., The Trend Toward Dictatorship in Japan. in Foreign Pol1cy Reports,
Vol. X, No. 25, February 13, 1935: p. 322.

-86-
When these murders occurred, the world waited to hear whether a military dictatorship would be
established, or whether the rebels would be suppressed. The latter happened. A conservative minis-
try was finally formed, many of the minor rebel leaders committed suicide, and more important army
officers advocating the same ideas as the rebels were removed from the active service lists. But,
though the extremists among the army officers did not win at this time, other officers of the same
type remain on active service. Army pressure was recognized as the new cabinet was cautiously
formed. A decisive crisis has been only postponed.
The type of violent movements which have occurred in Japan has often been called fascist. Like
fascism elsewhore, the movement is opposed to radical social and economic reform; it uses terrorist
methods; it calls upon narrow nationalism, as well as prejudices against radicalism; it has "the emo-
tional appeal of sacrifice, in that it frankly admits the temporary necessity for hardships and even
suffering in the interests of the nation. . . It promises a glory of national triumph more than com-
pensatory for the initial sacrifices." 7
However, though any movement in Japan which may be la-
belled Fascism has these characteristics which distinguish European Fascism, there is in Japan no
separate Fascist army to force through, and support, a Fascist dictatorship. Moreover, "if the so-
cial basis of Fascism is rooted deep in the middle class, it can hardly flourish in countries where
that class has a short history, small power and few traditions. If Fascism is a device of the in-
dustrial and financial capitalists to defend their vested interests, 1t is likely to grow wherever
monopoly control is being challenged."8 In Japan, the middle class has a short history, small power
and few traditions, and in Japan the only challenge to monopoly control has come from the army,
which has been forced, because of the need of funds to develop Manchuria, to make a truce with
capital. Whether or not the trends to be observed in Japan are Fascist, they express the Japanese
struggle between the common man and the vested interests.
While this struggle is going on, the core of the reactionary point of view is expressed in the
words of the president of the House of Peers, "Many Japanese have now waked from their long period of
dreaming and have begun to advocate a return to ideas peculiar to that country." 9
A Japanese
writer, arguing against Marxism and Communism in Japan, expands this idea and says:
The Japanese Empire is a huge family, and the people are tied by close blood-relationships
into a tight spiritual unity. It is thus quite different from states in Europe and America
that have been organized to meet the rational needs of the people. The Imperial Family 1s the
head family, and all other families branch from it, tracing their descent either directly or
indirectly from the Imperial fountainhead. This is a characteristic of the Japanese state in
which we take pride. Instead of the principles of freedom and equality for individuals held
essential in occidental states, the Japanese rely on parental love and deep affection among
brothers and sisters. These feelings are more deeply rooted and permanent than the rational
claims for freedom and equality. Though dormant in the bosoms of the people in ordinary times,
they manifest themselves unmistakably in times of national emergency. Japan has adopted the
culture and institutions of the West to an amazing degree, but they have neither extirpated
nor changed the national spirit. All we need to do is to strengthen our consciousness of 1t.
Confucius, the great sage of the Orient, taught that filial piety is the source of all
other virtues. This is an eternal truth. To the Japanese, loyalty and filial piety are the
same; love between sovereign and subjects and affection between parent and child have a common
source. Through all ages this has been true. In its essentials, the Japanese social structure
1s not the exploiting organ of the bourgeoisie that the Marxists believe it to be. . .
Japan is at a crossroad. The national spirit will be conquered by capitalism and the com-
munistic doctrines sprouting from it, or it will triumph over capitalism and its evils. . . The
problem will be solved only when the cardinal principles of love and affection underlying the
family system, peculiar to the Japanese race, are reawakened in the minds of the people and
when our productive machinery, instead of benefiting the privileged minority, is devoted to the
welfare of the whole nation.
To bring this about, the people must be taught anew our traditional spirit, that they may
acquire unshakeable faith in it.10
pp.28-29.

In addition to generalizations of this type, there is a movement based on these and similar
ideas, which advocates a "Second Restoration." Supporters of this maintain that capitalists, corrupt
politicians and militarists have come between the emperor and his people; that all these elements
should be swept aside; that the emperor should be "restored" and, as father of his people, provide
for their welfare. To make this possible, all the people should return to agriculture and to the
simple economy of earlier times, to the forms of thought and behavior of the past.
Generalizations such as those quoted, or the impracticable propositions of those who advocate
the "Second Restoration," seem to be grounded in a strong desire to escape from the complex prob-
lems of the modern world, but they seem to take insufficient account of facts. The words quoted on
an earlier page, applied to Japan of the Nara period, appear not inapplicable today, as a description
of the type of facts which are not faced by those who wish a return to the life and ideals of the past:
It was too much to expect that a rich and varied culture could be, without difficulties and
breakdowns, borrowed from abroad and erected upon a social basis in which tradition was so strong,
and an economic base which was inadequate to support it.
In this period of difficulties, resulting from borrowing from abroad a rich and varied culture,
and erecting it upon a social basis in which tradition is strong and an economic base which is in-
adequate to support it, Japanese seek various solutions, and conflicting currents exert their influ-
ence. A personal interpretation of these conflicting currents is given in a recent book called Facing
Two Ways. The author, the Baroness Ishimoto, analyzing her own problems, casts light upon her hus-
band's difficulties as well, and indicates also the nature and strength of the various influences
affecting life in present-day Japan:
As I look back even over my short life I see there repeated challenges of the new against
the old, the perfect feminine in the old sense trying to put down the struggles of the new fem-
inine aspiring to express itself in a progressive world. It was my own mother who regarded it
as her great work to cast her daughter into the mold deemed so admirable by Occidental and
Oriental "philosophers." When mother bought a kimono or an obi for me, she was always partic-
ular to select one elegantly quiet in color and design. I was not to look younger than I was
actually; nor was I to be the focus of all eyes by reason of some splashing decoration in my
apparel. If my garments were costly, the fact was not to be too strident. My manner she hoped
to make accord with the refined modesty of my dress. A naive grace was the desired effect.
Even my speech was to be free of such assertions as "I think," "I like," "I want," "I, I, I..
the I never coming first, unlike the style of free Western girls. My mother warned me that I
must listen to others always, smile at whatever they said, and express as little as possible
of myself.
While my mother was eager to make a dainty bride of me, the man I married was writing in
his diary: ". . . I am not hoping that my wife, Shidzue, will be a baroness of the sort de-
picted in fiction or drama, leading an elaborate life amid luxurious surroundings; what I really
hope for her future is that she will concern herself with the great problems of her country-
women!"
After our marriage and while he found inspiration in working for labor, he watched with
interest my growth in social consciousness. As soon as we had settled in a cottage in the coal
mine district in western Japan, away from the traditions and complications of the old family
system in Tokyo and its guardian mother-in-law, my husband began his constructive task of edu-
cating his girl bride into a "real" person. He insisted on my changing my attitude even toward
him from a meek feudal wife to an alive, liberal and understanding companion. . . His persis-
tent call to me to rise from a stage "too delightful to behold" toward that of the "self-con-
scious woman" changed even my appearance.
After his long and hard effort to put spirit into a doll-like creature, and just as his
labor began to bear fruit. . . my husband said to me one day that he thought my appearance was
losing charm for him.
Now he frankly declared that the beauty of a Japanese woman lay only in her naivete. He
pointed to the delicate feminine pictures in the old prints, pronouncing them his ideal. What
a contradiction! After having so long admired the sturdy women of Millet and the powerful
masterpieces of Rodin! He who once had undertaken to educate his wife with a view to making
her as active and independent as any English or American woman was now gloating over Japanese
dolls in the old prints as types to emulate! But as my husband had always been ahead of his
time, so his reaction against liberalism was a sign of the newest national tendency. . .
In family life in Japan, as it must be everywhere, the husband's mental outlook directly
affects the life of his wife. This ancient truth, known to my ancestors of course, I now took
to my heart. Hardly had I become conscious of myself when I had to face this reactionary wave
at home.

=== Page 119 === (confidence 0.99)
-88-
If the ensuing domestic problem and struggle had been but an isolated private affair,
my melancholy plight would have been of little moment as a story. But my story is a common
one among the present-day Japanese women who are trying to emerge from the condition of non-
resistance to events however meaningful and take their place in the shaping of events in their
own interests, in the interests of the race and of the nation. So in talking about myself, I
am really talking about countless members of my sex in Japan.11
The young Baron Ishimoto had been a radical and an idealist. He had lived and worked among the
people, and had encouraged his wife to understand social problems. He later became discouraged be-
cause of conditions about him and moved from progressivism to conservatism. His wife observes:
Having believed in the swift reconstruction of Japanese life from top to bottom, he was
unprepared for the slow and tedious march of events toward that goal. As the reactionary
forces at home grew bolder, he grew correspondingly discouraged and soon felt that idealism
had been irrevocably betrayed. Immediate realities curbed his imaginative flights and even-
tually he was completely overcome by the influences of his bourgeols environment. There he
was at last - a mere man of aristocratic urban culture, captivated by the conventions of his
own class! 12
Here we have a concrete picture of a Japanese who, under pressure of conflicting influences,
lost his courage, surrendered the liberal and radical ideas he had valued, and gave in to the
forces of reaction. Is this picture a typical one? Will a return to traditional forms of thought
and behavior serve as an adequate outlet for the conflicting currents in Japan today? Or will these
forces find some other outlet? The answer of course lies in the future, and any predictions which
might be ventured would be based on one's own philosophy and interpretation of history.

1. Factors favorable to espionage or counter-espionage on the

Delivery of mail to and from Japan; there being no law

Regular visits by Japanese commissioned parsonnel to
certain Japanese hotels, tea-houses, shrines, temples, and

Many of the visiting Japanese naval personnel have elose
relatives among the local Japanese residents.
Liberty parties are eautioned against accepting favors
fron mon-Japanese or strangers.
All of the vessels are equipped with range-finders,
whish they use freely on entering or leaving ports; and they
are frequently observed sketahing and photographing dooks
and utility plants.
m. Aside from the espionage aotivities of the visiting
Japanese vessels, they serve as a direct medium of contact between the
Japanese residents of lHawai1 and their homeland, and the personnel of
these vensels are naturally looked to for interpretation of conditions
and evente in Japan. The visiting naval personnel make most
of the opportunity. Through leotures, moving pictures, exhibitions,
ete., is borme home to the local Japanese the "greatness" of Jupan, her
virility, and her absolute superiority over all other countrics. In
fact, every effort of Japanese naval personnel ashore here appears to
be deliberately caloulated to advance Japanese nationalism and to
cement bonds of loyalty.

MORE JAPANESE PROPAGANDA IN THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS
The American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations, in official report of
its activities for the year 1936, refers at pp. 18 and 19 to what it has done in
Hawaii and California in introduction of text and reference books into the public
schools, and says in regard thereto:
 811. 13 Justitute g Paisn Relalion 118
"Work along this line on the west coast, because of the educational tradi-
tions which have been foisted on the schools by chauvinistic groups and by the hos-
tile newspapers and certain anti-Japanese elemcnts, is of necessity slow. Every
effort made by the American Council to introduce new material in California--and
this is true also of Hawaii--has been roundly denounoed by these propagandists. It
is encouraging to note that despite unscrupulous propaganda of this sort, the educa-
tional authorities themselves, the teachers and the vast majority of the adult pub-
lic, have staunohly supported the Council's efforts."
In the language quotod reference is made to the condemnation and final with-
drawal of a textbook on Japan, prepared under joint direction of the Instituto of
Pacific Relations, the Hawaiian Board of Education, and the Society for Cultural
Relations of Japan, usod in Honolulu public schools during 1935 and urgod for simi-
lar use in continental United States. Use of the book was protested to the Hawaiian
Board of Education, to the Hawaiian Logislature, and to the Superintendent of Public
Instruction of California, because of falso or misleading statements therein con-
tained as to the "Gentlemen's Agreement" and the Japanese immigration question, and
as to the part played by Japan in making history in Asia during the present contury.
The justice of the criticism was conceded and the withdrawal of the book announced
in letter of the Council's Secretary, June 30, 1936.
The I.P.R. report and the languago quoted doubtloss refers also to the with-
drawal and reissue in corrected editions of certain textbooks prepared for use in
the public schools of California in courses, credit for whose introduction is
claimed by the American Council of tho I.P.R. Those books were publicly charged as
containing misleading statements similar to those found in the Hawaiian textbook,
and substitution therefor of corrected cditions was mude under direction of the
California State Board of Education or thru voluntary offer of the publishers (see
C.J.I.C. Docs. #458-9-76).
The report also announces complction and contemplated appearance in l937 of
three new text books. One of them, "Japan, Where Ancient Loyalties Survive", was
written by Helen Pratt, co-author of the text book on Japan which it replaces. It
is now in use in sohools in Hawaii and possibly elsewhere. On examination it is
found to offend, at pp. 74, 75 and 84, in similar manner, tho with more subtlety
than its predecessor, the apparent intent being to mislead the reader by concoclment
or skillful treatment of selocted facts and to make thereby a case for Japan.
The complaints of Japan, therein voiced, will find full answer in the facts
which are concealed:• The intent and provisions of the Gentlemen's Agreement, ex-
plained carefully by President Theodore Roosevelt; the fact that Australia and other
British Dominions have even more rigorously excluded Japanese without any racture
of friendly relations; the enormous increase of our Japanese population vhile the
Agreement was in force and in violation of its terms; and the nocessity in conse-
quence for an exclusion law--all are ignored. Immigration statistics are juggled so
as to lead the reader to believe that our Japanese population roceived an incroase
of only about 8,Ooo thru immigration under the Agreemont. If thc author knows the
facts as set forth in "Japanese Exclusion, a Study of the Policy and tho Law", Jonn
B. Trevor, House Doc. #600, 1925, pp. 8 and 9, and in the statement of the California
Joint Immigration Committee to the Secrctary of State, June 18, 1937, and in C.J.I.C.
Doc. #499(and a book to guide students should not have beun written by one ignorant
of those facts)--then there is evidonce of an intent to deliberutely mislead publio
school students and instruotors.

Civil Personnel in Hawaii.
1. In compliance with the desires of the Working Committee of
the Interdepartmental Committee dealing with the above subject, as
expressed in conference on June 29, 1937, the following points are
submitted, as indicating practices and conditions which the War and
Navy Departments are particularly desirous of terminating in Hawaii:
a.
The practice of leaving presumably Japanese naval
and military personnel from Japanese naval vessels upon de-
parture of such vessels. This practice, strong indications
of which appear to have been observed during the current year,
in all probebility places trained observers in position to
gather important information on our military and naval ex-
ercises held in that area.
These exercises involve the
planned defense of Hawaii.
It is noted that such personnel
was probably present at the time of the recent Army - Navy
exercises there.
b. The illegal presence in the islands of any member
of the Japanese Irmy or Navy.
c. The presence of any craft in the Islands fitted
or designed for illegitimate purposes or with unidentified
personncl on board. This involves inspections as to the
equipment or design and positive identification of personnel.

=== Page 190 === (confidence 0.98)
DEPARTMENT OF STATE
DIVISION OF FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS
October 11, 1937.
I have been unable to find anything in the
record showing a reason for differentiating be-
tween the right of the Japanese Government to
refuse permission for our naval vessels to visit
open ports in the islands under mandate of
Japan and the right of this Government to re-
fuse permission for Japanese vessels to visit
open ports in Hawai1 or elsewhere in American
territory. The record shows thet originally
the Japanese Government was willing to allow
our vessels to visit the open ports in the man-
dated 1slands but in latter years permission
to visit even these ports h:s been withheld
by the Japanese Government.
While from the point of view of legitimate
retaliation we may be warranted in withholding
permission for Japanese vessels to visit open
ports in the Hawaiian Ielands, there is a ques-
tion in my mind whether now 1s an opportune
time to take such measures. Our naval vessels
have begun to make frequent visits to Kobe to
contact the Dollar Line there and no difficulty
has been experienced in obtaining the permis-
eion of the Japenese Government. If we resort
to restricting Japanese vessels visiting Ameri-
can ports this might cause irritation, lead-
ing the Japanese Government to make difficul-
ties over visits to Japenese ports, of our
naval veseels and over other matters.

Recom mendations
1 Recommend that when a Japanese naval vessel visits Honolulu an accurate
count be made of all individuals leaving the ship and of all individuals
going on board the ship, in order to ascertain definitely whether or not
such vessel is leaving personnel at Honolulu upon departure or is taking
on board personnel at Honolulu in excess of the numbers with which she
arrived.
2
Recommend that the count be taken independently by different covernment
agencies in Honolulu in order to check the eccuracy of results and that if
practicable a separate count be taken of officers in uniform, enlisted
men in uniform and individuals in civilian clothes. The count should be
taken under the supervision of the Commandant, Tourteenth Naval District,
utilizing such personmel of the Federal Governnent in iawaii as may be
agreed upon by the representatives of the various Executive Departments in
Hawaii. The count should be taken in such a manner that the fact that it
was being taken should not be known.
3. Reconmend that should a Japanese naval vessel be found, upon taking such a
count,to have left personnel behind upon departure or to have taken on ad-
ditional personnel at Honolulu, the tate Department be informed immediately
of the circunstances in order that proper representations cen be made to the
Japanese Government or other suitable actin be taken.
11
Inasmuch as the difficulty of maintaining efficient vatch cver the activities
of Japanese naval vessels in violetion of the usual courtesies extended to
public vessels is very great at any port in the Hawaiian Islands except at
Honolulu, reconmend that requests of the Japanese Government for its public
vessels to visit ports in the Hawaiian Island, other than Honolulu, be de-
nied, giving the same reason for denial that the Japanese Government hes
given to some requests of the United Stetes for its naval vessels to visit
open ports in the Mandated Territory - that is, that the visit would be
"inconvenient", or following t.e most recent practice of the Jepanese Govern-
ment in refusing such permission iving no reason.
Recommend that the Custous officers watch Japanese naval vessels, in a manner
so that the fact is not known, to assure that such vessels are not landing
material in violation of customs regulations and that should it become ap-
parent that such is the case that proper steps be taken to stop it.

894.20211A/
The Session Laws of Hawaii contain the following
894-20211a
provision:
"Sec. 5524. Waiver of jury. The defendant
in any criminal case other than a case in which
the death penalty may be imposed may, with the con-
sent of the court, waive the right to a trial by
3
jury either by written consent filed in court or
by oral consent in open court entered on the
3
minutes. Any case in which a trial by jury is
waived as aforesaid may be tried by the court with-
out a jury both as to the facts and the law, and
when the trial shall have been had there shall be
no further trial upon the facts, except upon the
granting of a new trial according to law. [L. 1903,
c. 9, 8. 1; R.L. 1925, 8. 4028; Am. L. 1931, c. 36,
s. 1.]" (Revised Laws of Hawai1, 1935, page 858.)
Article III, Section 2, Clause 3 of the Constitution
F/MR
of the United States provides that:
"The Trial of all Criminals, except in Cases
of Impeachment, shall be by Jury."
The sixth amendment to the Federal Constitution also
Confidential File
provides that:
"In all criminal prosecutions, the accused
shall enjoy the right to a speedy and public trial,
by an impartial jury of the State and district
wherein the crime shall have been committed", etc.
It
e

=== Page 225 === (confidence 0.99)
-2-
It has been held that the provision in Article III
of the Constitution just quoted applies only to criminal
proceedings in the Federal courts and does not govern
trials in State courts (The Constitution of the United
States of America (1924), Senate Document No. 154, 68th
Congress, lst session, pages 483, 484). The provisions
of the sixth amendment to the Constitution have also been
interpreted as restrictive of the power of the Federal
Government alone and to mean that the jury referred to
is a jury constituted as it was at common law, i.e.,
twelve men. (Ibid., 615, 617.)
Willoughby states in his treatise on the Constitution
that:
"The right of trial by jury provided for in
the Constitution applies only in the Federal courts,
and in them it applies only to those cases in which,
by common practice at the time the Constitution was
adopted, it was employed in the colonies and in
England. Thus it does not apply to equity causes,
to cases in an admiralty and to military courts,
nor where the special prerogative rights of courts
are involved, as, for example, in proceedings for
disbarment or for contempt."  (II, Willoughby, The
Constitutional Law of the United States (1929) 1142.)
Willoughby also states that:
"The law governing the waiver by the accused
of his constitutional right to a trial by jury in
criminal actions, or to a trial by less than twelve
jurors, and, indeed, the waiver of any constitutional
guaranty, is not in a clearly determined condition.
In cases arising under State constitutions, inhar-
monious doctrines have been declared. In some juris-
dictions the position has been taken that the guaran-
ties are intended merely for the benefit of the
accused

=== Page 226 === (confidence 0.99)
-3-
accused and may, therefore, be waived. In other
States the courts have held that the guaranty of
jury trial in criminal cases is one in which the
State also has an interest, and which for that
reason may not be waived.
"In the United States Supreme Court it was
held in Schick v. United Statee [195 U.S. 65] that
jury trial might be waived in the trial of minor
offences.
"The right of the accused to waive jury trial
in cases of felony has never come before the Supreme
Court; but in Lewis v. United States [146 U.S. 370]
that Court held that, in felonies, the presence of
the accused could not be waived either by himself
or by counsel. ..." (Ib1d., 1l46-ll47.)
Dobie, in his work on Federal procedure, also states
that:
"Whether the accused can waive a jury trial
and be tried before the Federal judge is a question
that has occasioned grave debate. Schick v. United
States seems to have settled the question by hold-
ing that there can be such a waiver in (but only in)
'petty offenses', which are not 'crimes' in a consti-
tutional sense." (Dobie, Handbook of Federal Juris-
diction and Procedure (1928), 86.)
The Act of April 30, 1900, entitled "An Act To pro-
vide a government for the Territory of Hawaii", contained
the provision in Section 5 thereof that:
"The Constitution, and, except as herein other-
wise provided, all the laws of the United States
which are not locally inapplicable, shall have the
same force and effect within the said Territory as
elsewhere in the United States ..."
and Section 6 thereof states:
"The

=== Page 227 === (confidence 0.99)
-4-
"The laws of Hawaii not inconsistent with
the Constitution or laws of the United States or
the provisions of this Act shall continue in force,
subject to repeal or amendment by the Legislature
of Hawaii or the Congress of the United States."
(31 Stat. 141-142.)
By the Act of May 27, 1910, Section 5 of the Act
just quoted was amended to read:
"The Constitution, and, except as herein
otherwise provided, ali the laws of the United
States, including laws carrying general appropri-
ations, which are not locally inapplicable, shall
have the same force and effect within the said
Territory as elsewhere in the United States", sub-
ject to certain provisos. (36 Stat. 433.)
Attention should be called to a case decided by the
Supreme Court upon an appeal from the District Court of
the United States for the Territory of Hawaii in 1903
(Hawaii v. Mankichi, 190 U.S. 197). In that case Mankichi
had been tried on a charge of having committed the crime
of murder on March 26, 1899. He was found guilty of man-
slaughter in the first degree by a verdict of nine jurors.
The statutes of Hawaii prior to July 7, 1898, provided for
such trial and conviction. It therefore became important
to determine whether the Joint Resolution of Congress "To
provide for annexing the Hawaiian Islands to the United
States", approved July 7, 1898, which provided that the
municipal legislation of the Hawaiian Islands not incon-
sistent with the Joint Resolution nor contrary to the
Constitution or the treaties of the United States should
remain

=== Page 228 === (confidence 0.99)
-5-
remain in foroe until the Congress of the United States
should otherwise determine (30 Stat. 750-751), imposed
upon the Islands the provisions of the United States
Constitution. The Supreme Court held by a five to four
decision that the conviction was lawful. Justice Brown,
in delivering the opinion of the majority, stated that:
"... Under the conditions named in this reso-
lution [July 7, 1898] the Hawaiian Islands remained
under the name of the 'Republic of Hawaii' until
June 14, 1900, when they were formally incorporated
by act of Congress under the name of the 'Territory
of Hawaii'. 31 Stat. 14l. By this act the Const1-
tution was formally extended to these islandg, sec. 5,
and special provisions made for empanelling grand
juries and for unanimous verdicts of petty juries.
Sec. 83. [Underscoring added.]
"The question is whether, in continuing the
municipal legislation of the islands not contrary
to the Constitution of the United States, it was in-
tended to abolish at once the criminal procedure
theretofore in force upon the islands, and to substi-
tute immediately and without new leglslation the com-
mon law proceedings by grand and petit jury, which
had been held applicable to other organized Terri-
tories.
"... Of course, for the reasons already stated,
the questions involved in this case could arise only
from such as occurred between the taking effect of
the joint resolution of July 7, 1898, and the act
of April 30, l900, establishing the territorial
government." (Ibid., 210-211, 218.)
It appears, therefore, that the majority of the
Supreme Court had no doubt that after June 14, 1900, the
Constitution of the United States was formally extended
to

=== Page 229 === (confidence 0.98)
-6-
to the Hawaiian Islands and that the case of Hawaii v.
Mankichi was decided as it was because of the fact that
it arose prior to that Act.

My dear Miss Kaltenbaoh:
I am sure you will fulfill the expectations of many who know your
past experiences in the type of work Mr. MoClatchy was engaged in.
Yes, I shall gladly cooperate with you and will send you whatever
information that may be of interest to America and to the Commission.
At the moment I am organizing the various Korean leaders to take
direot steps in demanding from the Japanese Goverment a plebiscite
for Korea's autonomy. I mean, to send Korean leaders to Japan and
make direot demands instead of only telling the Americans to help
them. I for one shall gladly go to Japan. Many say I am foolish
and a suicide -- well yes, it may sound foolish and seemingly
suicidal; however, one cannot do any work without risking one's life.
The time is ripe for action. Koreans in Korea (confidential) are
ready to maroh on to the battlefield if the proper time could be
reasonably decided.
According to my best knowledge and the confidential reports coming
from the fronts, this move is a timely one.
Thus far I am getting strong help and I believe I shall soon soe
the movement come into action.
Before going to Japan I am planning to visit America for four to
6 weeks to lay before the American public our side of the story and
also why we are taking this step (suicidal) to demand from Japan our
froedom. I believe in about the later part of August or September
of this year I shall be in the Pacific Coast region on my way to the
East. I have few more details to settle in the Fast; cn my way back
I hope to spend a week in California calling on various leaders.
Would it be humanly possible for you to find out if I can meet some
of the leading organizations in California. I shall be glad to
speak on the subjects which they are taking interest. I also wish
to meet the Mcclatchy family members and tope to get some place in
the Sacramento Bee.
If you can make the necessary arrangements as to time, place and
subjeot (statohood for Hawaii, Japanese in Hawaii, etc.) sometime
in the later part of September or the End week of October, I shall

of my duration in America.

ENT ON JAPANESE LANGUAGE SCHOOLS IN ISLES.
In February number of Mita Hyoron, the organ of Keio
Gijuku, the famous University founded in Tokyo by Fukuzawa,
appears a leading article appraising Japanese Language Schools
in Hawaii.
"In Hawa1i no less than 200 schools attended by 40,000
pupils out of a total population of Japanese in the islands of
140,000, three or four of the schools have an enrollment of
over 1,O00. Professor Ktyooka is impressed by the superiority
of the girls to the boys in the Makkalei School,due to the
fact that the girls are under restraint at home and retain
more of the ancestral decorum while the boys are allowed
to run about and pick up undesirable habits."
Honolulu, Hawaii.

JAPANESE THREATEN TO DOMINATE HAWAII
The following exaerpts from an article in Hawaii Hochi (a Japanese newspaper of Hon-
olulu) and reprinted in the Japanese New World Sun of San Francisoo, September 26,
1938, indicate a situation that well merits the most serious oonsideration.
"The total Japanese population of Hawaii at present (1938) is ostimated at 153,539,
representing 37.31% of the whole. Out of the total Japanese population there are
116,584 who are Amerioan citizens. This is nearly 76% of the entire racial bloc.
. . . alien Japanese make up only 9.2% of the whole population of the territory . .
. . so it would appear that the Japanese hloc that could vote if it wanted to do so,
that could rogister as ε qualified group of electors . . . amounts to about 35% of
the total eligible eleotorate.
"That suoh a group would be in a position to swing elections if it aoted in a solid
bloo is beyond question. The Japanese are in a position to hold the balance of
power and to use it effectively if they ohoose. So far they have not functioned as
a racial bloo, which is the best proof of their Amoricanzation.
"But what if they should decide to use their strength in the only truly Amerioan way
in whioh mass solidarity oan be demonstrated--at the ballot box?
"an any issue that affected them as a racial group, affeoted their interests as a
partioular seotion representing one-third of the citizenship, they would have a per-
feot right to stiok together and fight for their own oandidates. They would be saps
if they didn't.
Figures do not lie. Amerioan citizens of Japanese ancestry are approaching the point
of strongth at which it will be possible for them to ohallenge any party, any oandi-
date, any platform or any polioy."
Hore is expressed in no unoertain terms the threat of the Japanese to use their
racial plurality to dominate Hawaii. It is not stated, however, that two-thirds of
these American citizens of Japanese ancestry who have the power to "challenge any
party, any candidate, any platform or uny policy" have failed to expatriate and
are therefore also citizens of Jupan, and bound to obey her orders in peaoe and in
war.
Should statehood be granted to Hawaii, and should the prinoiple of self detormina-
tion become effeotive, what may be the future of our western outpost, where a large
majority of Amerioan citizens of tho proponderant racc, who threaten openly to use
their politioal power for their own purposes, are, thru choice, oitizens alsoof a
powerful and joalous nation which demands and roceives aotivo loyalty from its sub-
jeots in whatever portion of the world they may reside.

My dear Secretary:
This will serve to introduce to
you Mr. Kilsoo Haan of Honolulu, T.H.
I had occasion to become acquainted
with Mr. Haan on the visit to the Territory last year
made by the Hawaiian Territory Commission, appointed
from both Houses of the Congress pursuant to a resolution
creating it and whose duties were to investigate
conditions in the Territory relative to statehood. In
our hearings which were much extended, Mr. Haan was a
valuable and helpful witness and it seemed to me and
several of us that he was in possession of information
and in control of certain channels of information that
not only aided the Committee but would be of interest
to the State Department. I am informed that he is
now in Washington and I am sending this letter in
the hopeful anticipation that you will accord him
every courtesy and consideration to which he is
entitled.
Respectfully submitted,

America is now facing a strong villanous competitor in the

consented rather reluotantly even to the absorption of Korea, she now

We feel that America's Ostrich Diplomacy for temporal commercial
profit out of the sale of arms, munitions and materials essential for war
will aid the comtempt and disrespect of Japanese militarists against
America. They will not appreciate merica's help but instead they believe
America's desire for profit is tne "lack of merican intelligence and de-

Japan now has proven that all the declaration with respect to

Diplomacy?
Under the present international situation, it seems to us that
the United States should interpose its "Good Offices" in protest against
this wholesale oppression of the Koreans, and it should, in good faith
at least, use ali its moral influence toward breaking the morale of the

"Asia for Japan" policy.
The following suggestions are humbly submitted for your early
consideration:
A. Extend your sympathy to the Chinese, the Koreans, and the
liberal-minded Japanese peasants, thus uplifting their morale in
resisting Japanized Fascism in Asia.
B. Refuse to sell to Japan, arms, munitions, and materials
essential to carry on the war of aggression in China for two years.
We believe the total cost will not exceed 30o0 or 400 million dol-
lars.
C. Encourage and aid tne Sino-Korean organization in Hawaii
and America with the expressed purpose of having these organiza-

the Army and the Navy.
Explanation in detail of A, B, and C.
In reference to A.
The morale of the Chinese and the Koreans can be lifted through
issuing letters of sympathetic understanding as requested and through
publio statements mentioning the hopes of reviewing the American-Korean
Treaty of May 22, 1882, eto.
There are 22,O00,O00 Koreans in Korea, in between China, Siberia,
and Japan -- they will drink in like thirsty men in a desert dying of
thirst. Sympathy will go a long way -- in reality, its effect will be
greater than supplying quantities of arms, munitions, or other aid.
In reference to B.
If the United States Congress would enact a law pronibiting the

In reference to C.
By aiding the Chinese and Korean organizations in Hawaii and
America to cooperate with the American intelligence departments. Un-
doubtedly you will agree with me that the time and ciroumstances call
for such activities, largely for self-defense measures.
The Sino-Korean Peoples League has, in a small way, succeeded in
exposing Japanese activities in Hawaii. The thought naturally comes to
us, why not expand our activities in America? The American intelligence
departments are spending much money and time and many admit that they
meet many difficulties and get less favorable results. Our service will
aid Amerioa.
The Japanese activities in Hawaii and on the Pacific Coast are
numerous and vitally important. No one can deny the need of watching
their activities.
The Koreans are significantly placed. These young men and women
can be used most advantageously to America. Why not do it? Are there
any reasons why they should not be used? As far as I know, many are
qualified and are willing. They will gladly serve America if such op-
portunities are granted them.
Among the thousands of Korean youths, there are about 250 to 300
boys and girls who are best suited for this type of work. These young
men and women are the ones who have arrived in america since 1924. These
men are required to leave the U. S. A. after the academic requirements
have been fulfilled. Because of tne prospect of going back to Korea un-
der the Japanese rule, very few would dare say or do anything political
in nature.
Nearly 99 percent of these young men who have returned to Korea
have been put in prison because of some alleged remark made against Japan
during their sojourn in America. Many, after serving prison terms, have
become mentally and physically unfit for society. many of them are forced
to go about, against their will, preaching the wonders of Japanese rule
and Japan's future as the master of the world.
(If need bg, I shall be glad to have honorable men come to Wash-
ington and testify to this effect.)
These Korean students today are so afraid to go back to Korea.
They dread the day. They hate to even think about going. These men
and women are potential materials who would give voluntary service if
America could grant them the privilege of remaining in America as
"Political Refugees" until such time as Korea becomes free. Granting
them the privilege to reside in America as "Political Refugees" is jus-
tifiable, humanitarian, and in accord with the spirit of America's
expressed policy of giving aid to political refugees.
May I submit the following factors for further consideration:
a. There are less than 300 of these young men and women in
American schools, who come under this law.
b. They are all here in America at their own expense. Nearly
all of them are graduates of american universities or are going to
graduate from some university soon.

c. One hundred percent of these men are well versed in spoken

d. They are best suited and qualified for this type of work.
They can be made to cooperate with such organizations as ours, giv-

I also have had the honor and privilege of addressing 38 American

Kindly grant us our plea and let us serve america in these times of un-

We believe america is the beacon light of democracy and the

America falls or is in constant danger, threatened with insecurity.
Those who are concerned with the peace of the Pacific realize
that unless the people of the Pacific stand up for democracy now, we
will suffer the consequences. That is why we believe that the present
war between Japan and China is more than a war for territories or for
raw materials. This is a war between two political philosophies --
Democracy vs. Japanized Fascism.
Japanized Fascism means the fulfillment of "Asia for Japan"
and the beginning of an economic and military war between the white and
the yellow races.

It has been the national belief that Japan is a divinely protec-
ted nation and that she can never be conquered by a foreign power. So
strongly are the militarists involved with this faith that there is ab-
solute confidence in the ultimate success and justification of all her
causes and claims in any dealings with foreign nations. Furthermore,
the Japanese Militarists' faith in the Emperor as "the incarnate god
who governs the universe" and he himself as divinely commissioned to
spread Japan's "kultur" as far as his sword can reach, has been the
constant source of danger toward peace and stability in the Pacific.
Internationally speaking, Korea has become both the exponent
and the finished example of Japanese militarists' ambition. Today 85
percent of imports are from Japan. The people have no rights, not even
the universally recognized elementary human rights. This is the second
time in our history Japan has and is now trying to wipe out rorean
civilization.
The Japanese author, Dr. Yoshi S. uno, writes:
"The Seven Years' War was one of tne most cruel and un-
provoked wars that the world has ever witnessed. korean civiliza-
tion was completely destroyed. The Lorean people suffered to such
a degree that even the graves of their kings were molested and
rifled. At the close of the war rorea was a land of the ruins, so
great had been the devastation."
There is today in the city of Kyoto, where the 38, 700 pairs of
ears and 38,700 noses of their victims are buried -- it is called the
"Ear Mound". Curious travelers still stand before this "Ear Mound"
and wonder - wonder.
Dr. Kuno further stresses the wholesale spoilation of Lorean
civilization, 1592-1597:
"At the time of Hideyoshi's invasion, the civilization
of Korea had reached its peak. She had metallic movable type of
her own invention; in Korea they had movable type several years
before its invention in the Occident. The Japanese gathered up
most of this type and took it to Japan, it was only after her in-
vasion of Korea that Japan learned to print books with any facility.
From Korea, Japan also learned the art of weaving various kinds of
goods, The most noteworthy industrial knowledge that Japan gained
from Korea was the manufacture of porcelain ware. Such famous wares
as those of Satsuma, Hirado, Rukusan, Cgano, Takatori, and Hagi, which
are famous today as special products of Japan, were originated by
skilled laborers in Korea whom various Japanese feudal lords took
prisoners and settled permanently in the various provinces. It is
said that the process is now a lost art in Korea. World history
contains no parallel to this wholesale uprooting of the civiliza-
tion of one nation and its transplantation in another."
The success of Japan's "Asia for Japan" policy spells with
capital letters a racial war in the near future. We believe this war
will come within two decades. Can you pioture the mass of Orientals
working under the new political philosophy believing the white race is
the curse to the world's happiness? Industrially and militarily
America will face a monster, whose characteristics are of the Shinto
Gods, a wolf, a fox, a tiger, a dove, a loving mother, etc. With all
its cunningness, its foxiness added with measured politeness, Japan will
play the "jujitsu" dipbmacy with America. When she is ready, she will
come with fury and with such military might america will then realize
the plea and the continual warnings of the Koreans since 1905.

fear and disappointment even as far back as April, l906, less than five
months after the withdrawal of American Legation from Seoul, Korea.
America's fear is well justified. America must take action now or it

The Japanese preach the coming Holy War with America in Hawaii
to their children as they do now in Japan. The present war is considered
another Holy War. Japan's war is not only in the sense of military con-
quest but it also must have the "Kultural Conquest" over the whites. That
is one reason why you see so much of the so-called cultural propaganda
in Hawaii and in California. That is why they have launched out with
the Society of International Cultural Relations -- with agents all over
Amerioa. They are ven now working to convert the great financiers of
America, witn a new headquarters in New York City at the Rockefeller

ready she will strike back.
Lt. General kenji Doihara recently wrote in the Chuo Koran (Cen-
tral Review) Nov. 1938 - quote:
"Japan must win a victory in this holy war and for that
purpose she must also carry out and win a cultural war. ---- the
present incident is a war for the renaissance of the civilization
of the Orient against that of the West. ---- Japan alone which has
preserved the culture and tradition of the Orient on the one hand,
and, on the other by absorbing the new civilization of the West, has

The Japanese Imperial Rescript, taught to Japanese children in
Hawaii and America, reads:
"We shall build our capitol all over the world and make
the whole world our domain."
The object of the Institute of Overseas Peoples Education is,
quote:
"To educate the children of Japanese living abroad, in
order to establish a foundation for their oversea development
and by solving the problems of the education of these children
to encourage overseas expansion. They teach their children the

Mr. Haan called at 1l:00 this morning by arrangement
made by the Secretary's office. He showed me a copy of a
letter which he had addressed to the Secretary setting forth
his desire that the State Department manifest an interest in
the situation of the Koreans, that this Government adopt
measures of economic pressure against Japan, and that this
Government make arrangements whereby some three hundred
Korean students who are now in this country might remain
here after completion of their studies. He also handed me
the attached letter of April 28, with enclosure.
I glanced over these documents and returned to Mr. Haan
the copy of the letter to the Secretary. Mr. Haan then com-
F
A
mented orally at some length on a number of the subjects
discussed in the documents.
I

=== Page 323 === (confidence 0.97)
- 2 -
I made comment to the effect that this Department
was essentially a department of policies; that the policies
of this Government in the field of foreign affairs had been
set forth publicly by the Secretary of State and by the
President; that I assumed that Mr. Haan was familiar with
those public statements; and I intimated that I could make
no comment in addition to and going beyond those statements.
With reference to Mr. Haan's desire that arrangements be made
whereby certain Korean students might remain in the United
States, I said thet that matter seemed to me to be one for
consideration and determination by the Department of Labor
and by Congress. I added that the Visa Division would be
the Division in this Department best qualified to offer
suggestions on that subject and I arranged for Mr. Haan to
see Mr. Coulter of the Visa Division.

I have the houor to inform the Department that I have this
morning received from the Office of the Clerk of the Circuit
Court-First Judicial Circuit, Territory of Hawaii, e letter
deted March 30, 1939, enclosins a Court Order in the case en-
titled "Kil Son Hahn, also known as Kil Soo Haan, versus Nippu
403
Jiji Co., Ltd., L.15541 - First Circuit Court, T.H." to take
the testimony of Kanekazu Okada (Consul-General) - December, l932,
5
to August 1934, whose present address is the Japanese Legation,
43 Pretorius Street, Pretoria, Union of  outh fricn. In view of
the most unusual circumstances surroundins this case I am for-
warding the entire set of papers, including a copy of the letter
from the Chief Clerk of Court, to the Depertment with the request
that, if the Department perceives no objection, a copy of this deapatch
may be forwarded with the papers to the said Clerk of Court. I would
F/A
ask on the other hand thet, if the Department does see en objection
to the subject matter of part of my despateh, it will forward the
papers together with an eppropriate letter to the Clerk of Court.
In brief, this Consulate General does not feel that any action
can be teken in this metter for the following reasons, one,technical
the other political.
In the first place, the order of the Court runs to "the Consul
- Generel -

=== Page 326 === (confidence 0.97)
一2-
General of the United States or his Deputy or any United States
Consul or his Deputy residing in Pretoria, Union of South Africa."
If the person whose testimony is desired was at present in Pretoria,
the technical side of my objections might feil. However, he is
at present in Capetown and will be until presumably the end of the
Parliamentary Session about mid-July. The wording of the Court
Order does not allow the Consul at Capetown or eny of his officers
to take the Deposition.
Furthermore, the person in question whose testimony is desired
is an official of the Jepanese Government. He was presumably at
some time in the past Consul General or Acting Consul General of
Jepan in Hawaii. At the present time he is Envoy Extraordinary and
Minister Plenipotentiary of Japan to the Union of South Africa.
For this reason alone J should hesitate most seriously to approach
him for his testimony. I would also have hesitated considerably
even if he had been a Consul General.
The most serious point of my objections arises in the nature
of the questions asked in the direct Interrogatories, notably
questions 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10. The substance of those questions
clearly indicates that the testimony has to do with an alleged
plot of some kind of a racial nature certainly and probably of
a higher political nature. I could not consider, in view of this
fact, asking the questions that are put forward. Furthermore,
it is extremely likely that even if I did reguest answers to such
questions he would decline to answer them either on general political
grounds or on the grounds that the rules of his Foreign Service
forbade his appearance as e witness in a case. In this respect I
have in mind the general rules of our own Foreign Service.
I extremely regret my inability to oblige the Clerk of Court
of the First Judicial District of Haweii, but I do not feel that
the Deposition could be taken even if the technical objection could
be avoided.

fees for the taking of the Deposition, and I have not been in-
formed from any official source that the cese is one in which the
United States Government is interested which would excuse the
charging of fees.
Respectfully yours,
