Sir:
This office has received your letter of March 30,
1939, transmitting (1) a Commission to take Deposition
and (2) Proposed Direct Interrogatories in the case of
Kil Son Hahn, also known as Kil Soo Haan vs. Nippu Jiji
Co., Ltd.; L 1554l - First Circuit Court, T. H. I was
requested to arrange for taking the deposition of Kazue
Kuwashima whose address is Japanese Embassy, 75 Rua dos
Voluntarios da Patria, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
With every reasonable disposition to comply with the
order of the Court, I regret that it is not practicable
to execute this commission. Mr. Kuwashima is the Japanese
Ambassador to Brazil and the diplomatic immunity attached
to his position prevents him from giving testimony in
relation to litigation in any foreign court whatsoever.
He cannot forego this right except by the express consent
to his Government. Furthermore, some of the interrogatories
would seem to be objectionable as tending to question
matters which in his official character are exempt from
examination.
Consequently, the commission and proposed direct
interrogatories are returned herewith.
Respectfully yours,

The purpose of this writing is to present as

=== Page 366 === (confidence 0.99)
JAPAN'S NATIONAL MISSION AND HAWAII
National or racial conflicts do not become aoute until
the nation or race kept in a weaker position is animated by
national tendenoy to ohange its status and strive for equality
with the nation or race deemed superior. Commodore Mathew C.
Perry kindled this very kind of spark when he forcefully opened
the ports of Japan to the world.
The Japanese race accepted the supremacy of the white
race with solemn mental reservation. She buried her pride and
humiliation and austuciously adopted the spirit of popular educa-
tional system from America, military, medical and scientific train-
ing from Germany and the naval strategy and diplomatic tactios from
England. In a good sense, these learnings were fittingly blended
into the teachings and culture of Japan. She took every nutriment
in order to develop Japan's racial civilization.
Today Japan is a new dynamic military power which makes
itself felt not only in the revolt all over Asia against the white
race but she is making forceful penetration into the western homi-
sphere and has captured many of the rich commercial markets.
The greatest statesman of Japan, Count Okuma, declared:
"To brand us Japanese as inferior because we are a colored race
is bigotry, -- we must combat and destroy through the fulfillment
of our national mission."
What is then, the national mission of Japan?
It is fairly arguable, basing on historical facts that
Japan's national mission is world's supremacy and racial equality.
With this in view she has played a role of an expert strategist,
she has judiciously applied the art of jiugitsu, seizing and claim-
ing all the strategic points in the continent of Asia and in the
Pacific, directly obatruoting America's advance to the rioh com-
meroial El-Dorado of the Far East. She stretohed her steady arm
up to the north and gripped Kurile and half of Sakhalin, threaten-
- 2 -

=== Page 367 === (confidence 0.98)
Americoa's future northern air-route. She annexed Korea, the
stepping stone to Asiatio continent, and in l931, she forcefully
seised the three eastern provinoes of Manchuria and the rich
opium province of Jehol. She also possesses the island of Formosa
and the chain of islands north of Formosa to Japan proper, blook-
ing China's front door. She now holds the key to the western half

EXPATRIATION A HOAX
Recently the Japanese and many of their American friends
have proudly pointed out to the expatriated Japanese boys and girls
as a proof of their loyalty to America.
Peculiarly, the Japanese law of nationality is based on
the principle of jus sanguines, while the American laws are based
on the prinoiple of jus soli. Dual nationality usually arises
through a conflict between the law of jus soli -- the law determining
nationality according to the place of birth -- and the law of jus
sanguines by which nationality as traced through blood relationship.
Whenever these two principles conflict dual nationality arises.
To ease this unfortunate situation, the 1924 Expatriation
Law was put into effect by the Japanese government. Unfortunately
the result has been proven, beyond a reasonable doubt, a hoax.
The Japanese Consulate Official stated that although the
Japanese children may register only at the Territorial Board of Health,
the status of the child may not be "necessary to say that such children
hold American citizenship only." One of the indirect means of bringing

countries has recently been organised in Tokyo. The preamble of the

Colonisation, seems to be the prime mover of the organisation. Among

1. To invite once a year representatives from various

officials and exchange views on immigration, etc.
2. To enlist the support of Japanese in various countries
for the propaganda of our country.
3. To promote the developmert of our vernacular pepers
in foreign countries and to establish some sort of
closer link between papers in Japan and those in
foreign countries.
4. To offer assistance to the settlement of all disputes
among Japanese in foreign countries.
5. To offer aid to the Japanese in foreign countries
when they file any petition to the government.
6. To act as arbitrators in all disputes between organi-

7. To offer assistance to the problem of immigration in

To render assistance to the solution of second

JAPAN'S NATIONAL MISSION AND HAWAII
National or racial confliots do not become acute until the nation or race kept
in a weaker position is animated by national tendenoy to ohange its status and
strive for equality with the nation or race deemed superior. Commodore Matthew C.
Perry kindled this very kind of spark when he foroefully opened the ports of Japan
to the world.
The Japanese raoe accepted the supremacy of the white race with solemn mental
reservation. She buried her pride and humiliation and austuciously adopted the
spirit of popular educational system from America, military, medical and scientific
training from Germany and the naval strategy and diplomatio tactics from England. In
a good sense, these learnings were fittingly blended into the teaohings and culture
of Japan. She took every nutriment in order to develop Japan's racial civilization.
Today Japan is a new dynamio military power which makes itself felt not only in
the revolt all over Asia against the white race but she is making forceful penetra-
tion into the western hemisphere and has captured many of the rioh commeroial
markets.
The greatest statesman of Japan, Count Okuma, declared: "To brand us Japanese
as inferior because we are a colored race is bigotry -- we must combat and destroy
through the fulfillment of our national mission."
What is then, the national mission of Japan?
It is fairly arguable, basing on historical facts that Japan's national mission
is world supremacy and racial equality. With this in view she has played a role of
an expert strategist, she has judiciously applied the art of jiugitsu, seizing and
olaiming all the strategic points in the continent of Asia and in the Pacific,
directly obstruoting America's advance to the rich commercial El-Dorado of the Far
East. She stretched her steady arm up to the north and gripped Kurile and half of
Sakhalin, threatening Amerioa's future northern air-route. She annexed Korea, the
stepping stone to Asiatic continent, and in l93l, she forcefully seized the three
eastern provinces of Manchuria and the rich opium province of Jehol. Since July 7,
1937 - North and South China. She also possesses the island of Formosa and the
chain of islands north of Formosa to Japan proper. blocking China's front door. She
now holds the key to the western half of the Paoifio, by virtue of taking over all
the former German Pacifio Islands north of equator, even the island of Yap. This
chain of islands for thousands of miles stretches from Bonin to the Marshalls, two
thousand miles nearer to the Hawaiin Islands. Strategically these islands are nat-
ural air bases for her large air forces, coaling station for her navy and the step-
ping stone for her army to maroh toward the white man's country. Unquestionably the
proximity of these islands makes the Amerioan possessions vulnerable!
Japan will never rest until the fulfillment of her dream is ended. To her,
time is no question. Like the 47 ronin who awaited years for an opportunity to
avenge the dishonor of their master, she will do likewise. For 26 years she prepar-
ed for the eventful march from Mukden to Shanghai. It will be a matter of time that
she will attempt to sail from Bonin via Marshalls to Hawaii, then to California, or
from Kurile via Unalaska to the Paoifio Coast.
The Japanese fishing interests are scanning the Marshalls and the Carolines with
hundreds of fishing sampans. In July of 1934, Japan moved her northern fishing base
800 miles nearer to Alaska. The fishing industry employs about 18,O00 men. With
twenty tenders and more than 400 vessels. Hawaii's large fleet of 400 or more sam-
pans and about 15,O00 reservists will be another vital factor. These unique and
strategic positions will be an added advantage to Japan's navy. Not long ago in a
meeting at the Buddhist temple, an American Shintoist, Dr. Mason, remarked, "I have
been told that in the event of war between Japan and the United States you have
enough food supply to last only for six weeks." When he was asked from whom he re-
ceived the information, he answered, "The Japanese leaders told me." For all prac-
tioal purposes the Japanese are fervently pushing Japanization in Hawaii.
Japan is the only world power possessing a first class army as well as navy.
this faotor combined with the compactness of super-strategic position, a naval at-
tack on Hawaii would be reasonably successful. No one can deny that the Pacific
situation is fraught with dangerous possibilities. The indecisive policy of the
United States may enoourage the Japanese militarists to take sudden action. In
which event, What Can Be The Consequenoes?

JAPAN's PREVIOUS ATTEMPT
Hawaii was annexed to the U. S. while Japan was too busy recovering between
wars with China and Russia. To this day the Japanese regret that Japan did not an-
nex these islands prior to her major wars. However, this does not mean that she did
not make any attempt.
In 1894, during the sitting of Constitutional Convention of Hawaii, Japan made
a diplomatio demand that Japanese be given rights to vote. To avoid granting fran-
ohise, the Republic of Hawaii was forced to frame its constitution in such a manner
as to stop all naturalization for the time being, making this matter subject to
further treaty negotiation.
In 1895, the far-sighted Japanese government made strong formal protest against
allowing large number of Chinese to enter Hawaii. Japan's representative stated
that the coming of Chinese to Hawaii was "detrimental to the Japanese interest". It
is said similar protest was made to the Korean government by Prince Ito, ending
further immigration of Koreans to Hawaii.
In 1897, after the unsuocessful attempt to intimidate the Hawaiian government,
the Japanese government seized an opportunity to protest an alleged ill-treatment
and discriminative act toward the Japanese immigrants. She made a formal demand for
an indemnity. Soon after the ultimatum was forwarded to the Hawaiian government,
Japan sent her cruiser, S. Naniwa, under the oommand of Captain Kuroda. On his
arrival Minister Shimamura of Japan immediately asked for a permit to have Captain
Kuroda and his orew to exercise in target practice with the tube guns and rifles ad-
jacent outside of the harbor of Honolulu for 20 days, under the very nose of the
Hawaiian capitol. This dramatio incident hastened the move of annexation of Hawaii
to the United States and temporarily halted Japan's advancement.
"DUCK DIPLOMACY"
Japan's continental policy has been termed the "duck diplomaoy" by the Chinese,
because it typifies a duok, which appears calm and serene above water, while it
paddles busily beneath, making steady progress. Likewise, Japan's diplomacy in
Hawaii oan be termed as such. Outwardly, the Japanese seem very peaceful and loyal
to Amerioa. Yet behind the scene one may find their programs filled with question-
able aotivities.
There are two distinot factors which aid the promotion of Japanization in Hawa-
ii. They aro -- first, the heredity of national traits of the Japanese race. Second
the Japanized environment, created by the Japanese leaders. These two factors have
been so oleverly harmonized and blended into such a degree that the result of collab-
oration is astonishing. It should be borne in mind that the success of Japanization
is largely due, if not entirely, to the correlationship of these two factors.

issues constantly bob up to disturb the community. Enter the business world in

HIS IMPERIAL HIGHNESS, PRINCE FUSHIMI'S FUND
Among the many Japanese institutions and agencies, perhaps the Prinoe Fushimi
Scholarship Association of Hawaii can be considered a representative one, direotly
sponsoring an effeotive action in promoting leadership for the fulfillment of Japan's
mission. The material aid received from a Prince of Japan, in the form of prizes
and soholarship by the American citizens of Japanese ancestry, has created the de-
sired results.
In the year of 1907, after the successful consummation of Anglo-Japanese Alli-
ance, His Imperial Highness, Prince Fushimi of Japan, visited Hawaii on his homeward
voyage as the guest of the British government. Fifteen leading Japanese with Consul-
General Saito, met tho Prinoe and his military aides at the home of Mr. Araki, the
manager of the Yokohama Specie Bank. It is said that General Nishi and Admiral
Yamamoto insisted on an aggressive, typical Japanese program, but the two militarists
were prevailed to compromise to a milder, but an effective program. Prinoe Fushimi
gave a modest amount of $200.00 with the promise of more and the local leaders were
asked to inorease the fund according to the needs from time to time. Prizes and
other recognitions were given to the outstanding young Japaneso student leaders for
meritorious efforts and in excellance of school work. Since l9l9 scholarships wore
awarded, sending outstanding Japanese student leaders to various universities. The
recipients of this fund now hold the key positions in the City, County and
Territorial governments.
JAPANESE CHRISTIANS
Mr. Yusuki Tsurumi, one of the well-known parliamentarian and Christian leaders,
said, "I doubt very much whether Christianity, as developed in America and Europe,
will be aocepted as such by a large number of Japanese ....... Japanese will not
accept a foreign thought without impressing upon it their own stamp."
The foregoing statement by an eminent Japanese Christian leader confirms our
belief that the Japanese Christians in Hawaii cannot be truly Americanized through
Christianity alone. Unfortunately, the American missionaries and many leading fin-
anoiers are of the belief that this seems to be the best means to Americanize the
Amerioan citizens of Japanese ancestry. Looking over the statistics of the various
Japanese religious sects in Hawaii, one will find the sorrowful fact that, in spite
of large expenditures donated by American missionaries, Christianity has been
embraced by the Japanese leaders for a purpose -- a Japanese Front. The following
table will give the reader some idea of the number of Japaneso Christians compared

EXPATRIATION A "HOAX"
Recently the Japanese and many of their Amerioan friends have proudly pointed

CONCLUSION
A few years ago the vice-minister Yasujiro Tsutsumi, of Japan's Overseas Af-
fairs, urged upon Japanese abroad to build up their own civilization and industrial
development, rather than become assimilated in the local population. He stated that
"where Japanese had maintained their identity, the result had been beneficial to
Japan."
General Araki said, "The urgent need of the Japanese nation is to realize justly
and effectively the power of the spirit of the Japanese." He further declared, "The
spirit of Japan must be spread over the seven seas and the five continents. Every-
thing that opposes its expansion is to be overwhelmed if necessary by force. The
countries of eastern Asia have been oppressed by the white people. Japan will not
tolerate this any longer. It is the duty of the Japanese people to oppose any action
of the Powers that run counter to Japanese rule."
Judging from these official attitudes and the subsequent events since l910, it
is apparent that America will soon face a momentous period of her history. The ideals,
politioal philosophies, and economic standards of the two great nations are bound to
test their supremacy. Our national security and the security of these islands will
be wholly contingent upon Japan's military policy in the Pacific. Japanization ac-
tivities should not be considered as mere academic interest; we should follow as
closely as possible the course of events and development of public opinion in Japan
and America.
Amerioans may recall the Wood-Forbes mission in l92l to the  Philippine Islands.
General Wood is said to have had a frank talk with Baron Tanaka (author of Tanaka's
memorial). He told the Japanese militarists "that if she continued to fortify the
Bonins, the Loochoos and the Pesscaadores to the point where at any time it would in-
terfere with or stop American commerce with mainland (China). the U. S. would go to
war". Baron Tanaka answered just as frankly and emphatically, "that if anyone inter-
fered with them in Manchuria, Japan would fight. Japan will not arbitrate on Man-
churia and will fight before she surrenders her hard won rights in the territory she
holds as vital to her security as the U. S. does the Panama Canal."
Since the exohange of this frank declaration, Japan not only fortified the Bonin
and Loochoos, but it is said that she is improving harbors and building large air-
plane landing fields in the Pelews, Carolines and the Marshalls. In the name of
Manchukuo she is building a puppet navy and forcing military training on Manchukuan
and the Koreans. The most recent threat is the "Hands off China" policy which is as
much as to say. Amerioa you keep off from China; this deolaration is a direct threat
and an act of interferenoo to American commerce. Will America go to war with Japan
as declared by General Wood? Thus far America has not taken any effective action,
but if Japan insists to aggravate and demand the equality of naval ratio, elimination
of American commercial and economic interests in China; secretly construct fortifica-
tions in the Pacific Mandates and continue the Japanization of Hawaii, America will
have no alternative.
In the face of all these perplexing contingencies, the strategical value of
Hawaii cannot be too highly stressed. Hawaii is the Heligoland to U. S. Navy and
Gibraltar to U. S. Army. Therefore, the necessity of Americanization in Hawaii is
doubly significant. Our security will wholly depend upon the satisfactory and ra-
tional settlement of political and military problems between Japan and America. The
Japanization of Hawaii is no longer an issue only for the people of Hawaii but it has
become national and as such it should be dealt with.
Japan's continued aggressive movement into the continent of Asia and particular-
ly Japan's insistence of Japanization of her subjects residing in the North and South
American countries and Hawaii are the outcome of the intense desire of the Japanese
race to change their racial, social, economic, and political and military status
equal to the status of America and of the white race. This spirit of Japan will
never rest till her national mission is attained.
More than three decades ago American hearts were oaptivated by the eloquence of
Senator Beveridge. He declared in the Senate -
"Our largest trade henceforth must be with Asia. The Pacific is our ocean.

have no alternative.
In the face of all these perplexing contingencies. the strategical value of
Hawaii cannot be too highly stressed. Hawaii is the Heligoland to U. S. Navy and
Gibraltar to U. S. Army. Therefore. the necessity of Americanization in Hawaii is
doubly significant. Our security will wholly depend upon the satisfactory and ra-
tional settlement of political and military problems between Japan and America. The
Japanization of Hawaii is no longer an issue only for the people of Hawaii but it has
become national and as such it should be dealt with.
Japan's continued aggressive movement into the continent of Asia and particular-
ly Japan's insistence of Japanization of her subjects residing in the North and South
American countries and Hawaii are the outcome of the intense desire of the Japanese
race to change their racial, social, economic, and political and military status
equal to the status of America and of the white race. This spirit of Japan will
never rest till her national mission is attained.
More than three decades ago American hearts were oaptivated by the eloquence of
Senator Beveridge. He deolared in the Senate -
"Our largest trade henceforth must be with Asia. The Pacific is our ocean.
- - - And the Pacific is the ocean of the commerce of the future.
"Most future wars will be conflicts of commerce. The Power that rules the
Pacific, therefore, is the Power that rules the world."

Twenty-three years ago Mr. Chokume Matsuo said: "Japan and America are pitted
against each other not only as regards China but also with regards to the mastery of
the Pacific Ocean. There is always a possibility of the outbreak of war between
Japan and America. Frankly speaking, there is no prospect for America's emerging
victorious, judged both from her military and naval preparedness.
"Remember the position of the country before the outbreak of Russo-Japanese War.
There might have been not a soul in the world who dreamed of Japan's defeating Rus-
sia."
Can America arrest Japanization of Asia and Hawaii without going into a racial
war with Japan? Thinking Americans fully know when Japan is in full control of Asia,
with countless man power and with all the rich resources under their command, America
will be forced to lower the white man's standard of living, and submit to much
humiliation.
The writer sinoerely believes that America can arrest Japanization of Asia and
Hawaii if she so desires. The following course of aotion will force Japan's milita-
rists to their senses, eventually bringing peace and security in the Pacific:
First: Embargo the necessary arms, munitions, machinery, and materials
essential for war to Japan through a planned subsidy for two years.
Second: Extend positive moral aid to China and Korea to resist Japan's
militarists.
America's present policy of supplying 57 peroent of all war essentials to
Japan is parallel to America's aid to Japan when annexing Korea in 1910. Japan
used Korea as a stepping stone in the conquest of China. If history repeats,
Japan will use China in the conquest of Alaska, Hawaii, and possibly the Pacific
Coast.
Remember the American-Korean Treaty, May 22, 1882?

JAPAN'S NATIONAL MISSION AND HAWAII
National or racial confliots do not become acute until the nation or race kept
in a weaker position is animated by national tendency to change its status and
strive for equality with the nation or race deemed superior. Commodore Matthew C.
Perry kindled this very kind of spark when he foroefully opened the ports of Japan
to the world.
The Japanese race accepted the supremacy of the white race with solemn mental
reservation. She buried her pride and humiliation and austuciously adopted the
spirit of popular educational system from America, military, medical and scientific
training from Germany and the naval strategy and diplomatic tactics from England. In
a good sense, these learnings were fittingly blended into the teachings and culture
of Japan. She took every nutriment in order to develop Japan's racial civilization.
Today Japan is a new dynamic military power which makes itself felt not only in
the revolt all over Asia against the white race but she is making forceful penetra-
tion into the western hemisphere and has captured many of the rich commercial
markets.
The greatest statesman of Japan, Count Okuma, declared: "To brand us Japanese
as inferior because we are a oolored race is bigotry -- we must combat and destroy
through the fulfillment of our national mission."
What is then, the national mission of Japan?
It is fairly arguable, basing on historical facts that Japan's national mission
is world supremacy and racial equality. With this in view she has played a role of
an expert strategist, she has judiciously applied the art of jiugitsu, seizing and
olaiming all the strategic points in the continent of Asia and in the Pacific,
directly obstructing Amerioa's advance to the rich commercial El-Dorado of the Far
East. She stretched her steady arm up to the north and gripped Kurile and half of
Sakhalin, threatening Amerioa's future northern air-route. She annexed Korea, the
stepping stone to Asiatic continent, and in l93l, she forcefully seized the three
eastern provinces of Manchuria and the rich opium province of Jehol. Since July 7,
1937 - North and South China. She also possesses the island of Formosa and the
chain of islands north of Formosa to Japan proper. blocking China's front door. She
now holds the key to the western half of the Pacific, by virtue of taking over all
the former German Pacific Islands north of equator, even the island of Yap. This
chain of islands for thousands of miles stretches from Bonin to the Marshalls, two
thousand miles nearer to the Hawaiin Islands. Strategically these islands are nat-
ural air bases for her large air forces, coaling station for her navy and the step-
ping stone for her army to march toward the white man's country. Unquesti onably the
proximity of these islands makes the American possessions vulnerable!
Japan will never rest until the fulfillment of her dream is ended. To her,
time is no question. Like the 47 ronin who awaited years for an opportunity to
avenge the dishonor of their master, she will do likewise. For 26 years she prepar-
ed for the eventful march from Mukden to Shanghai. It will be a matter of time that
she will attempt to sail from Bonin via Marshalls to Hawaii, then to California, or
from Kurile via Unalaska to the Pacific Coast.
The Japanese fishing interests are scanning the Marshalls and the Carolines with
hundreds of fishing sampans. In July of 1934, Japan moved her northern fishing base
800 miles nearer to Alaska. The fishing industry employs about 18,O00 men. With
twenty tenders and more than 400 vessels. Hawaii's large fleet of 400 or more sam-
pans and about 15,Ooo reservists will be another vital factor. These unique and
strategic positions will be an added advantage to Japan's navy. Not long ago in a
meeting at the Buddhist temple, an American Shintoist, Dr. Mason, remarked. "I have
been told that in the event of war between Japan and the United States you have
enough food supply to last only for six weeks." When he was asked from whom he re-
ceived the information, he answered, "The Japanese leaders told me." For all prac-
tioal purposes the Japanese are fervently pushing Japanization in Hawaii.
Japan is the only world power possessing a first class army as well as navy,
this factor combined with the compactness of super-strategic position, a naval at-
tack on Hawaii would be reasonably successful. No one can deny that the Pacific
situation is fraught with dangerous possibilities. The indecisive policy of the
United States may oncourage the Japanese militarists to take sudden action. In

One. That the American fleet will be forced to wage a defensive war.

JAPAN's PREVIOUS ATTEMPT
Hawaii was annexed to the U. S. while Japan was too busy recovering between
wars with China and Russia. To this day the Japanese regret that Japan did not an-
nex these islands prior to her major wars. However, this does not mean that she did
not make any attempt.
In 1894, during the sitting of Constitutional Convention of Hawaii, Japan made
a diplomatio demand that Japanese be given rights to vote. To avoid granting fran-
ohise, the Republic of Hawaii was forced to frame its constitution in such a manner
as to stop all naturalization for the time being, making this matter subject to
further treaty negotiation.
In 1895, the far-sighted Japanese government made strong formal protest against
allowing large number of Chinese to enter Hawaii. Japan's representative stated
that the coming of Chinese to Hawaii was "detrimental to the Japanese interest". It
is said similar protest was made to tho Korean government by Prince Ito, ending
further immigration of Koreans to Hawaii.
In 1897, after the unsuocessful attempt to intimidate the Hawaiian government,
the Japanese government seized an opportunity to protest an alleged ill-treatment
and discriminative act toward the Japanese immigrants. She made a formal demand for
an indemnity. Soon after the ultimatum was forwarded to the Hawaiian government,
Japan sent her cruiser, S. Naniwa, undor the command of Captain Kuroda. On his
arrival Ministor Shimamura of Japan immediately asked for a permit to have Captain
Kuroda and his orew to exercise in target practice with the tube guns and rifles ad-
jacent outside of the harbor of Honolulu for 20 days, under the very nose of the
Hawaiian capitol. This dramatic incident hastened the move of annexation of Hawaii
to the United States and temporarily halted Japan's advancement.
"DUCK DIPLOMACY"
Japan's continental policy has been termed the "duck diplomacy" by the Chinese,
beoause it typifies a duck, which appears calm and serene above water. while it
paddles busily beneath, making steady progress. Likewise, Japan's diplomacy in
Hawaii can be termed as suoh. Outwardly, the Japanese seem very peaceful and loyal
to America. Yet behind the scene one may find their programs filled with question-
able activities.
There are two distinot factors which aid the promotion of Japanization in Hawa-
ii. They aro -- first, the heredity of national traits of the Japanese race. Second.
the Japanized environment, created by the Japanese leaders. These two factors have
been so oleverly harmonized and blended into such a degroe that the result of collab-
oration is astonishing. It should be borne in mind that the success of Japanization
is largely due, if not entirely, to the correlationship of these two factors.

issues constantly bob up to disturb the community. Enter the business world in
Hawaii and one will find that race prejudice still controls its human emotions. Very

HIS IMPERIAL HIGHNESS, PRINCE FUSHIMI'S FUND
Among the many Japanese institutions and agencies, perhaps the Prince Fushimi
Scholarship Association of Hawaii can be considered a representative one, direotly
sponsoring an effective action in promoting leadership for the fulfillment of Japan's
mission. The material aid received from a Prince of Japan, in the form of prizes
and scholarship by the American citizens of Japanese anoestry, has created the de-
sired results.
In the year of 1907, after the successful consummation of Anglo-Japanese Alli-
ance, His Imperial Highness, Prince Fushimi of Japan, visited Hawaii on his homeward
voyage as the guest of the British government. Fifteen leading Japanese with Consul-
General Saito, met tho Prinoe and his military aides at the home of Mr. Araki, the
manager of the Yokohama Specie Bank. It is said that General Nishi and Admiral
Yamamoto insisted on an aggressive, typical Japanese program, but the two militarists
were prevailed to compromise to a milder, but an effective program. Prince Fushimi
gave a modest amount of $2o0.00 with the promise of more and the local leaders were
asked to increase the fund according to the needs from time to time. Prizes and
other recognitions were givon to the outstanding young Japanese student leaders for
meritorious offorts and in excellonce of school work. Since l919 scholarships woro
awarded, sending outstanding Japanese student leaders to various universities. The
recipients of this fund now hold the key positions in the City, County and
Territorial governments.
JAPANESE CHRISTIANS
Mr. Yusuki Tsurumi, one of the well-known parliamentarian and Christian leaders,
said, "I doubt very much whether Christianity, as developed in America and Europe,
will be accepted as such by a large number of Japanese ....... Japanese will not
accept a foreign thought without impressing upon it their owm stamp."
The foregoing statement by an eminent Japanose Christian leader confirms our
belief that the Japanese Christians in Hawaii cannot be truly Americanized through
Christianity alone. Unfortunately, tho American missionaries and many leading fin-
anciers are of the belief that this seems to be the best means to Amerioanize the
American citizens of Japanese ancestry. Looking over the statistics of the various
Japanese religious sects in Hawaii, one will find the sorrowful fact that, in spite
of large expenditures donated by Amorican missionaries, Christianity has been
embraced by the Japanese leaders for a purpose -- a Japanese Front. The following
table will give the reader some idea of the number of Japaneso Christians compared

EXPATRIATION A "HOAX"
Recently the Japanese and many of their American friends have proudly pointed
out to the expatriated Japanese boys and girls as a proof of their loyalty to America.
Peculiarly, the Japanese law of nationality is based on the principle of jus
sanguines, while the Amerioan laws are based on the principle of jus soli. Dual

=== Page 411 === (confidence 0.99)
nationality usually arises through a confliot between the law of jus soli -- the law
determining nationality according to the place of birth -- and the law of jus san-
guines by which nationality is traced through blood relationship. Whenever these
two prinoiples conflict dual nationality arises.
To ease this unfortunate situation, the 1924 Expatriation Law was put into
effect by the Japanese government. Unfortunately the result has been proven, beyond
a reasonable doubt, a hoax.
The Japanese Consulate Official stated that although the Japanese children may
register only at the Territorial Board of Health, the status of the ohild may not be
"necessary to say that such children hold American citizenship only". One of the in-
direct means of bringing the expatriated Japanese youths back to their own national-
ity is that they are urged to register their marriage certificates at the Japanese
Consulate, thus regaining their nationality from the Japanese government. Another
way is the general practice of the parents of the Japanese ancestry registering their
names at the Consulate when they become of military age, without their son's knowl-
edge. It is said "the parents are forced to do it, for otherwise their relatives
residing in Japan would be punished, fined or otherwise made to suffer." Approx-
imately two-thirds of the Amerioan citizens of Japanese ancestry in Hawaii retain the
status of dual citizenship.

CONCLUSION
A few years ago the vice-minister Yasujiro Tsutsumi, of Japan's Overseas Af-
fairs, urged upon Japanese abroad to build up their own civilization and industrial
development, rather than become assimilated in the local population. He stated that
"where Japanese had maintained their identity, the result had been beneficial to
Japan."
General Araki said, "The urgent need of the Japanese nation is to realize justly
and effectively the power of the spirit of the Japanese." He further deolared, "The
spirit of Japan must be spread over the seven seas and the five continents. Every-
thing that opposes its expansion is to be overwhelmed if neoessary by force. The
countries of eastern Asia have been oppressed by the white people. Japan will not
tolerate this any longer. It is the duty of the Japanese people to oppose any action
of the Powers that run counter to Japanese rule."
Judging from these official attitudes and the subsequent events since l910, it
is apparent that America will soon face a momentous period of her history. The ideals,
political philosophies, and economic standards of the two great nations are bound to
test their supremacy. Our national security and the security of these islands will
be wholly contingent upon Japan's military policy in the Pacific. Japanization ac-
tivities should not be considered as mere academic interest; we should follow as
closely as possible the course of events and development of public opinion in Japan
and America.
Americans may recall the Wood-Forbes mission in 192l to the  Philippine Islands.
General Wood is said to have had a frank talk with Baron Tanaka (author of Tanaka's
memorial). He told the Japanese militarists "that if she continued to fortify the
Bonins, the Looohoos and the Pesscaadores to the point where at any time it would in-
terfere with or stop American commerce with mainland (China), the U. S. would go to
war". Baron Tanaka answered just as frankly and emphatically, "that if anyone inter-
fered with them in Manchuria, Japan would fight. Japan will not arbitrate on Man-
churia and will fight before she surrenders her hard won rights in the territory she
holds as vital to her security as the U. S. does the Panama Canal."
Since the exchange of this frank declaration, Japan not only fortified the Bonin
and Loochoos, but it is said that she is improving harbors and building large air-
plane landing fields in the Pelews, Carolines and the Marshalls. In the name of
Manchukuo she is building a puppet navy and forcing military training on Manchukuan
and the Koreans. The most recent threat is the "Hands off China" policy which is as
much as to say. America you keep off from China; this deolaration is a direct threat
and an aot of interferenoo to American commeroe. Will America go to war with Japan
as declared by General Wood? Thus far America has not taken any effective action,
but if Japan insists to aggravate and demand the equality of naval ratio, elimination
of Amerioan commercial and economic interests in China; secretly construct fortifica-
tions in the Pacific Mandates and continue the Japanization of Hawaii, America will
have no alternative.
In the face of all these perplexing contingencies, the strategical value of
Hawaii cannot be too highly stressed. Hawaii is the Heligoland to U. S. Navy and
Gibraltar to U. S. Army. Therefore, the necessity of Americanization in Hawaii is
doubly significant. Our security will wholly depend upon the satisfactory and ra-
tional settlement of political and military problems between Japan and America. The
Japanization of Hawaii is no longer an issue only for the people of Hawaii but it has
become national and as suoh it should be dealt with.
Japan's continued aggressive movement into the continent of Asia and particular-
ly Japan's insistence of Japanization of her subjects residing in the North and South
American countries and Hawaii are the outcome of the intense desire of the Japanese
race to change their racial, social, economic, and political and military status
equal to the status of America and of the white race. This spirit of Japan will
never rest till her national mission is attained.
More than three decades ago American hearts were captivated by the eloquence of
Senator Beveridge. He declared in the Senate -
"Our largest trade henceforth must be with Asia. The Pacific is our ocean.

JAPAN'S NATIONAL MISSION AND HAWAII
National or raoial oonfliots do not become acute until the nation or race kept
in a weaker position is animated by national tendency to change its status and
strive for equality with the nation or raoe deemed superior. Commodore Matthew C.
Perry kindled this very kind of spark when he forcefully opened the ports of Japan
to the world.
The Japanese race accepted the supremacy of the white race with solemn mental
reservation. She buried her pride and humiliation and austuciously adopted the
spirit of popular educational system from America, military, medical and scientific
training from Germany and the naval strategy and diplomatic tactics from England. In
a good sense, these learnings were fittingly blended into the teaohings and culture
of Japan. She took every nutriment in order to develop Japan's racial civilization.
Today Japan is a new dynamic military power which makes itself felt not only in
the revolt all over Asia against the white race but she is making forceful penetra-
tion into the western hemisphere and has captured many of the rich commercial
markets.
The greatest statesman of Japan, Count Okuma, declared: "To brand us Japanese
as inferior because we are a colored race is bigotry -- we must combat and destroy
through the fulfillment of our national mission."
What is then, the national mission of Japan?
It is fairly arguable, basing on historioal facts that Japan's national mission
is world supremacy and racial equality. With this in view she has played a role of
an expert strategist, she has judiciously applied the art of jiugitsu, seizing and
olaiming all the strategic points in the continent of Asia and in the Pacific,
directly obstructing America's advance to the rich commercial El-Dorado of the Far
East. She stretched her steady arm up to the north and gripped Kurile and half of
Sakhalin, threatening Amerioa's future northern air-route. She annexed Korea, the
stepping stone to Asiatic continent, and in 193l, she forcefully seized the three
eastern provinoes of Manchuria and the rich opium province of Jehol. Since July 7,
1937 - North and South China. She also possesses the island of Formosa and the
chain of islands north of Formosa to Japan proper. blocking China's front door. She

JAPAN's PREVIOUS ATTEMPT
Hawaii was annexed to the U. S. while Japan was too busy recovering between
wars with China and Russia. To this day the Japanese regret that Japan did not an-
nex these islands prior to her major wars. However, this does not mean that she did
not make any attempt.
In 1894, during the sitting of Constitutional Convention of Hawaii, Japan made
a diplomatio demand that Japanese be given rights to vote. To avoid granting fran-
chise, the Republic of Hawaii was forced to frame its constitution in such a manner
as to stop all naturalization for the time being, making this matter subject to
further treaty negotiation.
In 1895, the far-sighted Japanese government made strong formal protest against
allowing large number of Chinese to enter Hawaii. Japan's representative stated
that the coming of Chinese to Hawaii was "detrimental to the Japanese interest". It
is said similar protest was made to the Korean government by Prince Ito, ending
further immigration of Koreans to Hawaii.
In 189~: after the unsuccessful attempt to intimidate the Hawaiian government,
the Japanese government seized an opportunity to protest an alleged ill-treatment
and discriminative act toward the Japanese immigrants. She made a formal demand for
an indemmity. Soon after the ultimatum was forwarded to the Hawaiian government,
Japan sent her oruiser, S. Naniwa, under the command of Captain Kuroda. On his
arrival Minister Shimamura of Japan immediately asked for a permit to have Captain
Kuroda and his orew to exeroise in target praotice with the tube guns and rifles ad-
jacent outside of the harbor of Honolulu for 20 days, under the very nose of the
Hawaiian capitol. This dramatio inoident hastened the move of annexation of Hawaii
to the United States and temporarily halted Japan's advancement.
"DUCK DIPLOMACY"
Japan's continental policy has been termed the "duck diplomacy" by the Chinese,
because it typifies a duck, which appears calm and serene above water, while it
paddles busily beneath, making steady progress. Likewise, Japan's diplomacy in
Hawaii oan be termed as suoh. Outwardly, the Japanese seem very peaceful and loyal
to Amerioa. Yet behind the scene one may find their programs filled with question-
able activities.

ii. They are -- first, the heredity of national traits of the Japanese race. Second
the Japanized environment, created by the Japanese leaders. These two factors have

is largely due, if not entirely, to the correlationship of these two faotors.

HIS IMPERIAL HIGHNESS, FRINCE FUSHIMI'S FUND
Among the many Japanese institutions and agencies, perhaps the Prince Fushimi
Scholarship Association of Hawaii can be considered a representative one, directly
sponsoring an effective action in promoting leadership for the fulfillment of Japan's
mission. The material aid received from a Prince of Japan, in the form of prizes
and soholarship by the American citizens of Japanese anoestry, has oreated the de-
sired results.
In the year of 1907. after the successful consummation of Anglo-Japanese Alli-
ance, His Imperial Highness, Prince Fushimi of Japan, visited Hawaii on his homeward
voyage as the guest of the British government. Fifteen leading Japanese with Consul-
General Saito, met tho Prince and his military aides at the home of Mr. Araki, the
manager of the Yokohama Specie Bank. It is said that General Nishi and Admiral
Yamamoto insisted on an aggressive, typical Japanese program, but the two militarists
were prevailed to compromise to a milder, but an effective program. Prince Fushimi
gave a modest amount of $200.00 with the promise of more and the local leaders were
asked to increase the fund according to the needs from time to time. Prizes and
other recognitions were givon to the outstanding young Japaneso student leaders for
meritorious efforts and in excellonce of school work. Since l9l9 scholarships woro
awarded, sending outstanding Japanese student leaders to various universities. The
reoipients of this fund now hold the key positions in the City, County and
Territorial governments.

A few years ago the vice-minister Yasujiro Tsutsumi, of Japan's Overseas Af-
fairs, urged upon Japanese abroad to build up their own civilization and industrial
development, rather than become assimilated in the local population. He stated that
"where Japanese had maintained their identity, the result had been beneficial to
Japan."
General Araki said, "The urgent need of the Japanese nation is to realize justly
and effectively the power of the spirit of the Japanese." He further declared, "The
spirit of Japan must be spread over the seven seas and the five continents. Every-
thing that opposes its expansion is to be overwhelmed if necessary by force. The
countries of eastern Asia have been oppressed by the white people. Japan will not
tolerate this any longer. It is the duty of the Japanese people to oppose any action
of the Powers that run counter to Japanese rule."
Judging from these official attitudes and the subsequent events since 1910, it
is apparent that America will soon face a momentous period of her history. The ideals,
political philosophies, and economic standards of the two great nations are bound to
test their supremacy. Our national security and the security of these islands will
be wholly contingent upon Japan's military policy in the Pacific. Japanization ac-
tivities should not be considered as mere academic interest; we should follow as
closely as possible the course of events and development of public opinion in Japan
and America.
Americans may recall the Wood-Forbes mission in 192l to the Philippine Islands.
General Wood is said to have had a frank talk with Baron Tanaka (author of Tanaka's
memorial). He told the Japanese militarists "that if she continued to fortify the
Bonins, the Loochoos and the Pesscaadores to the point where at any time it would in-
terfere with or stop American commerce with mainland (China), the U. S. would go to
war". Baron Tanaka answered just as frankly and emphatically, "that if anyone inter-
fered with them in Manchuria, Japan would fight. Japan will not arbitrate on Man-
churia and will fight before she surrenders her hard won rights in the territory she
holds as vital to her security as the U. S. does the Panama Canal."
Since the exchange of this frank declaration, Japan not only fortified the Bonin
and Looohoos, but it is said that she is improving harbors and building large air-
plane landing fields in the Pelews, Carolines and the Marshalls. In the name of
Manchukuo she is building a puppet navy and forcing military training on Manchukuan
and the Koreans. The most recent threat is the "Hands off China" policy which is as
much as to say. Amerioa you keep off from China; this declaration is a direct threat
and an aot of interferenoe to American commerce. Will America go to war with Japan
as declared by General Wood? Thus far America has not taken any effective action,
but if Japan insists to aggravate and demand the equality of naval ratio, elimination
of Amerioan commeroial and economic interests in China; secretly construct fortifioa-
tions in the Pacific Mandates and continue the Japanization of Hawaii, America will
have no alternative.
In the face of all these perplexing contingencies, the strategical value of
Hawaii cannot be too highly stressed. Hawaii is the Heligoland to U. S. Navy and
Gibraltar to U. S. Army. Therefore. the necessity of Americanization in Hawaii is
doubly significant. Our seourity will wholly depend upon the satisfactory and ra-
tional settlement of political and military problems between Japan and America. The
Japanization of Hawaii is no longer an issue only for the people of Hawaii but it has
become national and as such it should be dealt with.

Amerioan countries and Hawaii are the outcome of the intense desire of the Japanese

equal to the status of America and of the white race. This spirit of Japan will

JAPAN'S NATIONAL MISSION AND HAWAII
National or racial conflicts do not become acute until the nation or race kept
in a weaker position is animated by national tendoncy to change its status and
strive for equality with the nation or race deemed superior. Commodore Matthew C.
Perry kindled this very kind of spark when he foroefully opened the ports of Japan
to the world.
The Japanese race accepted the supremacy of the white race with solemn mental
reservation. She buried her pride and humiliation and austuciously adopted the
spirit of popular educational system from America, military, medical and scientific
training from Germany and the naval strategy and diplomatic tactics from England. In
a good sense, these learnings were fittingly blended into the teachings and culture
of Japan. She took every nutriment in order to develop Japan's racial civilization.
Today Japan is a new dynamio military power which makes itself felt not only in
the revolt all over Asia against the white race but she is making forceful penetra-
tion into the western hemisphere and has captured many of the rich commercial
markets.
The greatest statesman of Japan, Count Okuma, declared: "To brand us Japanese
as inferior because we are a oolored race is bigotry -- we must combat and destroy
through the fulfillment of our national mission."
What is then, the national mission of Japan?
It is fairly arguable, basing on historical facts that Japan's national mission
is world supremacy and racial equality. With this in view she has played a role of
an expert strategist, she has judiciously applied the art of jiugitsu, seizing and
claiming all the strategic points in the continent of Asia and in the Pacific,
directly obstruoting Amerioa's advance to the rich commercial El-Dorado of the Far
East. She stretohed her steady arm up to the north and gripped Kurile and half of
Sakhalin, threatening Amerioa's future northern air-route. She annexed Korea, the
stepping stone to Asiatic continent, and in l931, she forcefully seized the three
eastern provinces of Manchuria and the rich opium province of Jehol. Since July 7,
1937 - North and South China. She also possesses the island of Formosa and the
chain of islands north of Formosa to Japan proper. blocking China's front door. She
now holds the key to the western half of the Pacific, by virtue of taking over all
the former German Pacific Islands north of equator, even the island of Yap. This
chain of islands for thousands of miles stretches from Bonin to the Marshalls, two
thousand miles nearer to the Hawaiin Islands. Strategically these islands are nat-
ural air bases for her large air forces, coaling station for her navy and the step-
ping stone for her army to march toward the white man's country. Unquesti onably the
proximity of these islands makes the American possessions vulnerable!
Japan will never rest until the fulfillment of her dream is ended. To her,
time is no question. Like the 47 ronin who awaited years for an opportunity to
avenge the dishonor of their master, she will do likowise. For 26 years she prepar-
ed for the eventful march from Mukden to Shanghai. It will be a matter of time that
she will attempt to sail from Bonin via Marshalls to Hawaii, then to California, or
from Kurile via Unalaska to the Pacific Coast.
The Japanese fishing interests are scanning the Marshalls and the Carolines with
hundreds of fishing sampans. In July of 1934, Japan moved her northern fishing base
800 miles nearer to Alaska. The fishing industry employs about 18,000 men. With
twenty tenders and more than 400 vessels. Hawaii's large fleet of 400 or more sam.
pans and about 15,O00 reservists will be another vital factor. These unique and
strategic positions will be an added advantage to Japan's navy. Not long ago in a
meeting at the Buddhist temple, an American Shintoist, Dr. Mason, remarked, "I have
been told that in the event of war between Japan and the United States you have
enough food supply to last only for six weeks." When he was asked from whom he re-
ceived the information, he answered, "The Japanese leaders told me." For all prac-
tical purposes the Japanese are fervently pushing Japanization in Hawaii.
Japan is the only world power possessing a first class army as well as navy,
this factor combined with the compactness of super-strategic position, a naval at-
tack on Hawaii would be reasonably suocessful. No one can deny that the Pacific
situation is fraught with dangerous possibilities. The indecisive policy of the
United States may encourage the Japanese militarists to take sudden antion

JAPAN's PREVIOUS ATTEMPT
Hawaii was annexed to the U. S. while Japan was too busy recovering between
wars with China and Russia. To this day the Japanese regret that Japan did not an-
nex these islands prior to her major wars. However, this does not mean that she did
not make any attempt.
In 1894, during the sitting of Constitutional Convention of Hawaii, Japan made
a diplomatio demand that Japanese be given rights to vote. To avoid granting fran-
ohise, the Republic of Hawaii was forced to frame its constitution in such a manner
as to stop all naturalization for the time being, making this matter subjeot to
further treaty negotiation.
In 1895, the far-sighted Japanese government made strong formal protest against
allowing large number of Chinese to enter Hawaii. Japan's representative stated
that the coming of Chinese to Hawaii was "detrimental to the Japanese interest".
It
is said similar protest was made to the Korean government by Prince Ito, ending
further immigration of Koreans to Hawaii.
In 1897, after the unsuccessful attempt to intimidate the Hawaiian government,
the Japanese government seized an opportunity to protest an alleged ill-treatment
and discriminative act toward the Japanese immigrants. She made a formal demand for
an indemnity. Soon after the ultimatum was forwarded to the Hawaiian government,
Japan sent her cruiser, S. Naniwa, under the command of Captain Kuroda. On his
arrival Minister Shimamura of Japan immediately asked for a permit to have Captain
Kuroda and his orew to exeroise in target practice with the tube guns and rifles ad-
jacent outside of the harbor of Honolulu for 20 days, under the very nose of the
Hawaiian capitol. This dramatic incident hastened the move of annexation of Hawaii
to the United States and temporarily halted Japan's advancement.
"DUCK DIPLOMACY"
Japan's continental policy has been termed the "duck diplomaoy" by the Chinese,
because it typifies a duck, which appears calm and serene above water, while it
paddles busily beneath, making steady progress. Likewise, Japan's diplomacy in
Hawaii can be termed as suoh. Outwardly, the Japanese seem very peaceful and loyal
to America. Yet behind the scene one may find their programs filled with question-
able activities.
There are two distinct factors which aid the promotion of Japanization in Hawa-
ii. They are -- first. the heredity of national traits of the Japanese race. Second.
the Japanized environment. created by the Japanese leaders. These two factors have
been so oleverly harmonized and blended into such a degree that the result of collab-
oration is astonishing. It should be borne in mind that the success of Japanization
is largely due, if not entirely, to the correlationship of these two factors.

underlying its peaceful surface, the problem of racial equality and its contemporary
issues constantly bob up to disturb the community. Enter the business world in

ohise, the Republic of Hawaii was forced to frame its constitution in such a manner
as to stop all naturalization for the time being, making this matter subjeot to
further treaty negotiation.
In 1895, the far-sighted Japanese government made strong formal protest against
allowing large number of Chinese to enter Hawaii. Japan's representative stated
that the coming of Chinese to Hawaii was "detrimental to the Japanese interest". It
is said similar protest was made to the Korean government by Prince Ito, ending
further immigration of Koreans to Hawaii.
In 1897, after the unsuocessful attempt to intimidate the Hawaiian government,
the Japanese government seized an opportunity to protest an alleged ill-treatment
and discriminative act toward the Japanese immigrants. She made a formal demand for
an indemnity. Soon after the ultimatum was forwarded to the Hawaiian government,
Japan sent her cruiser, S. Naniwa, under the command of Captain Kuroda. On his
arrival Minister Shimamura of Japan immediately asked for a permit to have Captain
Kuroda and his orew to exeroise in target practice with the tube guns and rifles ad-
jacent outside of the harbor of Honolulu for 20 days, under the very nose of the
Hawaiian capitol. This dramatio incident hastened the move of annexation of Hawaii
to the United States and temporarily halted Japan's advancement.
"DUCK DIPLOMACY"
Japan's continental policy has been termed the "duck diplomaoy" by the Chinese,
because it typifies a duck, which appears calm and serene above water. while it
paddles busily beneath, making steady progress. Likewise, Japan's diplomacy in
Hawaii can be termed as suoh. Outwardly, the Japanese seem very peaceful and loyal
to America. Yet behind the scene one may find their programs filled with question-
able activities.
There are two distinot factors which aid the promotion of Japanization in Hawa-
ii. They arc -- first. the heredity of national traits of the Japanese race. Second.
the Japanized environment, created by the Japanese leaders. These two factors have
been so oleverly harmonized and blended into such a degree that the result of collab-
oration is astonishing. It should be borne in mind that the success of Japanization
is largely due, if not entirely, to the correlationship of these two factors.
RACIAL HARMONY?
Although Hawaii is called the "melting pot" in the crossroad of the Pacific,
underlying its peaceful surface, the problem of racial equality and its contemporary
issues constantly bob up to disturb the community. Enter the business world in
Hawaii and one will find that race prejudice still controls its human emotions. Very
often the question of racial equality is fully discussed in the classrooms of the
public schools, and among missionaries. To be sure, the politicians loudly speak of
it on the stumps, during the political campaigns.
- 3 -

=== Page 445 === (confidence 0.99)
The elder citizens consider the question of racial equality merely an academic
bjeot, while the youngsters of the teen age make a reasonable practice of it. How-
over, as soon as the two races venture out into the business world as competitors,
they find the common ground on which they had stood has suddenly disappeared. In-
wardly, both races wish to exclude each other in order to prevent a rapid rise or to
exclude dissimilar customs as a means of promoting national solidarity. Whether
this prejudice is intentional or not, the aotual praotice still persists in Hawaii
and it will continue to fight for supremaoy of race so long as the Japanese race de-
mands equal raoial status -- Americanism vs. Japanism.
HIS IMPERIAL HIGHNESS, PRINCE FUSHIMI'S FUND
Among the many Japanese institutions and agencies, perhaps the Prince Fushimi
Scholarship Association of Hawaii can be considered a representative one, direotly
sponsoring an effective action in promoting leadership for the fulfillment of Japan's
mission. The material aid received from a Prinoe of Japan, in the form of prizes
and soholarship by the American citizens of Japanese ancestry, has created the de-
sired results.
In the year of 1907, after the sucoessful consummation of Anglo-Japanese Alli-
ance, His Imperial Highness, Prince Fushimi of Japan, visited Hawaii on his homeward
voyage as the guest of the British government. Fifteen leading Japanese with Consul-
General Saito, met the Prince and his military aides at the home of Mr. Araki, the
manager of the Yokohama Speoie Bank. It is said that General Nishi and Admiral
Yamamoto insisted on an aggressive, typical Japanese program, but the two militarists
were prevailed to compromise to a milder, but an effective program. Prinoe Fushimi
gave a modest amount of $2o0.00 with the promise of more and the local leaders were
asked to inorease the fund according to the needs from time to time. Prizes and
other recognitions were given to the outstanding young Japanese student leaders for
meritorious efforts and in excellence of school work. Since l919 soholarships woro
awarded, sending outstanding Japanese student leaders to various universities. The
recipients of this fund now hold the key positions in the City, County and
Territorial governments.
JAPANESE CHRISTIANS

will be accepted as such by a large number of Japanese ....... Japanese will not
accept a foreign thought without impressing upon it their own stamp."
The foregoing statement by an eminent Japanese Christian leader confirms our
belief that the Japanese Christians in Hawaii cannot be truly Americanized through
Christianity alone. Unfortunately, the Amerioan missionaries and many leading fin-

American citizens of Japanese ancestry. Looking over the statistics of the various
Japanese religious sects in Hawaii, one will find the sorrowful fact that, in spite

EXPATRIATION A "HOAX"
Recently the Japanese and many of their American friends have proudly pointed
out to the expatriated Japanese boys and girls as a proof of their loyalty to America.
Peculiarly, the Japanese law of nationality is based on the principle of jus
sanguines, while the Amerioan laws are based on the principle of jus soli. Dual

=== Page 447 === (confidence 0.99)
hationality usually arises through a confliot between the law of jus soli -- the law
determining nationality according to the place of birth -- and the law of jus san-
guines by whioh nationality is traced through blood relationship. Whenever these
two principles conflict dual nationality arises.
To ease this unfortunate situation, the 1924 Expatriation Law was put into
effect by the Japanese government. Unfortunately the result has been proven, beyond
a reasonable doubt, a hoax.
The Japanese Consulate Official stated that although the Japanese children may
register only at the Territorial Board of Health, the status of the child may not be
"necessary to say that such children hold American citizenship only". One of the in-
direot means of bringing the expatriated Japanese youths back to their own national-
ity is that they are urged to register their marriage certificates at the Japanese
Consulate, thus regaining their nationality from the Japanese government. Another
way is the general practice of the parents of the Japanese ancestry registering their
names at the Consulate when they beoome of military age, without their son's knowl-
edge. It is said "the parents are forced to do it, for otherwise their relatives
residing in Japan would be punished, fined or otherwise made to suffor." Approx-
imately two-thirds of the Amerioan citizens of Japanese anoestry in Hawaii retain the
status of dual citizenship.

Hawaii Sentinel, the fearless American Weekly, reported; (Less than two months

Japanese in Hawaii, including American citizens of Japanese ancestry "signed pledges
of loyalty to Japan in their own blood."

CONCLUSION
A few years ago the vice-minister Yasujiro Tsutsumi, of Japan's Overseas Af-
irs, urged upon Japanese abroad to build up their own civilization and industrial
development, rather than become assimilated in the looal population. He stated that
"where Japanese had maintained their identity, the result had been beneficial to
Japan."
General Araki said. "The urgent need of the Japanese nation is to realize justly
and effectively the power of the spirit of the Japanese." He further deolared. "The
spirit of Japan must be spread over the seven seas and the five continents. Every-
thing that opposes its expansion is to be overwhelmed if necessary by force. The
countries of eastern Asia have been oppressed by the white people. Japan will not
tolerate this any longer. It is the duty of the Japanese people to oppose any action
of the Powers that run counter to Japanese rule."
Judging from these official attitudes and the subsequent events since l9l0, it
is apparent that America will soon face a momentous period of her history. The ideals,
political philosophies, and economic standards of the two great nations are bound to
test their supremacy. Our national security and the security of these islands will
be wholly contingent upon Japan's military policy in the Pacifio. Japanization ac-
tivities should not be considered as mere aoademic interest; we should follow as
closely as possible the course of events and development of public opinion in Japan
and America.
Americans may recall the Wood-Forbes mission in 192l to the Philippine Islands.
General Wood is said to have had a frank talk with Baron Tanaka (author of Tanaka's
memorial). He told the Japanese militarists "that if she continued to fortify the
Bonins. the Loochoos and the Pesscaadores to the point where at any time it would in-
terfere with or stop American commerce with mainland (China), the U. S. would go to
war". Baron Tanaka answered just as frankly and emphatically, "that if anyone inter-
fered with them in Manchuria, Japan would fight. Japan will not arbitrate on Man-
churia and will fight before she surrenders her hard won rights in the territory she
holds as vital to her security as the U. S. does the Panama Canal."
Since the exohange of this frank declaration, Japan not only fortified the Bonin
and Loochoos, but it is said that she is improving harbors and building large air-
plane landing fields in the Pelews, Carolines and the Marshalls. In the name of
Manchukuo she is building a puppet navy and forcing military training on Manchukuan
and the Koreans. The most recent threat is the "Hands off China" policy which is as
much as to say, America you keep off from China; this declaration is a direct threat
and an act of interference to American commerce. Will America go to war with Japan
as declared by General Wood? Thus far America has not taken any effective action,
but if Japan insists to aggravate and demand the equality of naval ratio, elimination
of American commercial and economic interests in China; secretly construct fortifica-
tions in the Pacific Mandates and continue the Japanization of Hawaii. America will
have no alternative.
In the face of all these perplexing contingencies, the strategical value of
Hawaii cannot be too highly stressed. Hawaii is the Heligoland to U. S. Navy and
Gibraltar to U. S. Army. Therefore, the necessity of Americanization in Hawaii is
doubly significant. Our security will wholly depend upon the satisfactory and ra-
tional settlement of political and military problems between Japan and America. The
Japanization of Hawaii is no longer an issue only for the people of Hawaii but it has
become national and as such it should be dealt with.
Japan's continued aggressive movement into the continent of Asia and particular-
ly Japan's insistence of Japanization of her subjects residing in the North and South
Amerioan countries and Hawaii are the outcome of the intense desire of the Japanese
race to change their racial, social, economic, and political and military status
equal to the status of America and of the white race. This spirit of Japan will
never rest till her national mission is attained.
More than three deoades ago American hearts were oaptivated by the eloquence of
Senator Beveridge. He declared in the Senate -
"Our largest trade henceforth must be with Asia. The Pacific is our ocean.
- - - And the Pacific is the ocean of the commerce of the future.

JAPAN'S NATIONAL MISSION AND HAWAII
National or racial conflicts do not become acute until the nation or race kept
in a weaker position is animated by national tendenoy to change its status and
strive for equality with the nation or race deemed superior. Commodore Matthew C.
Perry kindled this very kind of spark when he forcefully opened the ports of Japan
to the world.
The Japanese race accepted the supremacy of the white race with solemn mental
reservation. She buried her pride and humiliation and austuciously adopted the
spirit of popular educational system from America, military, medical and scientific
training from Germany and the naval strategy and diplomatic tactics from England. In
a good sense, these learnings were fittingly blended into the teachings and culture
of Japan. She took every nutriment in order to develop Japan's racial civilization.
Today Japan is a new dynamic military power which makes itself felt not only in
the revolt all over Asia against the white race but she is making forceful penetra-
tion into the western hemisphere and has captured many of the rich commercial
markets.
The greatest statesman of Japan, Count Okuma, declared: "To brand us Japanese
as inferior because we are a colored race is bigotry -- we must combat and destroy
through the fulfillment of our national mission."
What is then, the national mission of Japan?
It is fairly arguable, basing on historioal facts that Japan's national mission
is world supremacy and racial equality. With this in view she has played a role of
an expert strategist, she has judiciously applied the art of jiugitsu, seizing and
claiming all the strategic points in the continent of Asia and in the Pacific,
directly obstructing America's advance to the rich commercial El-Dorado of the Far
East. She stretched her steady arm up to the nor th and gripped Kurile and half of
Sakhalin, threatening America's future northern air-route. She annexed Korea, the
stepping stone to Asiatic continent, and in 193l, she forcefully seized the three
eastern provinces of Manchuria and the rich opium province of Jehol. Since July 7,
1937 - North and South China. She also possesses the island of Formosa and the
chain of islands north of Formosa to Japan proper. blocking China's front door. She
now holds the key to the western half of the Pacific, by virtue of taking over all
the former German Pacific Islands north of equator, even the island of Yap. This
chain of islands for thousands of miles stretches from Bonin to the Marshalls, two
thousand miles nearer to the Hawaiin Islands. Strategically these islands are nat-
ural air bases for her large air forces, coaling station for her navy and the step-
ping stone for her army to march toward the white man's country. Unquesti onably the
proximity of these islands makes the American possessions vulnerable!
Japan will never rest until the fulfillment of her dream is ended. To her,
time is no question. Like the 47 ronin who awaited years for an opportunity to
avenge the dishonor of their master, she will do likewise. For 26 years she prepar-
ed for the eventful march from Mukden to Shanghai. It will be a matter of time that
she will attempt to sail from Bonin via Marshalls to Hawaii, then to California, or
from Kurile via Unalaska to the Pacific Coast.
The Japanese fishing interests are scanning the Marshalls and the Carolines with
hundreds of fishing sampans. In July of 1934, Japan moved her northern fishing base
800 miles nearer to Alaska. The fishing industry employs about 18, O00 men. With
twenty tenders and more than 400 vessels. Hawaii's large fleet of 400 or more sam-
pans and about 15,O00 reservists will be another vital factor. These unique and
strategic positions will be an added advantage to Japan's navy. Not long ago in a
meeting at the Buddhist temple, an American Shintoist, Dr. Mason, remarked, "I have
been told that in the event of war between Japan and the United States you have
enough food supply to last only for six weeks." When he was asked from whom he re-
ceived the information, he answered, "The Japanese leaders told me." For all prac-
tical purposes the Japanese are fervently pushing Japanization in Hawaii.
Japan is the only world power possessing a first class army as well as navy,
this factor combined with the compactness of super-strategic position, a naval at-
tack on Hawaii would be reasonably successful. No one can deny that the Pacific
situation is fraught with dangerous possibilities. The indecisive policy of the
United States may enoourage the Japanese militarists to take sudden action Tn

JAPAN's PREVIOUS ATTEMPT
Hawaii was annexed to the U. S. while Japan was too busy recovering between
wars with China and Russia. To this day the Japanese regret that Japan did not an-
nex these islands prior to her major wars. However, this does not mean that she did
not make any attempt.
In 1894, during the sitting of Constitutional Convention of Hawaii, Japan made
a diplomatio demand that Japanese be given rights to vote. To avoid granting fran-
ohise, the Republic of Hawaii was forced to framo its constitution in such a manner
as to stop all naturalization for the time being, making this matter subject to
further treaty negotiation.
In 1895, the far-sighted Japanese government made strong formal protest against
allowing large number of Chinese to enter Hawaii. Japan's representative stated
that the coming of Chinese to Hawaii was "detrimental to the Japanese interest". It
is said similar protest was made to tho Korean government by Prince Ito, ending
further immigration of Koreans to Hawaii.
In 1897, after the unsuccessful attempt to intimidate the Hawaiian government,
the Japanese government seized an opportunity to protest an alleged ill-treatment
and discriminative act toward the Japanese immigrants. She made a formal demand for
an indemnity. Soon after the ultimatum was forwarded to the Hawaiian government,
Japan sent her cruiser, S. Naniwa, undor the command of Captain Kuroda. On his
arrival Minister Shimamura of Japan immediately asked for a permit to have Captain
Kuroda and his orew to exercise in target practice with the tube guns and rifles ad-
jacent outside of the harbor of Honolulu for 20 days, under the very nose of the
Hawaiian capitol. This dramatio incident hastened the move of annexation of Hawaii
to the United States and temporarily halted Japan's advancement.
"DUCK DIPLOMACY"
Japan's continental policy has been termed the "duck diplomaoy" by the Chinese,
because it typifies a duck, which appears calm and serene above water, while it
paddles busily beneath, making steady progress. Likewise, Japan's diplomacy in
Hawaii can be termed as such. Outwardly, the Japanese seem very peaceful and loyal
to America. Yet behind the scene one may find their programs filled with question-
able activities.
There are two distinot factors which aid the promotion of Japanization in Hawa-
ii. Thoy aro -- first, the heredity of national traits of the Japanese race. Second.
the Japanized environment. created by the Japanese leaders. These two factors have
been so oleverly harmonized and blended into such a degree that the result of collab-
oration is astonishing. It should be borne in mind that the success of Japanization
is largely due, if not entirely, to the correlationship of these two faotors.

underlying its peaceful surface, the problem of racial equality and its contemporary
issues constantly bob up to disturb the community. Enter the business world in
Hawaii and one will find that race preiudice still controls its human emotions. Very

HIS IMPERIAL HIGHNESS, PRINCE FUSHIMI'S FUND
Among the many Japanese institutions and agencies, perhaps the Prince Fushimi
Scholarship Association of Hawaii can be considered a representative one, directly
sponsoring an effective action in promoting leadership for the fulfillment of Japan's
mission. The material aid received from a Prince of Japan, in the form of prizes
and scholarship by the American citizens of Japanese ancestry, has created the de-
sired results.
In the year of 1907, after the sucoessful consummation of Anglo-Japanese Alli-
ance, His Imperial Highness, Prince Fushimi of Japan, visited Hawaii on his homeward
voyage as the guest of the British government. Fifteen leading Japanese with Consul-
General Saito, met tho Prince and his military aides at the home of Mr. Araki, the
manager of the Yokohama Specie Bank. It is said that General Nishi and Admiral
Yamamoto insisted on an aggressive, typical Japanese program, but the two militarists
were prevailed to compromise to a milder, but an effective program. Prince Fushimi
gave a modest amount of $2o0.00 with the promise of more and the local leaders were
asked to inorease the fund according to the needs from time to time. Prizes and
other recognitions were givon to the outstanding young Japaneso student leaders for
meritorious efforts and in excellonce of school work. Since 19l9 soholarships woro
awarded, sending outstanding Japanese student leaders to various universities. The
reoipients of this fund now hold the key positions in the City, County and
Territorial governments.
JAPANESE CHRISTIANS
Mr. Yusuki Tsurumi, one of the well-known parliamentarian and Christian leaders,
said, "I doubt very much whether Christianity, as developed in America and Europe,
will be accepted as such by a large number of Japanese ....... Japanese will not
accept a foreign thought without impressing upon it their owm stamp."
The foregoing statement by an eminent Japanese Christian leader confirms our
belief that the Japanese Christians in Hawaii cannot be truly Americanized through
Christianity alone. Unfortunately. the American missionaries and many leading fin-
anciers are of the belief that this seems to be the best means to Americanize the
Amerioan citizens of Japanese ancestry. Looking over the statistics of the various
Japanese religious sects in Hawaii, one will find the sorrowful fact that, in spite
of large expenditures donated by Amorican missionaries, Christianity has been
embraced by the Japanese leaders for a purpose -- a Japanese Front. The following
